#9144. Matteo Thun designs Torre Velasca interiors using "building itself as the starting point"

Photography by Alberto Strada (unless stated otherwise)

Italian architect Matteo Thun looked to the original materials and colours of Milan’s iconic Torre Velasca when creating its new interiors, which feature pink hues inspired by the tower’s dusky facade.

Thun has designed 72 flats in the upper floors of the tower, ranging from suites to duplex penthouses. He approached the interior design of the skyscraper, built in the 1950s by the architecture studio BBPR, with a focus on reinterpretation.

“We allowed the masters and the building itself to speak, imagining a way of living within it that would carry the building a little further into the future, adding a new chapter to its history,” Thun told Dezeen.

“We did not seek contrast: our design was informed directly by the materials and colours of Torre Velasca, and we chose not to intervene where we felt the architecture had already achieved a sense of completeness.”

His studio preserved original details, including doors, window frames, loggias and tiles in the bathrooms and kitchens. These were then juxtaposed with modern furniture and evergreen design classics.

“The interiors bring together new furniture designed by the studio and design references spanning the 1950s to the 1980s, including iconic pieces developed in new colourways in collaboration with historic Milanese companies,” Thun said.

“With a deep appreciation for craftsmanship and a strong attention to detail, these designs share an ability to evolve without losing their identity.”

The colour palette, too, was inspired by the original hues of the Torre Velasca.

In the living rooms, walls are covered in custom-made velvet wall coverings by textile company Dedar in a pale pink colour that resembles the pink plaster on Torre Velasca’s facade.

“The building itself was our starting point,” Thun said.

“The pink plaster, developed and patented specifically for the tower, together with the blue and green floor tiles found both inside and in the loggias, formed the basis of our colour palette,” he continued.

“We developed different gradations of these tones, opting for darker shades of green and blue to define the entrance areas and bedrooms. “

As well as the apartments, Thun also designed the interior of the reception, lobby and the corridors on the ground floor.

And while this was an interior project, Thun says it ended up becoming “a lesson in architecture” for his studio.

“Working with a building as distinctive as Torre Velasca challenged us to think and work first and foremost as architects,” Thun said.

“The challenge was not to reinvent the building, but to find ways to make its original character feel relevant today, while remaining true to BBPR’s vision,” he continued.

“In this sense, the project became a process of discovery, with the building itself serving as our greatest teacher. It was, in many ways, a lesson in architecture for us.”

Thun has previously designed the interior of the boutique hotel The Julius Prague and “hotel-like” rooms for a German hospital.

Photography by Alberto Strada (unless stated otherwise)

#9143. 39 Award-Winning Photos From the 1839 Awards Photographers of the Year Contest

39 Award-Winning Photos From the 1839 Awards Photographers of the Year Contest

The 1839 Awards has announced the winners of its annual Photographer of the Year contest, celebrating exceptional, creative photography across multiple categories. Photographers from nearly 80 different countries entered the 2026 edition.

Giacomo Marchione was named the International Photographer of the Year 2026 for his series, The Invisible. Marchione’s five striking photos show underwater sea creatures, illuminated by light against a stark black background.

“At night, the sea doesn’t sleep,” Marchione says. “When the sun sets and the sea seems to fall silent, one of nature’s most extraordinary spectacles begins: the vertical migration of plankton. Millions of organisms rise from the depths to the surface in this upward migration.”

Marchione is a celebrated Italian underwater photographer as well as a practicing orthopedic surgeon. Marchione’s passion for underwater photography began in 1992 when he obtained his first scuba diving certification on vacation. He has photographed underwater all over the globe, including in the Maldives, Indonesia, Malaysia, and, of course, off the coast of Italy.

Marchione is not only the overall contest winner, but he also won the Underwater category.

On the Non-Professional side of the competition, photographer Dammy Twitch took top honors for his series, What If We Lived Among Gods. It’s a medium-format 120 film analog series exploring “myth, divinity, and everyday Nigerian life.”

Apampa Oluwadamilola, known professionally as Dammy Twitch, was born in 1995 and raised in Oyo State, Nigeria. Twitch relocated to Lagos and built his fine art photography, film, and music career. He was named to the Forbes 30 Under 30 list in 2022 and has received numerous accolades since, including the Rolling Stone Africa Mwamkom Vanguard Award for Visual Storytelling this year.

Twitch’s directorial debut, Call of My Life, has become one of the top five highest-grossing films ever in West Africa.

In total, there are many category winners across both Professional and Non-Professional sections. They can all be viewed on the 1839 Awards website. PetaPixel has selected a smattering of award-winning photos to share below, but everyone is highly encouraged to go view them all, organized by category, on the 1839 Awards website.

#9142. Peruvian senator calls for removal of large-scale replicas of Moche erotic sculptures from public park

One of the huaco erótico sculptures in Fertility Park, near Trujillo, Peru Photo: Richard Avila, via Wikimedia Commons

A controversy over 3m-tall erotic sculptures in northern Peru reignited recently after a senator requested that the cultural ministry remove them from a public area. Located in a park outside the city of Trujillo, the sculptures are replicas of ceramics from the pre-Incan Moche civilisation.

“What happens when children see these images? Neurological and psychological factors are affected, because they see body dimensions that are completely different from how they see themselves,” Milagros Jáuregui, a conservative senator from the Renovación Popular party, said in a speech on 26 October.

The sculptures are located in Parque de la Fertilidad (Fertility Park), a public space where in 2021 then-mayor Arturo Fernández of the Moche district began installing giant fibreglass reproductions of ceramic depictions of sexual acts to promote tourism.

Known as huacos eróticos, the much smaller original ceramics date from the 3rd to 8th century AD. No more than 30cm in height, they were placed in tombs as burial offerings. But the debate about their much larger versions in the park goes beyond political prudishness.

“It’s a complicated issue,” the Peruvian archaeologist Walter Alva tells The Art Newspaper. “There’s freedom to express or re-create themes from the past, but these ceramics were created to be placed as offerings to the dead, with a sense of revitalising life. They are associated with both fertility and an entire system of beliefs.”

An original huaco erótico ceramic offering made by the Moche civilisation, Larco Museum, Lima Photo: László Varga, via Wikimedia Commons

The Moche civilisation covered 700km of the coast of what is now Peru, between the regions of Piura and Ancash, centuries before the Inca dominated the area. “Moche art is primarily ceramic, and these vessels depict erotic scenes or concepts of sexuality from that era,” Alva says. “The sculptures in the park were created outside of their historical context.”

One of the greatest archaeological discoveries from the Moche civilisation was that of the Lord of Sipán near the city of Chiclayo—a discovery Alva made in 1987. A 3rd-century monarch, the Lord of Sipán’s body was found covered with gold along with eight other people, a dog and two llamas and nearly 500 objects including ceramic vessels, ornaments and textiles.

The Moche have the largest number of erotic representations among pre-Hispanic civilisations. The most complete collection of its ceramics is in Lima, at the Larco Museum of pre-Columbian art, which celebrated its centennial in July. Before the 1960s, children were forbidden from entering the room that housed the huacos. Today, minors must be accompanied by an adult. The institution’s Erotic Gallery is one of its most popular attractions.

Jáuregui, an evangelical pastor as well as a senator, believes these Moche sculptures should only be in closed spaces. “Displaying these types of images in public is harmful to children,” she told congress. “We should have them in museums, where high-school students can observe a part of our culture that is a national treasure with the help of teachers or some kind of tutor.”

The well-preserved statue is one of the oldest artefacts discovered in the Chan Chan archaeological site

Excavations at the Cerro Mayal site in the north of the country show it was an important production facility for Moche ceramics around the seventh century

This major London show, marking the 200th anniversary of the country's independence, does not flinch from the bloodiest aspects of Inca culture

The so-called “Hall of the Moche Imaginary” is one of two elaborately decorated spaces archaeologists recently uncovered at Pañamarca

#9141. Five examples of Mesoamerican modern architecture

Mexican architects have been combining principles from ancient architecture with modern techniques. Curator and writer Su Wu picks five examples of this phenomenon from her Mesoamerican Modern book.

Wu’s book, Mesoamerican Modern: Ancient Ideas in Contemporary Mexican Homes, details projects that illustrate this trend, from the 1970s to today, with a focus on residential architecture.

“These homes reflect the complex aesthetic cultures of Mesoamerica,” Wu told Dezeen. She chose the phrase that titles the book over “pre-Columbian” because she wanted to demonstrate that the monumentalism and logic of pre-Columbian Mexican architecture did not end with colonisation.

“I think these homes show instead that rather than being relegated to the past, these Mesoamerican materials, techniques, typologies, and forms are alive in the present and also perhaps inspiration or guides for the future.”

Each shows aspects of monumentalism that recall the stone architecture of the wider Mesoamerican culture, while acknowledging the diversity.

The book tries to depart from projects that just use symbols and focus on the logic of the buildings, noting specific characteristics such as patios as intrinsic the the design.

“For me, the most defining characteristics of Mesoamerican architecture are the ones that reflect underlying principles, rather than the disjunction when symbols become separated from their meaning,” Wu said.

“So throughout the book I wanted to highlight forms that arise from ideas such as the use of light or shadow as a physical object, or how homes are aligned to natural features, or the everyday presence of craft and the handmade, with an expanded sense of beauty as an attenuating consequence.”

Read on for five examples of the Mesoamerican modern style in Mexico with commentary by Wu.

“This 1973 home is one of a few 20th-century homes in Mesoamerican Modern, built by architect Agustín Hernández for his sister Amalia, the founder of Mexico City’s Ballet Folklorico.

“A poet as well as an architect, Hernández is celebrated for injecting ‘Mesoamerican semantics into the brute vocabulary of modernism’, but  wrote most of all about the geometric and cosmic principles at the heart of Mesoamerican architecture, and the ‘mathematical, almost symphonic rhythm’ of Mesoamerican structures and cities.

“His sister Amalia’s home was inspired by the convex forms of seashells as well as by the prominent ocular motifs in Mesoamerican imagery. “

Casa Mobius by Ernesto Gómez Gallardo, 1974

“Built by the architect for his own family in 1974, this house in Mexico City’s San Jeronimo neighborhood is today the studio and home of ceramicist Perla Valtierra.

“Shaped loosely like a mobius strip, with a triangular lattice allowing spaces to fold in upon themselves and a cantilevered living room, the home reconsiders both volumes and typologies, in rooms that are anything but square.

“The house is furnished with an eclectic mix of iconic Japanese, Brasilian and Mexican furniture, including a chair originally designed for the Museo Experimental El Eco in Mexico City by its founder Matthias Goeritz, a close friend and frequent collaborator of Luis Barragan.”

“Architect Teodoro González de León once described the patio as a defining characteristic of a Mesoamerican home, a space that is at once enclosed and exterior, and open to the elements.

“In this house in Estado de Mexico, Mexico City-based architect Fernanda Canales reclaimed land that had been devastated by cattle overgrazing, creating an interlocking series of patios that, in their deliberately undefined sense of function, create more space without having to build more of it.

“Each room in the home, which is approached through a pyramidal foyer with an opening to the sky, looks out onto courtyards or landscape, replete again with plants of the Americas.”

Casa Cometa by Taller Mauricio Rocha + Gabriela Carrillo, 2019

“In this home inspired by the spatial organization of ceremonial Mesoamerican sites, communal areas extend horizontally, while private spaces descend and rise vertically, like a dramatic bedroom tower with a daily view of both the sunrise and the sunset over the Pacific.

“With its overlapping platforms and passageways, the space designed by Gabriela Carrillo and Mauricio Rocha reflects the multiple planes of existence in Mesoamerican cosmology.

“In this house, a walkway weaves under the swimming pool, which itself slips under a long orthogonal platform, cut through with a descending staircase.”

“Casa Monte is a one-bedroom house with no exterior doors. Instead, the house deliberately discourages approach by appearing like a fortress over the tree line, and by its placement on a stepped platform, which creates a sense of separation from the jungle floor below.

“The open space with a pool cutting across the interior suggests the idea that architecture exists foremost as a way to engage with nature.

“Cast by Matos himself in earth-tinted cement on the beach where the house now sits, the home’s hundreds of individual forms were fitted together on-site.”

#9140. New Sensor Tech Could Replace Bayer Color Filter and Transform Mobile Photography

New Sensor Tech Could Replace Bayer Color Filter and Transform Mobile Photography

Metalenz has acquired Israeli startup PxE Imaging. PxE’s claim to fame is its Holocoder technology, a replacement for the Bayer color filter found on traditional image sensors.

As Metalenz explains in its press release, the Holocoder “eliminates the need for the Bayer filter and sorts light without absorption, increasing the light delivered to a standard image sensor by 2.5x.”

As expected, significantly increasing the light delivered to an image sensor will, all else equal, dramatically improve camera performance and image quality across the board—in dark scenes and bright ones alike.

Like PxE Imaging, Metalenz has been focused on technologies that adhere directly to an image sensor. A few years ago, Metalenz brought its groundbreaking metasurface optics to market, which are ultra-thin optics that can be printed like semiconductor wafers. The key is how the thin lens bends light.

That’s true, too, of Holocoder technology. The Holocoder “harnesses the wave nature of light to physically decode information such as wavelength and depth, enabling simultaneous capture of color and depth information in the same image with a single camera.”

A Bayer filter, which is how traditional digital image sensors capture and reconstruct color, also absorbs about 60% of the light coming into a sensor, Metalenz says. With its acquisition of PxE, Metalenz can now add sophisticated color and depth information to the material and surface data its products already capture, all without significantly increasing manufacturing complexity or computational demands.

“Metalenz has strategically expanded its IP from unique hardware to full-stack solutions co-designed with our metasurfaces,” says Rob Devlin, Co-founder and CEO of Metalenz.

“We’ve deployed into the most demanding customer devices, built a supply chain at mass-market scale, and built a software stack that takes information delivered to a sensor all the way through AI decisions. With PxE’s technology and team, we’re expanding our capabilities into visible sensing, addressing a longstanding problem of low light performance while solving the new physical AI problem of obtaining richer information beyond conventional RGB imagery,” Devlin continues.

“Owning hardware that brings new information to sensors is the real moat for differentiated AI models. Our combined capability with PxE extends that same principle across all of machine vision, so people and machines can see and understand more about the world without relying on heavy computation.”

“We developed the Holocoder to capture information in light that conventional sensors discard or cannot see, giving cameras greater light sensitivity and the ability to capture color and depth together,” adds Yoav Berlatzky, Co-founder and CEO of PxE Imaging.

“Joining Metalenz gives us the manufacturing platform and commercial reach to bring this technology to everyday devices. Together, we can give people better images and machines a richer understanding of the world.”

The terms of the transaction have not been disclosed.

Devlin spoke to WIRED about the acquisition, shedding more light, pun intended, on PxE Imaging’s technology.

“Apple, Samsung, Google — everyone is fighting to improve the visible camera every year, right?” Devlin tells WIRED.

“A lot of what they’re doing is investing hundreds of millions of dollars into software to try to somehow improve it, but the downside of that is that once information is lost when you’re absorbing all of that light, you can’t really buy it back, even if you’re throwing all of the software into the world at it.”

As of right now, Metalenz cannot directly combine PxE’s Holocoder technology with its commercial Metalenz optics. However, it is absolutely in the cards for the long term. PxE’s technology itself could hit the market as soon as the end of next year, thanks to Metalenz’s manufacturing capacity.

The potential use cases here are manifold. In scenarios where tiny cameras are very important, like autonomous vehicles for example, it’s obvious that a smaller camera that can absorb more light is beneficial.

Another obvious situation is smartphone cameras. As Devlin notes, there is a physical problem that image sensors of all sizes must try to overcome: getting more, better light data. The more light that reaches the sensor, the better. The Bayer color filter is an incredible technological achievement, but it’s getting very long in the tooth. Perhaps, if PxE is correct, there’s a better way.

Image creditsMetalenz, PxE Imaging. Header photo licensed via Depositphotos.com.

#9138. This Retro-Inspired Waist-Level Digital Camera Already Raised $270K on Kickstarter

This Retro-Inspired Waist-Level Digital Camera Already Raised $270K on Kickstarter

A new retro-inspired digital camera with a waist-level viewfinder has quickly raised nearly $270,000 on Kickstarter, absolutely shattering its meager $4,996 funding target.

The Campix, as Kosmo Foto writes, is made by Hong Kong-based photo brand Fotorgear. As Kosmo Foto notes, the Campix is “heavily influenced by the East German Exakta Varex camera,” including its waist-level prism. For its part, Fotorgear says the Campix is “inspired by the timeless design of classic waist-level film cameras.”

The company adds that its new camera combines a retro waist-level viewfinder and an analog-like experience with the convenience of digital. To that end, the Campix embraces tactile manual controls, film-inspired digital simulations, and a virtual “film” roll experience.

The Campix is far from the first camera to offer a “roll” style shooting experience, with perhaps the most famous example being the Fujifilm X half. The idea is that users select their preferred “film” look and then shoot through an entire 36-shot “roll” of digital images using that style. Photographers can also customize these looks in an accompanying app and save them to one of six filter slots, which can be cycled through on the camera using a physical dial.

Notably, the Campix does two things very differently from other film-inspired digital cameras—beyond its signature waist-level viewfinder. First, the camera features interchangeable lenses thanks to its proprietary T-mount design. Second, the Campix captures RAW files, a feature missing from many style-focused, film-emulation digital cameras.

As for its optics, users can swap between an 8mm fisheye, 16mm wide-angle, 60mm portrait, 75mm macro, and a 1.55x anamorphic lens. Fotorgear also sells these same lenses for use with smartphones. The stock lens is a 26mm-equivalent f/2.2 prime.

The Campix includes a Xenon flash with TTL support; Fotorgear states the flash has an effective range of about one to three meters.

Internally, the camera is built around a 13-megapixel Sony IMX258 image sensor. This Type 1/3.06 sensor is similar in size to the ultra-wide and telephoto sensors found in many smartphones, carrying a crop factor of roughly 7.4x. The camera offers Auto ISO (100–3,200) alongside automatic exposure, while white balance can be set to automatic or manual.

As mentioned, the Campix pairs with a mobile companion app available for iOS and Android, as well as a dedicated desktop app for RAW processing.

The Campix Basic starts at $109 for early-bird backers and will retail for $209, bundled with the 26mm lens. The Campix Set—priced at $199 for super-early birds and $319 at retail—includes the camera body, the standard 26mm lens, plus the 75mm Macro, 60mm Portrait, and 16mm Wide-Angle lenses. It also comes with a Star Filter, CPL, and UV filter set. The lenses can also be purchased individually.

#9137. Photogenic ‘One-in-a-Million’ Fish With Xanthochromism Caught in New York

Photogenic ‘One-in-a-Million’ Fish With Xanthochromism Caught in New York

U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) biologists caught a one-in-a-million fish in Oswego, New York, and it sure is a looker.

Biologists performing a routine Aquatic Invasive Species Survey in Oswego Harbor, New York, caught a burbot (Lota lota) with xanthochromism, a “rare biological condition” that turns the fish bright yellow-orange. Burbot are typically brown with dark spots, making this almost entirely yellow-orange specimen a remarkable find.

Xanthochromism is a rare genetic mutation that suppresses normal dark pigmentation, producing a distinct yellow-orange appearance. Scientists note that xanthochromism is “considerably less common” in wild fish populations than albinism or melanism.

In 2024, an orange shark made headlines and scientists later determined that it had an even rarer combination of albinism and xanthochromism. Its unusual eyes the result of the former and the neon-orange skin the latter.

Because burbot are a native species, they are not the primary target of the Aquatic Invasive Species Early Detection and Monitoring Program. As the USFWS explains, this program deploys advanced technology and targeted surveillance strategies to locate “watchlist species” across New York’s Great Lakes, rivers, and harbors.

Most fish caught during these surveys are native species, which biologists inspect and safely release. Burbot—even typical specimens—are notable catches due to their low populations in the Great Lakes. Finding a burbot with xanthochromism is exceptionally rare.

According to United States Geological Survey (USGS) biologists on the team, this particular individual appeared emaciated and in poor health. Consequently, scientists transported it to the Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine for detailed analysis.

“The discovery could turn out to be lucky for the species too; this exceptionally rare fish may provide valuable insight into the health of the species’ populations throughout the basin that can inform management actions,” USFWS says.

While scientists documented this recent discovery, wildlife photographers have also captured extraordinarily rare animals over the years. In 2024, wildlife photographer Yves Adams photographed an ultra-rare all-black penguin.

It was not Adams’ first time photographing extremely rare birds. A few years prior, he photographed what he believes was a “never-before-seen” yellow penguin — not unlike the burbot recently found in New York.

#9136. Plan Ahead: Seven Places to Point Your Camera in 2028

Plan Ahead: Seven Places to Point Your Camera in 2028

What makes a great photography adventure? People travel with their cameras for different reasons. For some, travel itself is the main attraction, with photography opening the door to longer, richer experiences. For others, it is the chance to develop new skills by photographing new landscapes, wildlife, or cultures around the world.

Full disclosureThis article was brought to you by Muench Workshops.

Both motivations run through seven destinations selected from Muench Workshops’ newly launched 2028 calendar. Each presents a different photographic challenge, from finding abstraction in familiar landscapes in the United States to learning about wildlife storytelling while on safari in Africa.

In winter, Yellowstone sheds much of the activity and visual clutter of its summer season, revealing a quieter, more graphic landscape. Deep snow reduces forests and valleys to clean layers of white and pale blue, while thick blankets of steam drift quietly through the valleys.

Nearby, heavily snowed-in forests naturally simplify a busy landscape into striking shapes and negative space, and ice crystals and geothermal textures reward close, macro-style work. Even wildlife can become part of the abstraction, whether through motion or the contrast of dark forms against luminous snow.

“Yellowstone in winter feels like the park has rebooted into its original operating system,” says photographer and Muench Workshops leader Matt Payne. “Fewer people, more steam, sharper light, and wildlife that does not care about your comfort level.”

Pro tip: when you get close to frost or ice crystals, depth of field shrinks to just a few millimeters, even at f/16 or f/22. Positioning the camera’s sensor plane parallel to the detail you want sharp can help maximize depth of field. For subjects with greater depth, consider focus stacking rather than relying on an extremely narrow aperture.

On Hokkaido, Japan’s northernmost main island, rolling farmland disappears beneath deep snow, leaving lone trees, distant farm buildings, and narrow roads as isolated subjects across a broad white canvas.

Farther south in the mountains of Tohoku, the photographic challenge changes. Open horizons give way to dense forest, where finding order among overlapping trees becomes an exercise in composition. On Mount Zao, heavy snow and powerful winds encase the trees in ice, forming the eerie shapes known as “snow monsters.”

Photographer David Thompson sums up Japan in winter as “two extremes of winter landscape photography: the very clean, minimalist landscapes of Hokkaido and then those graphic, chaotic snow monsters.”

Simplifying a scene and organizing a busy one are opposite skills, and it’s worth being able to do both.

Pro tip: Bright snow can trick your camera’s meter into rendering white as gray. If you’re using an automatic exposure mode, try +1 to +2 stops of exposure compensation as a starting point, adjusting for the conditions. Check your histogram and highlight warnings to ensure the snow looks bright without losing important texture and detail. Shooting RAW provides additional flexibility when fine-tuning exposure afterward.

The Drakensberg is a titan among Africa’s great mountain ranges and one of South Africa’s most dramatic landscapes. The photographic conditions here can shift quickly, which is part of what makes the location so powerful.

A clear morning can vanish in seconds and clouds can mass throughout the day, culminating in dramatic afternoon thunderstorms. On other dawns, the world flips entirely: a cloud inversion traps a sea of mist within the valleys, leaving only the highest peaks to pierce the first light of day.

Photographer Marc Muench, who will co-lead the workshop, describes the appeal of the region, “This is a place where the atmospheric conditions make it pretty otherworldly. I can’t wait to photograph somewhere with such rapidly changing weather patterns and see shafts of light shooting down into these spectacular spires.”

The photographic challenge is scale: finding structure in vast, complex scenes and using clouds, mist, and ridgelines to create a sense of depth. The high summit plateau is difficult to access, so Muench Workshops uses a chartered helicopter to reach a pre-established camp, allowing photographers to return to the same compositions over several mornings and evenings, observing how changing weather and light transform the landscape.

Pro tip: When sunlight breaks through a downpour, a rainbow can materialize directly opposite the sun, forming an arc centred on the shadow of your own head. Position the sun behind you and watch the storm with a wide lens. Because rainbows are most visible when the sun is low, they are often a spectacle of early mornings and late afternoons.

In Bhutan’s high valleys, prayer flags drift across mountain passes and monks in crimson robes move between cliffside monasteries. In spring, rhododendrons bring color to the mountain slopes, while jacaranda trees bloom in the warmer valleys around Punakha.

Photographing cultural traditions requires a different approach to storytelling, particularly during celebrations such as the Ura Yakchoe Festival.

Through sacred masked dances, ceremonies, and community gatherings in the mountains of central Bhutan, the festival offers opportunities to document both the rituals and the quieter moments surrounding them.

“Bhutan was almost a blank canvas for me,” recalls photographer and workshop leader Joseph Roybal. “I was surprised by how the landscape, people, and culture came together and drew me into photographs I never expected to make. Our guides and their Buddhist outlook also taught me to let go when a photograph doesn’t happen as envisioned, trust that things unfold as they’re meant to, and simply be present behind the camera, a lesson that has changed how I approach photography.”

Pro tip: ask permission before you photograph a person, especially a monk or an elder; a smile and a nod toward your camera often make your request clear. Photography restrictions vary between temples and monasteries, so it’s important to check the rules at each location, particularly before photographing religious ceremonies or entering sacred spaces.

In Katmai National Park, on the Alaska Peninsula, the brown bears don’t stay in one place. Like any wild animal, they go where the food is, so where you find them changes with the season.

In June, on the coast at Hallo Bay, brown bears spend long stretches grazing on sedges and spring grasses in the coastal meadows before the salmon arrive. It’s also mating season, and a good time to spot spring cubs learning from their mothers.

By August, at Moraine Creek, the salmon have returned from the North Pacific and gather at the creek mouths and the bears follow, patrolling the channels and fishing the streams.

Successful bear photography begins with understanding behavior: recognizing how animals feed, interact, and move, and learning to anticipate the moments that make compelling images. The workshop’s camp is situated beside small lakes near important salmon spawning streams, allowing photographers to spend extended periods observing the bears and their behavior.

Pro tip: decide what you want before the action starts, because bears move faster than you can change settings. To freeze a leaping salmon, use a shutter speed of 1/1000 second or faster. If you would rather show motion, such as a bear shaking water from its head, set a much slower shutter speed in advance.

A compelling wildlife photograph doesn’t always need to be a tight portrait of a lion or leopard. Looking beyond the obvious subjects to include behavior, habitat, and smaller interactions can turn an individual photograph into part of a much broader story. In Zambia’s Lower Zambezi, the variety of habitats provides opportunities to place wildlife encounters within a much broader environmental story.

The river breaks into channels, lagoons, islands, and sandbars, and just to the north the valley opens into plains and mature winterthorn forest. You may spend a morning following a leopard, find wild dogs moving across the plains, or watch lion cubs playing in the dust.

Beside those moments are the frames that make a sighting a story: an alert impala under trees, oxpeckers moving across a buffalo’s hide, or animal tracks crossing the sand.

For wildlife photographer and workshop leader Richard Bernabe, understanding animal behavior is fundamental to anticipating the moments that make compelling photographs.

“Once you’ve got the first portraits out of your system, start looking for gesture and body language. It can be incredibly subtle: a yawn, a raised paw, a stretch. A lion that has been lying down may yawn several times before getting up. You begin to recognize those signals and get yourself ready for what might happen.”

Pro tip: think like a photo editor. A common way to build a story is to gather an establishing wide shot, a medium shot, a portrait, a close detail, and some action. The detail is the one photographers most often forget, and in a place like this it might be the animal tracks or a beetle working its way through some dung. After a morning, look at what you have and ask which of those you’re missing.

Indonesia offers two dramatically different environments for wildlife photography: the open, sunlit islands of Komodo, home to the world’s largest living lizard, and the dense lowland rainforests of Borneo, where orangutans move through the canopy.

Boats provide access to both environments, but photographing their wildlife presents very different challenges, from working at ground level with Komodo dragons to finding clear compositions among Borneo’s dense rainforest foliage. In Komodo National Park, a private traditional sailing vessel means you can reach the islands early in the morning, when the dragons are most active. The main photographic challenges are shooting a dark subject against a bright background and finding the low angles that convey a dragon’s scale.

In Borneo, a dual-level riverboat allows you to shoot at eye level with the rainforest canopy. The challenges here are timing frames for eye contact and interaction, separating the subject from the foliage, managing high ISO cleanly, and holding a long lens steady from a boat.

Pro tip: when you photograph orangutans through the canopy, autofocus will often lock onto the nearest leaves instead of the animal. Use a small autofocus area to target the animal’s eye, and try a wide aperture to soften distracting foreground foliage. When autofocus struggles with dense vegetation, manual focus can offer greater control.

These are just seven of the photographic experiences featured in Muench Workshops’ newly announced 2028 calendar. From wildlife and landscapes to cultural photography, the collection spans all seven continents, with each workshop designed around small groups, experienced photographic leaders, and time in the field.

Explore the full 2028 photography workshop collection.

Muench Workshops offers small-group photography journeys across all seven continents, built around being in the right place at the right time. Led by experienced photographers who share their knowledge in the field, each workshop combines expert guidance, thoughtful planning, and exceptional care, allowing guests to focus on developing their skills, exploring their creativity, and connecting more deeply with the places they visit.

#9135. Annie Leibovitz Photographs Florence Pugh for Jaguar’s New Type 01

Annie Leibovitz Photographs Florence Pugh for Jaguar’s New Type 01

Annie Leibovitz has teamed up with Hollywood star Florence Pugh and British carmaker Jaguar.

Jaguar has undergone a rebrand in recent years, culminating in the launch of the Type 01, a bold electric GT that doesn’t look like classic Jags. The British car firm will start taking orders for the Type 01 in 2027.

Pugh is an English actress, known for films like Oppenheimer, Black Widow, and Little Women. She has signed on to become Jaguar’s first-ever brand ambassador.

Jaguar says that it brought together the three “distinctive creative forces” of Leibovitz, Pugh, and the Type 01 to reflect the “originality, bold and creative spirit driving Jaguar’s reimagined identity.”

“Leibovitz’s compelling portrait series explores individuality, confidence and creative ambition — values that underpin both Type 01 and Jaguar’s transformation,” says Jaguar.

The photos were shot at STORIED in New York, a building that once housed Leibovitz’s studio.

“What interested me most about this portrait series was photographing two extraordinary and contrasting subjects,” Leibovitz says, per Haute Living.

“Florence brings warmth, presence and humanity, while Type 01 is sculpted, precise and striking in its form. Rather than treating the car as a backdrop, I wanted to photograph them both with the same curiosity, exploring their relationship as two distinct characters within the frame.”

“I’ve always been drawn to people and brands that are unapologetically original, which is one of the reasons this partnership with Jaguar feels so natural,” adds Pugh.

“Collaborating with Annie Leibovitz on these images was a remarkable experience. She has an incredible ability to capture character and individuality, and bringing that together with the bold vision of Type 01 made this a truly special creative collaboration.”

The starting price for the Jaguar Type 01 is expected to be $130,000.

Last month, Leibovitz photographed Sam Altman for Vanity Fair, channeling the German Romantic painter Caspar David Friedrich, specifically his famous 1818 work Wanderer Above the Sea of Fog, which features a man staring out over a landscape, high above the clouds. OpenAI CEO Altman was photographed looking out over the Bay Area bluffs.

#9134. Collector Elie Khouri to create physical home for his private foundation in Dubai

A rendering of the Elie Khouri Art Foundation in Dubai

The Dubai-based art collector Elie Khouri is building a space in the city for his eponymous foundation. The Elie Khouri Art Foundation (Ekaf) will be located in the coastal district of Jumeirah 1, in a villa renovated and redesigned by Counterspace, a firm led by the architect Sumayya Vally. The space, expected to open in 2028, will host public exhibitions and educational programmes.

Khouri is one of the Unite Arab Emirates (UAE)’s biggest and best-known collectors. Originally from Lebanon, he made his name as the chief executive officer of Omnicom Media in the Middle East and North Africa, and has been based in Dubai since the 1990s.

He began making plans for the foundation around five years ago, as one of the London-based Deflina Foundation’s collectors-in-residence, a programme launched in 2017 that considers collecting as a practice and seeks to support more ambitious implementation. With them he conducted feasibility studies to better understand what Dubai needs.

“The whole idea is to give back and foster exchange of ideas, challenge thinking and bring new perspectives,” he tells The Art Newspaper. “Dubai is about entrepreneurship. They support people like me, people coming to fulfil their ambitions. And what Dubai needs is private institutions, because that's how they will build their own version of culture.”

Despite Dubai’s large number of artists and galleries, it has never had a major museum, and private foundations have become a significant part of its infrastructure. The Jameel Arts Centre and Alserkal Avenue, each backed by individuals, are the two pillars of the art scene, in addition to smaller foundations such as Ishara, which focuses on art from South Asia.

Ekaf has an emphasis on global contemporary art, though one in which art from the Middle East will play an important role.

“We are here to support talent internationally,” says Khouri. “We're not about the region, but since we are in the Middle East, we also look at the best talent here. We have a responsibility to the ecosystem and the galleries.”

Ekaf will take Khouri’s collection, comprising works by more than 300 artists, as its starting point, drawing from it for initial exhibitions. Later shows will increasingly involve loans and collaborations. Ultimately, Khouri intends to establish an Ekaf collection that is separate to his personal holdings.

The veteran art strategist Caroline Louca, who was formerly at Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism and Christie’s Middle East, has been appointed as the director of the foundation. Louca and Khouri are looking to hire a curatorial team closer to the completion date for the museum.

Louca underlines that community engagement will be a major part of the foundation, with plans for talks, lectures and education streams. The foundation’s location, in Jumeirah 1, is a bonus in this respect. Jumeirah 1 is one of the oldest neighbourhoods in Dubai, where many affluent long-time residents live. Ekaf’s villa was home to an Emirati family in the 1980s, and Vally’s designs retain the elements of old-school Gulf architecture that is a source of nostalgia for many in the UAE.

"We are focusing on how we can make a place become part of the community—and not just focus on what we’re showing,” says Louca. “You can see beautiful artworks everywhere, but we want people to be a bit daring. We want them to walk in and ask questions—and not be embarrassed to ask questions—and then come back and ask more. If we can achieve that, it will be our barometer of success.”

The private institution, funded by Al Futtaim Group, will be built on a jetty

#9133. Customer Tried to Scam LA Pizza Shop With AI Image

Customer Tried to Scam LA Pizza Shop With AI Image

A pizza shop customer used AI to edit a photo of their pizza in a bid to get a refund — but it ultimately failed.

Masa in Echo Park, Los Angeles, is a popular neighborhood pizzeria renowned for its Chicago-style deep-dish pizzas.

KTLA reports that a DoorDash customer by the name of “Dani B” ordered a pizza from Masa but later demanded a full refund after Dani B sent a picture of a severely burnt pizza, claiming it was inedible.

The owner of the restaurant, Rhonda Reynolds, immediately suspected something was wrong. Masa says it takes great care over its quality control, and delivering a blackened pizza would simply never be allowed to happen.

Suspecting the customer had manipulated the image, Reynolds ran it through an app called “Is This AI” in an attempt to verify its authenticity. The program returned a 96 percent certainty that it was AI, citing “unnatural lighting effects on the pizza crust and inconsistent shadow directions within the pizza box.” The image doesn’t appear to contain a SynthID invisible watermark.

To be extra certain, Reynolds reviewed security footage taken inside the pizzeria, which captured the customer’s order being made in the kitchen. The footage showed that at the moment it was taken out of the oven and put into a delivery box, it did not appear to be burned at all.

“It’s the principle because it’s our reputation [being attacked] and it’s what we do here,” Reynolds tells KTLA.

“They went back and checked the footage,” says Jose Tapa, the employee who boxed the order. “The box clearly says the name of the person with the order number and [the pizza] was not what it was in their picture.”

A refund was initially sent to the scammer, but Reynolds successfully fought the claim and the refund was reversed.

Reynolds tells KTLA that this is the first time she’s ever encountered a scam involving AI tools. She worries that as AI tools become more advanced, small businesses like hers could increasingly fall victim to them and the scammers using them.

“We’ve been here 22 years and we’re considered a busy restaurant,” she adds. “It’s a struggle, that if this is a new frontier, we’re not gonna make it through to the other side if all of our time is spent [dealing with this]. So in that respect, it’s scary.”

Feeling frustrated on a Monday morning is not a reason to quit. But persistent patterns that affect your health, relationships, and long-term career growth are legitimate signals worth examining. The challenge is separating temporary frustration from genuine misalignment.

The FI community approaches this differently from mainstream career advice. Instead of asking "Am I happy at work?" — which fluctuates daily — we ask: "Is this role aligned with my long-term financial and personal goals?" That reframe turns an emotional decision into a strategic one.

Before you submit your resignation, your finances need to be ready regardless of how miserable you are. Quitting without financial preparation trades one source of stress for another.

The FI community has a massive advantage here. If you have been building toward financial independence — even if you are not there yet — your savings provide a runway that most people do not have. A $200,000 investment portfolio at a 4% safe withdrawal rate provides $8,000 per year in sustainable income, which dramatically reduces the pressure of a job search.

The worst time to make a career decision is when you are emotionally overwhelmed. A terrible meeting, a passed-over promotion, or a toxic interaction with a coworker can make quitting feel urgent when the situation may actually be temporary or fixable.

Use the 30-day test: if you have wanted to quit for fewer than 30 consecutive days, it is likely a temporary frustration. If the feeling has persisted — or intensified — for 30+ days, it is a pattern worth taking seriously.

How you leave a job matters as much as why you leave. Your professional reputation follows you for your entire career, and the people you work with today may be the hiring managers, clients, or references of tomorrow.

Two weeks notice: This is the minimum professional standard in the United States. For senior roles, three to four weeks is more appropriate. Check your employment contract — some roles require 30, 60, or 90 days notice.

The resignation conversation: Schedule a private meeting with your direct manager. Keep it brief and positive. Say: "I have decided to move on to a new opportunity. I want to thank you for [specific positive thing], and I am committed to making the transition as smooth as possible. My last day would be [date]."

The transition plan: Document your ongoing projects, key contacts, passwords, and processes. Offer to train your replacement. Complete as much outstanding work as possible. A strong exit creates goodwill that pays dividends for years.

What not to do: Do not badmouth the company, your boss, or your coworkers — not in the resignation meeting, not in your exit interview, not on social media. Even if your grievances are legitimate, airing them publicly hurts your reputation more than theirs.

Conventional advice says never quit without another job lined up. The FI community takes a more nuanced view: it depends on your financial position and the severity of the situation.

If you are leaving due to company changes — layoffs, restructuring, or role elimination — negotiate your severance package. Many employees accept the first offer without realizing severance is negotiable. Key leverage points include your tenure, difficulty of replacement, willingness to sign a non-compete or non-disparagement clause, and any outstanding commissions or bonuses.

Common severance components to negotiate: extended pay (push for 2-4 weeks per year of tenure), continued health insurance coverage, outplacement services, vesting acceleration for equity, and a positive reference commitment.

Health insurance is often the biggest financial concern when leaving a job. You have two primary options:

COBRA: Continues your employer plan for up to 18 months. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer was paying) plus a 2% administrative fee. COBRA typically costs $500-$700 per month for individual coverage and $1,400-$2,000+ for family coverage. It is expensive but familiar.

ACA Marketplace: Depending on your income after leaving, you may qualify for substantial subsidies. If your annual income drops below 400% of the federal poverty level, premium tax credits can reduce your monthly cost to $100-$400 for comprehensive coverage. FI seekers who leave jobs often qualify for significant subsidies because their earned income drops even if their net worth is high — ACA subsidies are based on income, not wealth.

Here is where financial independence changes everything. When you have significant savings — even if you have not reached full FI — you have leverage that most employees lack. You can negotiate from strength, take career risks, and walk away from toxic situations without financial desperation.

A $500,000 portfolio at a 4% withdrawal rate provides $20,000 per year indefinitely. That is not enough to live on for most people, but combined with a working spouse, reduced expenses, or part-time work, it transforms "should I quit my job" from a terrifying question into a strategic calculation. FI is not just about never working again — it is about having the financial security to make career decisions based on alignment and purpose rather than desperation and fear.

The FI community has a saying: financial independence is not about quitting your job — it is about having the freedom to choose whether to keep it. Every dollar you save and invest is a vote for your future autonomy. When you have 12-24 months of expenses saved, you negotiate from strength. When you reach Coast FI or beyond, a bad job becomes a choice, not a trap. Build your FI runway and the question changes from "Can I afford to quit?" to "Does this role still serve my goals?"

Work through these steps before making your decision.

Have you consistently wanted to leave for 30+ days? If no, wait. Temporary frustration is not a reason to upend your career. If yes, proceed to step two.

Pro tip: Keep a brief daily journal noting your satisfaction level 1-10. Data beats feelings for decision-making.

Is the issue your boss, your role, your compensation, the culture, or the industry? Some problems follow you to the next job. A bad manager is fixable by transferring. An industry you hate requires a bigger change.

Verify your emergency fund, health insurance options, debt situation, and FI runway. If you are not financially ready, keep working while you build your safety net and search for alternatives.

Before quitting, have you requested a transfer, a raise, a role change, or a conversation with HR? Many solvable problems go unaddressed because employees assume the answer will be no.

Pro tip: A direct conversation with your manager about your concerns resolves the issue 40% of the time.

If you decide to leave, secure your next opportunity (if possible), give appropriate notice, document your work for your successor, and maintain every professional relationship.

Pro tip: Never burn bridges. The colleague you leave today may be the hiring manager at your dream company in three years.

At minimum, 3-6 months of essential expenses in a liquid savings account. If you are quitting without another job lined up, aim for 6-12 months. The FI community recommends having your emergency fund fully funded, health insurance secured, and ideally some progress toward financial independence to provide a psychological safety net.

If your job is causing persistent anxiety, depression, or physical health symptoms that do not improve with coping strategies, therapy, or workplace changes — yes, your health must come first. But do it strategically: secure health insurance, build your financial runway, and consult a therapist or career coach before making the leap. Never make a permanent career decision during a temporary emotional crisis.

Generally, quitting gives you more control over the narrative, timing, and terms. Being fired can qualify you for unemployment benefits (quitting usually does not), but it can also create a negative reference. If you sense a termination is coming, consider whether negotiating a mutual separation with severance is an option. Document everything and consult an employment attorney if you believe the termination may be discriminatory or retaliatory.

Be honest and frame it positively. Acceptable explanations include: career transition (took time to retrain or earn a certification), personal development (traveled, volunteered, or cared for family), or strategic job search (took time to find the right fit rather than settling). Employers increasingly accept career gaps — especially post-2020 — as long as you can articulate what you did during the time off.

COBRA (Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act) lets you continue your employer health plan for up to 18 months after leaving. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer contributed) plus a 2% admin fee. Individual coverage typically costs $500-$700/month and family coverage runs $1,400-$2,000+/month. The ACA marketplace is often cheaper, especially if your income drops after leaving.

FI savings transform the equation entirely. With a substantial portfolio, you have a financial runway that removes the urgency and desperation from the decision. Even partial FI — having 2-5 years of expenses invested — means you can quit a toxic job, take time to find the right next role, or transition to lower-paying but more fulfilling work. FI is not just about retiring early; it is about having the leverage to make career decisions from a position of strength rather than fear.

The question "should I quit my job?" deserves a framework, not an impulse. Apply the 30-day test, diagnose the real problem, verify your financial readiness, explore internal solutions, and then make a deliberate decision. If you have been building toward financial independence, your savings give you something most people lack: the freedom to walk away from a bad situation without financial panic. FI is the ultimate career insurance — it turns "I have to stay" into "I choose to stay or go." Build your runway, protect your reputation, and make the decision from a position of strength.

#9131. Fala Atelier embeds trio of playful volumes into Portuguese hillside for Cookie Cutter Retreat

Photography by Francisco Ascensão (unless stated otherwise)

Three semicircular volumes of different scales make up this retreat for digital nomads in Portugal, completed by Porto architecture studio Fala Atelier.

The three volumes are nearly identical, emerging from the site with blocky, blue chimneys and topped with grass roofs, which Fala Atelier said “almost disappear” into the landscape.

“The three buildings enjoy considerable freedom in their relationships with the site, the slope and one another, sharing a geometric vocabulary without submitting to a rigid overall composition,” the studio told Dezeen.

“From a distance, they almost disappear, leaving the windows and bright blue chimneys to announce their presence,” it added.

“Their placement makes the landscape a fluid game.”

The retreat’s three buildings were scaled as small, medium and large versions of the same semicircular volume. and built with the same materials and dimension ratios.

Each one is composed of a concrete frame, which is embedded into the landscape and incorporates round columns. These are adorned with glazed fronts and tilted metal canopies.

Diagonal walls slice through each of the volumes to distinguish the public and private areas, behind which are spaces that draw on houses by architects Frank Gehry, Toyo Ito and Alvaro Siza, according to Fala Atelier.

“Each [volume] is divided by a diagonal wall, placing a dense collection of small rooms beside an expansive, almost empty space,” the studio said.

“We treated fragments of [Gehry, Ito and Siza’s] plans as objets trouvés, borrowing their internal formal relationships almost verbatim.”

The hall, which is the largest of the three spaces, was designed by Fala Atelier to “host almost any activity”.

Its front portion is open plan, while private spaces sit behind, finished with a combination of white-painted and tile-clad walls contrasted by blue and fluorescent-yellow details.

This same materiality and colour palette is repeated throughout the retreat’s private and shared dwellings to create a consistent visual language across the site.

“The consistency allows the differences to become more intriguing,” the studio said. “You recognise the family immediately, even if you briefly wonder which relative you have entered,” it added.

Elsewhere in Portugal, Corkinho used solid cork to construct a pavilion dedicated to silence in Alentejo and António Costa Lima Arquitectos has completed a warehouse-style housing block in Lisbon.

#9130. Prize dedicated to African women artists expands to Senegal and announces 2026 winners

Centre: Fatoumata Sy and Kwama Frigaux’s uncle, Mr. Pacx, representing the artist at the award ceremony. To their left (from left): prize jury members Dominique Heyse-Moore, Touria El Glaoui and Alexa Waley-Cohen. To their right (from left): Leila Zakhem, the prize director, and Valerie Lesbros, the director of the Institut Français du Sénégal

The Ghanaian-French artist Kwama Frigaux and the Senegalese Fatoumata Sy have been announced as the joint winners of the Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize. The prize, founded by the London and Accra-based Gallery 1957 in 2021 to support women artists in Ghana and its diaspora, has this year expanded to include artists from Senegal, in partnership with Institut Français du Sénégal. Frigaux and Fatoumata have been awarded $5,000 each, as well as a three-month residency (in Senegal for the Ghanaian and in Ghana for the Senegalese), and solo exhibitions.

The prize is named after the former Ashanti queen mother, renowned for her anti-colonial resistance when Ghana was under British rule. The call for applications for this year’s edition opened in June and ran until September, and was open to Ghanaian and Senegalese women artists aged 18 or older, based either in their home countries or in the diaspora. The winners were announced during Accra Cultural Week (29 October-2 November), which is organised by Gallery 1957. On view there until 5 December is The Lore of Care: Maternal Acts of Devotion, a solo show by Theresah Ankomah, the winner of the 2025 Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize.

Installation view of The Lore of Care: Maternal Acts of Devotion, Gallery 1957's show by Theresah Ankomah, who won the 2025 Yaa Asantewaa Prize

Frigaux and Sy were selected by a jury comprising Touria El Glaoui, the founder of the 1-54 Contemporary African Art Fair; the Ghanaian artist Serge Attukwei Clottey; Marie Hélène Pereira, a senior curator at Berlin’s Haus der Kulturen der Welt; Jeanne Barral, a curator at the Fondation Cartier; the collector Alexa Waley-Cohen; and Dominique Heyse-Moore, the senior curator of contemporary British art at Tate Britain.

Runners up participate in a mentorship programme, which provides support on topics such as grant applications and entrepreneurship. Mentors this year include the Nigerian artist Modupeola Fadugba and Aisha Ayensu, the founder of the Ghanaian luxury fashion brand Christie Brown.

"I think [it's] an incredible programme that helps drive the longevity of [the prize's] impact,” Leila Zakhem, the director of the prize, tells The Art Newspaper. “And it really creates a beautiful community.”

Zakhem explains that her team considered several countries for the expansion, including Nigeria. A key part of this search was finding a "very good implementing partner". The Institut Français du Sénégal, which is a non-commercial space, has a lot of credibility, she adds, “and they were very excited to partner with us on the prize”. Zakhem says that she hopes the expansion will help develop and create a bridge between art communities in English- and French-speaking West Africa.

The planned next steps are to expand further into West Africa, and then potentially beyond, with winners selected from different regions of the continent. “The goal is eventually to be the leading Pan-African female art prize on the continent,” Zakhem says.

#9129. Photographer Files $150K Copyright Lawsuit Against Sony Over His Image of Stevie Wonder

Photographer Files $150K Copyright Lawsuit Against Sony Over His Image of Stevie Wonder

A photographer has sued Sony, accusing the company of posting his “iconic” 1974 portrait of Stevie Wonder on Instagram without permission.

Longtime photographer Al Satterwhite filed a copyright infringement lawsuit against Sony Music Publishing (SMP) in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York on Sunday, seeking up to $150,000 in damages.

According to a report by Billboard, Satterwhite photographed Wonder sitting at a piano in 1974 and later registered the images with the U.S. Copyright Office. In 2023, SMP allegedly used one of the portraits in an Instagram carousel marking the 50th anniversary of Wonder’s 1973 album Innervisions.

Satterwhite’s lawsuit alleges that SMP posted his “iconic photograph” of Wonder on Instagram without first obtaining a license. He argues that the company’s use of the image cost him a licensing opportunity and potentially affected the market for his work. The complaint also claims that SMP benefited from sharing the photograph with its social media audience without paying him.

In court documents, the photographer claims the alleged infringement by SMP “has harmed, and continues to harm, the potential market for or value of the copyrighted work by robbing Plaintiff of his exclusive right to license the copyrighted work for illustrative and other purposes.”

The photographer is seeking up to $150,000 in statutory damages for copyright infringement, the maximum amount allowed under federal law for the willful infringement of a single work. Satterwhite’s argues that Sony knew, or should have known, that it needed a license to use the image, given its experience handling intellectual property rights in the music industry.

In the complaint, Satterwhite argues that SMP “is a sophisticated media company that understands copyright law and the need to obtain a license to publish the copyrighted works of others.”

According to Billboard, Satterwhite has filed more than a dozen previous lawsuits over the alleged unauthorized use of his photographs of Wonder and other well-known figures, including Arnold Schwarzenegger and Mel Brooks. Satterwhite also filed a lawsuit against Berklee College of Music last year, accusing the institution of using another photograph of Wonder from the same 1974 shoot without permission. He dropped the case voluntarily less than two months later.

#9128. Blackmagic’s $1,695 Spatial Audio Mic Has 108 Mics and Looks Super Sci-Fi

Blackmagic’s $1,695 Spatial Audio Mic Has 108 Mics and Looks Super Sci-Fi

Blackmagic Design has announced the Ambisonic Microphone, a new professional mic designed to capture spatial audio for immersive video productions.

“The Blackmagic Ambisonic Microphone is a 7th order ambisonic microphone array featuring 108 digital MEMS microphones that capture the entire sound field,” Blackmagic explains. “The MEMS microphones are mounted flush in a solid, faceted metal body, making the design extremely strong for professional use while remaining small enough to fit in the palm of your hand, and be mounted on top of a camera.”

Advanced audio processing technology is built directly into the microphone, and an internal processor runs Apple’s encoding filters, converting the 108 MEMS microphones to seventh-order ambisonics in real time. This means customers don’t need complicated software or a breakout box.

The mic is powered by a single USB-C cable, and it can quickly be mounted to an URSA Cine Immersive camera. Capturing spatial audio is as simple as plugging it in.

As Blackmagic Design explains, its new microphone started development when it was working with Apple on the Blackmagic URSA Cine Immersive camera, which was formally announced in June 2024 and billed as “the ultimate camera system for making immersive video for the Apple Vision Pro.”

Filmmakers have used the Blackmagic URSA Cine Immersive to capture all sorts of incredible things, including basketball games and rocket launches.

“This microphone started when we were collaborating with Apple on the Blackmagic URSA Cine Immersive camera. I heard a high resolution spatial audio capture for the first time and it was like hearing an acoustic reality, I was totally blown away,” says Blackmagic Design CEO Grant Petty.

“Apple licensed their array geometry and the ambisonic encoding filters, we did the engineering and design, and the result is an ambisonic microphone where you just plug in one cable and capture true spatial audio.”

The Blackmagic Ambisonic Microphone will be available next month for $1,695 through Blackmagic Design and its authorized retailers.

#9127. Leica Is Giving the M-A and M11-P Hammertone Special Edition Variants

Leica Is Giving the M-A and M11-P Hammertone Special Edition Variants

Leica has announced a new special edition version of both the M-A and M11-P cameras that brings what the company describes as a classic design that it also rarely uses: hammertone.

“Since the 1930s, the hammertone finish has symbolized the combination of durability and technical aesthetics. This distinctive texture is formed during the drying process when metal pigments and special additives create subtle variations in surface tension. In industrial design, particularly in Germany, this finish has come to symbolize functionality and reliability,” Leica says.

While it might be somewhat common generally in Germany, that’s not the case for Leica cameras – at least modern ones. It has appeared in the past, such as from the Leica MD documentation camera for the Leitz Reprovit system to the exceptionally rare Leica MD (of which only ten were produced in 1964), but it’s certainly unusual.

“With their distinctive finish, both variants draw inspiration from rare Leica special editions, including the 1964 Leica MD Hammertone, the 2003 MP LHSA, the 2011 Leica M9 Hammertone, and the 2016 Leica M-A Vienna Edition. The new Leica M-A Hammertone and the new Leica M11-P Hammertone continue this lineage in their own unique way, thereby adding two exceptional, valuable variants to the Leica M portfolio,” Leica says.

Leica says it has reworked the process of applying the pattern for these special editions to achieve a uniform finish of the texture across the entire camera.

Both the M-A and the M11-P have the hammertone finish on the top plate and base plate. It is made from solid brass with a cross knurling on the control elements and a shiny silver shutter-release plate. The cameras also have a black leatherette covering in a vulcanite style with white engravings.

The Leica M11-P Hammertone also has newly rounded, classically styled edges on the top plate and base plate to go with the hammertone texture, as well as a new version of the screw on the front featuring a silver-chrome finish.

This pattern has the special distinction of making every camera unique due to the way it is applied.

Both the Leica M-A Hammertone and the Leica M11-P Hammertone will be available starting on November 12 from Leica Stores, the Leica Online Store, and authorized dealers. The retail price for the Leica M-A Hammertone is $8,000, while the Leica M11-P Hammertone costs $10,950.

#9126. South Korean Photographers Demand Police Investigation After Politician Calls Them ‘Hyenas’ in Chatroom

South Korean Photographers Demand Police Investigation After Politician Calls Them ‘Hyenas’ in Chatroom

A leading South Korean politician is facing fierce backlash from the country’s media after referring to photojournalists as a “pack of hyenas” in an online chatroom — an insult that has prompted a formal police complaint from press photographers.

Representative Choi Min-hee is a South Korean politician and senior member of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK), serving in the country’s National Assembly. She has sparked outrage in South Korea after sharing an image of working press photographers in a group chat and making disparaging comments about the photojournalists.

Last week, Min-hee uploaded photos of photographers covering DPK events to a KakaoTalk group chat room for local party members in Namyangju, a city in South Korea. In the post uploaded to the chat room, which had over 500 participants, Min-hee referred to the photographers in the image as a “pack of hyenas.”

“These are journalists from media outlets with access to the National Assembly,” Min-hee writes in the post, according to numerous South Korean news outlets. “They’re doing this to capture divisive footage somehow.”

Min-hee’s disparaging post about South Korean photographers quickly spread online, sparking an angry backlash from members of the press. Amid the uproar, she held a press conference at the National Assembly on Wednesday and apologized for her remarks. However, the Korean Photographers Association has nonetheless decided to file a police complaint against Min-hee for disparaging photographers as a “pack of hyenas.”

The Korean Photographers Association says the politician’s remarks demean journalists, undermine legitimate press scrutiny of those in power, and cross the line from acceptable criticism into defamatory accusations.

“Condemning legitimate reporting activities as political divisiveness and ridiculing journalists by comparing them to animals is a clear insult to media professionals and an inappropriate act with potential for defamation,” the Korean Photographers Association writes in a statement to Wednesday, according to national news outlet Cho Sun Daily.

“Photographers do not exist to capture scenes that suit politicians’ preferences. They exist to monitor power through the eyes of the public and record history. Criticism of the media is free, but insults and baseless accusations against reporters cannot be justified.”

The association says the photographers pictured in Min-hee’s post have suffered significant emotional distress and humiliation as a result.

“We have finalized the decision to file a complaint with the police to prevent infringement on our members’ rights,” the Korean Photographers Association adds. “Photographers whose faces were exposed in the photos are currently experiencing severe humiliation and self-loathing, struggling to the point of being unable to continue their work.”

#9125. HP DesignJet T250 printer places professional printing in users’ hands

From printing menus to educational posters, technology company HP’s DesignJet T250 printer gives businesses the ability to design and print high-quality materials in house.

Described by the brand as the “world’s smallest plotters”, with HP DesignJet T250 users can customise thousands of professionally created templates and print content on-site when required.

The printer can be used for everything from designing large-format posters to advertising a new product or an event.

It can also print branded communications or create retail displays, among other materials. According to HP, this benefits multiple industries, from food and culture to education and design.

HP explained that this flexibility redefines the professional printing workflow by giving businesses control over the creative and operational process, reducing their reliance on external printing providers.

This also results in increasingly flexible timelines, with in-house designers able to tweak their design, then quickly print another copy.

According to HP, the printer also gives brands and companies greater control over costs.

This is particularly useful to smaller businesses, entrepreneurs and creative studios, it explained, where developing professional marketing materials can be expensive and time-consuming.

Instead, HP DesignJet T250 places control into user’s hands by giving them a fast and flexible way to bring creative ideas to life.

According to HP, click software incorporated into the device further streamlines workflow by providing an easy print experience and helping ensure prints are produced as intended.

“By bringing design and large-format printing together in one accessible solution, the HP DesignJet T250 helps small businesses and creative professionals create impactful visual communications without the complexity traditionally associated with professional printing,” the company said.

The HP DesignJet T250 is compact enough to be placed in small workspaces, offices or studios. It was made from at least 40-per-cent recycled plastic and is the first HP large-format plotter to contain recycled metal.

Users can also save 65 per cent energy when using the printer’s on/off auto-scheduler, according to the brand.

For a limited time, users can purchase an HP DesignJet T250 with a year’s worth of Canva Pro included. According to HP, this gives designers everything they need to create and print professional-quality posters from a single workflow.

“The combination of Canva’s intuitive design platform and the HP DesignJet T250 creates a seamless workflow that allows users to move from concept to final print with ease,” said HP.

To learn more about HP DesignJet T250, visit HP’s website.
