#9065. Dezeen Awards trophy updated using "one of humanity's oldest natural materials"

Photography courtesy of Corticeira Amorim

Portuguese manufacturer Corticeira Amorim has used sustainably harvested cork to refresh the latest edition of Dezeen’s iconic D-shaped trophy.

The trophies will be presented to this year’s winners at the Dezeen Awards party next week on 16 November at London’s Royal Opera House.

The event will bring together shortlisted studios, judges and the international architecture and design community to celebrate this year’s projects and reveal the 2026 winners, who will be the first to collect the new trophies.

Final tickets are available until 12pm London time on 11 November. Secure yours now.

An all-cork refresh for Dezeen Awards trophies

This year’s trophies have been produced in partnership with Corticeira Amorim, the world’s largest cork processing group, and mark the next material chapter for Dezeen’s trophy designs.

The updated design features an all-cork material palette that creates “a very direct encounter with the material”, according to Corticeira Amorim board member Cristina Amorim.

The group began by considering the trophy’s original design by Dutch studio Atelier NL, which was first created in 2018 and made from clay.

“The starting point was to preserve the recognisable form and graphic identity of the Dezeen Awards trophy, while allowing cork itself to become part of the design,” Amorim explained.

Cork is derived from the outer bark of the cork oak, which grows mainly in western Mediterranean countries such as Portugal, where Corticeira Amorim is based and has operated for over 150 years.

The material is renewable and recyclable. It is harvested without felling the tree, which naturally regenerates its bark to be harvested again at intervals of at least nine years.

Cork can also sequester carbon while replacing other, more polluting materials.

Beyond its sustainability credentials, the material is also remarkably light, resilient and adaptable in its nature.

“There is an interesting challenge in cork – it is one of humanity’s oldest natural materials, yet we are still discovering what it can do,” Amorim said.

This challenge spurred the development of different cork compositions, textures and finishes, after which a set of grains and colour references were selected to distinguish winner tiers while keeping a consistent visual language across the collection.

The winners of this year’s project categories, project of the year and Designers of the Year will each receive one of the bespoke cork trophies.

The project marks a continuation of Corticeira Amorim’s collaboration with architecture and design initiatives, revealing what Amorim sees as the “side of cork people may not expect”.

In 2024, the cork manufacturer produced the installations for City Cortex, a major arts programme that took place across the city of Lisbon.

The programme brought together internationally recognised architects and designers to create cork-based interventions for public and semi-public spaces, including Eduardo Souto de Moura, Diller Scofidio + Renfro and Yves Béhar.

Other notable projects also include Herzog & de Meuron and Ai Weiwei’s sunken 2012 Serpentine Pavilion, as well as product collaborations with designers including Jasper Morrison, the Bouroullecs and Naoto Fukasawa, showcasing the material’s broad potential.

“What makes cork surprising is its versatility: the same natural material can be transformed in so many different ways – some of them still unconceived,” Amorim said.

Reflecting on this year’s trophies, Amorim said: “cork is not simply associated with the awards – it becomes part of the award itself.”

“What we like about the final result is its simplicity,” she continued.

“The shape belongs unmistakably to the Dezeen Awards, but the texture, warmth, grain and natural variation belong unmistakably to cork.”

Previous editions of the Dezeen Awards trophy have explored materials including a compound of micro-paper, wood from London street trees and clay used to make the traditional yellow bricks found in the UK’s capital.

Dezeen Awards 2026 in partnership with TrimbleDezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology company Trimble. Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. Trimble’s collaboration with Dezeen Awards demonstrates its ongoing commitment to inspiring and supporting creative excellence across the globe.

Now a new update introduces an attempt to police generative AI content along with more complete AI declarations and more control over filtering. The aim is to make it easier to users to control what they see, but it's got a mixed response from artists so far.

We're introducing the next phase of generative AI content controls. Creators will have clearer AI declaration requirements when publishing, and AI filtering is now on by default, with options that give you finer control. Learn what's changing → https://t.co/cuHmcoAuhw https://t.co/64PevA0XjmNovember 9, 2026

When publishing content on ArtStation, users will now be asked to declare whether generative AI was used in the creation of the piece. Creators can identify their work as primarily generative AI, mixed generative AI and non-generative methods or 100% non-generative.

This relies on users being upfront, and ArtStation says that most are. However, it's recognised that there is a problem with people uploading AI-generated content without flagging it as such.

That leads to the second aspect of the latest update, which is a dedicated channel for reporting AI content. If users come across artwork they think is AI-generated but which isn't labelled, they can report it. ArtStation says that every report will help improve its AI filtering for the whole community.

Users also get more control over what they're shown: they can choose whether to hide declared generative AI content, or to allow mixed generative and non-generative workflows, and they can adjust how aggressively ArtStation filters content based on user reports of suspected generative AI.

The 'Strict' setting hides artwork when just a few reports suggest it may be AI-generated. 'Balanced' filters it out when there’s a moderate level of reports and 'Loose' removes it only when user signals are strongest. By default, the filter will be set to not show any project declared as AI-generated, tagged with 'CreatedwithAI' or tagged with generative AI tools, and suspected as AI will be set to strict.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

The platform risks becoming useless if it's impossible to find interesting work because of the sheer volume of low-quality AI-generated content. Many users have welcomed the latest update as a move in the right direction, while others have raised doubts about how effective the measures it will be.

There's a strong reliance on user moderation, which will depend on users accurately identifying AI art. Some may still go undetected completely, while the 'Strict' filtering could remove work falsely identified as AI.

It's not yet clear if artists will be notified if their work is flagged or whether they will have a way to contest that decision. That could be a concern when even long established digital artists like Loish have been falsely accused of using AI over on platforms like TikTok.

The update highlights the difficult balancing act of policing AI content. ArtStation has a big focus on concept art, and some in the industry now see generative AI as an inevitable part of the pipeline in this field. The new Disney deal with Adobe will focus on developing custom AI models specifically for concept work. In that context, KitBash probably sees banning AI art from the platform as counterproductive if not impossible.

#9063. Gustaf Westman unveils full Disney collection featuring Donald Duck bookstand and Pluto mirror

Swedish designer Gustaf Westman‘s full collaboration with media company Disney, which saw him reimagine familiar Disney details “through his own design language”, has been revealed.

The collection, which launches on 15 November, features homeware, accessories and glassware, alongside made-to-order furniture.

Among the furniture pieces are a bookstand designed to resemble Donald Duck, a Goofy coffee table and Mickey dresser, as well as a Pluto mirror.

Each takes recognisable features from the Disney characters and turns them into parts of the design object, with the Donald bookstand decorated with his hat and duck feet.

Westman told Dezeen he wanted to work with Disney because he grew up with the brand.

“Disney is part of so many people’s childhood, including mine,” the designer explained.

“Mickey’s ears and white gloves, Minnie’s bow, Goofy’s playful silhouette – they’re instantly recognisable shapes, and that made them really fun to work with,” he continued.

His aim was to create something new while using details that are deeply familiar to many.

“I wanted to take those familiar details and reimagine them through my own design language, with sculptural, playful forms in bold proportions, and bring that sense of joy into people’s homes,” Westman said.

The collection also includes smaller objects such as a vase designed to look like Mickey’s trousers, a glass that evokes Minnie Mouse and a candelabra resembling Donald Duck.

There is also merch, including a T-shirt, hoodie, keychains, hairbands and pins.

Westman’s own favourite object is the Mickey Tumbler, which was one of the first objects from the collection to be revealed.

“The Mickey Tumbler is my favourite,” he said.

“It combines my chunky shapes with Mickey’s signature colours and an ear-shaped lid, so both worlds are instantly recognisable without overcomplicating the design.”

Disney and Westman are hosting a series of pop-up experiences in Tokyo, New York and Paris to launch the collection before it is released online.

Disney also targeted the homeware and interior industries in 2022, when it launched its own homeware brand.

#9062. Why Are People Taking CoQ10 Supplements for Longevity, and Do They Work?

Coenzyme Q10, or CoQ10, was once a niche supplement, known best in wellness circles for its possible benefits for heart health and fertility. But now the antioxidant’s star is rising for a new reason: its purported longevity-boosting powers.

The appeal of CoQ10 has grown as researchers have explored its effects on various conditions, with small studies revealing, for example, it may help boost insulin sensitivity, cut the frequency of migraine attacks, and alleviate muscle aches from statins used for high cholesterol. But as of late, there’s excitement around its broader anti-aging potential because of how it supports our mitochondria, which you may remember from high school biology as the “powerhouse of the cell.”

That role has punched CoQ10’s ticket into the longevity club, alongside other supplements thought to lend a hand to mitochondria (like urolithin A and nicotinamide mononucleotide, or NMN). There’s even a synthetic derivative of CoQ10 designed specifically for better absorption by mitochondria, which is called mitoquinone (or MitoQ), that’s gaining hype among celeb trainers and athletes for boosting energy, recovery, and “cellular health.”

But is CoQ10 all it’s cracked up to be when it comes to longevity? Read on to learn more before grabbing a bottle of this supplement.

Our cells naturally produce CoQ10, a molecule that acts like a conveyor belt for charged particles inside our mitochondria, enabling them to “efficiently create adenosine triphosphate, or ATP,” the “currency for cellular energy,” Anthony Molina, PhD, a professor of medicine at UC San Diego who studies aging biomarkers, tells SELF. That’s a big deal, as all cells rely on that energy to complete their daily functions. As we age, both the number and energy-producing powers of mitochondria drop off—a process involved in the development of many age-related diseases, Dr. Molina points out. Meanwhile, CoQ10 levels also decline with age, leading to the idea that we should take it in supplement form for better mitochondrial (and, in turn, overall) health.

Beyond its role in energy production, CoQ10 is also an antioxidant that is “very powerful in capturing free radicals,” or volatile molecules that can harm cells, Daria Mochly-Rosen, PhD, a professor of chemical and systems biology at Stanford University and coauthor of The Life Machines: How Taking Care of Your Mitochondria Can Transform Your Health, tells SELF. By stabilizing those molecules, CoQ10 may help to keep that damage (a.k.a. oxidative stress) from piling up and also contributing to aging and the development of chronic disease.

Separately, CoQ10 has potential benefits as it relates to cardiovascular health: It’s anti-inflammatory and may also improve the function of blood vessels, helping regulate blood pressure, JoAnn E. Manson, MD, DrPH, chief of the division of preventive medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School, tells SELF. These upsides could lower risk for heart disease, the number-one killer in the US.

Despite the promising mechanisms above, “the evidence base just isn’t yet there,” Dr. Manson says. The studies we do have on CoQ10 and longevity are in mice and rats—and while a few suggest a lifespan-extending effect, or a way to reverse some cognitive decline once it starts, others show no anti-aging upsides in healthy animals. Besides, “we find again and again that humans are not just large, non-hairy mice,” Dr. Mochly-Rosen points out, “so we can’t assume the results transfer.”

Studies in people have been focused on CoQ10 as an intervention for specific diseases, particularly cardiovascular ones. All the experts say the strongest evidence for longevity is in those with heart failure, who have low CoQ10 levels—taking the supplement alongside standard treatment has been shown to reduce the need for hospitalization and risk of early death, possibly because of its mitochondrial perks.

But logistically, it’s a lot trickier to prove that CoQ10 prolongs life in healthy people versus in those with a medical condition or known CoQ10 deficiency. In the absence of these studies, it might be tempting to take a logical leap: If we know CoQ10 supports mitochondrial function, and levels of both dip with age and disease, supplementing with CoQ10 seems like it should help you live longer. But the problem is, we don’t know exactly what drives the mitochondrial issues that occur with age, Dr. Molina says. “So maybe you’re not taking a shot in the dark because we know that mitochondria has something to do with healthy aging, but using CoQ10 as the tool is like taking a shot in a dimly lit room,” he says. “It’s not clear whether you’re hitting the right target.”

As with any supplement, it’s best to ask your doctor before adding CoQ10 to your routine. While there’s a good deal of data to suggest it’s safe and well-tolerated, there are some people who shouldn’t take it, generally because of interactions with prescription drugs, Dr. Molina points out. The main concern is with blood thinners (a.k.a. anticoagulants) like warfarin (which are often prescribed after a blood clot)—CoQ10 could make these drugs less effective, Dr. Manson says. It’s also extra important to check in with your doctor first if you take insulin or are receiving treatment for cancer. Though CoQ10 doesn’t usually cause side effects, you could also wind up with some mild GI upset or insomnia, Dr. Manson adds.

There’s also the quality-control problem that comes with any supplement. These are not subjected to the same FDA regulations as medications are, meaning you can’t know for sure that you’re getting what the bottle promises. Studies of certain CoQ10 supplements have found that they contained less of the antioxidant than the amount listed on the label, Dr. Mochly-Rosen notes. Your best defense against winding up with a sugar pill is to find a product that’s been third-party verified, she says—look for the “NSF certified” or “USP verified” stamp.

The most accessible, repeatable high-value hotel redemption in travel rewards

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Picture this: You've been grinding toward your FI number, optimizing every dollar, and you've accumulated a stash of Chase Ultimate Rewards points sitting in your account. Now imagine checking into a clean, comfortable Hyatt Place in a city you're visiting for a wedding, a family reunion, or a long weekend — and the front desk agent hands you your keycard while your account balance drops by exactly 5,000 points. Not $150. Not $180. Five thousand points that you earned by buying groceries. That's the Category 1 Hyatt sweet spot — and it's the single most accessible, repeatable, high-value redemption in all of travel rewards. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A standard night at a Hyatt Place or Hyatt House in a mid-size U.S. city routinely runs **$100–$200 per night** in cash. At 5,000 points per night, you're redeeming at **2–4 cents per point (CPP)** — a range that demolishes the standard 1 cent per point benchmark that most casual rewards users never surpass. At 4 CPP on a $200 night, you're getting four times the value of a simple cash-back card. Every. Single. Time. The pricing inefficiency here is structural, not accidental. World of Hyatt uses a **fixed award chart** — meaning a Category 1 property costs 5,000 points whether it's a Tuesday in January or a Friday night during a sold-out college football weekend when cash rates are spiking. The loyalty program doesn't dynamically price awards the way airlines do. That fixed ceiling is your edge. For the ChooseFI community, this redemption isn't just good — it's foundational. It's the first sweet spot that proves the system works. Before you're ready to redeem 60,000 points for a business class flight to Tokyo, you need to feel what it's like to hand over a handful of points and walk into a hotel room that would have cost you real money. This is that moment. It builds the muscle memory, the confidence, and the conviction that travel rewards are real — and that you're playing the game correctly. This is where the journey starts.

World of Hyatt consistently delivers the highest cents-per-point value of any major hotel loyalty program. While Hilton and Marriott have moved to dynamic pricing — where award costs fluctuate based on demand — Hyatt maintains a fixed award chart. This structural difference is your edge. A Category 1 property costs 5,000 points whether it is a quiet Tuesday in February or a sold-out homecoming weekend. Combined with Chase Ultimate Rewards transfer ratios (1:1 from Sapphire Reserve, 4:3 from Sapphire Preferred) and instant transfer speed, Hyatt redemptions are the single best use of UR points for hotel stays. The ChooseFI community considers this the entry point that proves the entire travel rewards system works.

The core insight behind this sweet spot is deceptively simple: World of Hyatt uses a fixed-price award chart, and Category 1 is priced at a floor that hasn't kept pace with rising hotel cash rates.

Most hotel loyalty programs have moved to dynamic pricing — meaning award nights fluctuate with demand, just like cash rates. Marriott Bonvoy, Hilton Honors, IHG One Rewards — they've all largely eliminated fixed charts in favor of algorithms that squeeze more points out of you when demand is high. Hyatt has held the line on a fixed chart, and that stubbornness is your opportunity.

The Category 1 floor sits at 5,000 points per night. As cash rates for qualifying properties have climbed with inflation — many now regularly pricing at $150–$200+ — the points cost has remained anchored. The gap between what the market charges and what Hyatt charges in points is widening in your favor every year. That's not a bug in the system. It's a feature you're uniquely positioned to exploit by understanding it.

This redemption is built on two of the best transferable points currencies available to everyday consumers:

Both transfers are instant, which means you can search for availability before committing your points, confirm the room you want is bookable, and then initiate the transfer and complete the booking — all in one sitting. This is a critical distinction from some airline partners where transfers take 24–72 hours and you're transferring on faith. With Hyatt, there's no leap of faith required.

The transfer ratio matters. With a Sapphire Reserve, every UR point becomes one Hyatt point — 15,000 UR points covers three Category 1 nights with zero waste. With a Sapphire Preferred, the 4:3 ratio means you need 20,000 UR points for the same 15,000 Hyatt points. Bilt transfers at 1:1.

World of Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges on award bookings. This matters more for higher-tier redemptions, but it's worth internalizing as a feature of the program overall. When you book 5,000 points for a hotel night, that's your cost. You'll pay any applicable taxes at checkout — typically $10–$25 — but there are no program-imposed carrier fees or redemption surcharges eating into your value.

Hyatt's full chart runs from 3,500 points (Category 1 standard) up to 45,000 points (Category 8) per night. Understanding this structure helps you see the Category 1 sweet spot in context: it's the entry point, but it's not a consolation prize. Hyatt Place and Hyatt House properties are upper-midscale hotels — clean, well-maintained, often with free breakfast at Hyatt House locations and complimentary parking in suburban markets. These aren't budget motels. You're getting a genuinely comfortable night's sleep for points that most people have already earned without trying.

Booking a Category 1 Hyatt award is one of the smoothest processes in all of travel rewards. Here's exactly how to do it from start to finish.

Before anything else, log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards account at chase.com/ultimaterewards or your Bilt Rewards account at biltrewards.com and confirm your current points balance. You need a minimum of 5,000 points per night to execute this redemption. If you have 15,000 points, you can book up to three nights.

Go to hyatt.com and log in or create a free World of Hyatt account (it's free to join). Use the search bar to enter your destination city and travel dates. Once results populate, filter by "Points" or "Use Points" using the toggle at the top of the results page. This will display the award rate alongside the cash rate for every property.

Filter further by selecting "Category 1–2" under the Points filter to quickly surface the lowest-cost options. Availability is typically strong — Hyatt.com shows real-time award inventory, and Category 1 properties almost always have rooms open. The booking window extends 395 days out, so you can plan well in advance for travel around a specific event.

Once you've found the property and dates you want, note the exact points cost displayed. For Category 1 properties, this should read 5,000 points per night. Add the room to your cart and proceed — but do not check out yet if your Hyatt account currently has zero balance.

Open a new browser tab and navigate to your Chase Ultimate Rewards portal (chase.com/ultimaterewards) or Bilt dashboard. Select "Transfer to Travel Partners" and choose World of Hyatt from the list. Enter the number of points you need (5,000 per night, minimum), confirm your World of Hyatt membership number, and initiate the transfer.

Chase and Bilt transfers to Hyatt are instant. Note: Sapphire Reserve transfers at 1:1 while Sapphire Preferred transfers at 4:3 (4 UR = 3 Hyatt). Refresh your Hyatt account and your points will be there, ready to use.

Return to your Hyatt browser tab and complete the checkout process. Select "Redeem Points" as your payment method, confirm the points deduction matches what you expected, and finalize the reservation. You'll receive a confirmation email immediately.

If your preferred property shows no award availability on your dates, try these workarounds:

Go to hyatt.com and use the "Points + Cash" or "Use Points" search filter. Category 1 properties will display at 5,000 points per night. You can also browse by category directly — look for Hyatt Place and Hyatt House locations in secondary cities and suburban markets.

Always verify that your desired dates show award availability before initiating a transfer from Chase or Bilt. While transfers are instant, confirming availability first ensures you never have orphaned points sitting in your Hyatt account with no immediate use.

Log into your Chase or Bilt account, navigate to the transfer partners section, select World of Hyatt, and transfer the exact number of points needed. Transfers are instant. With a Sapphire Reserve, 5,000 UR points become 5,000 Hyatt points (1:1). With a Sapphire Preferred, you need approximately 6,700 UR points for 5,000 Hyatt points (4:3 ratio). Bilt transfers at 1:1.

Once the points land in your Hyatt account, complete the booking through hyatt.com or the World of Hyatt app. You will pay applicable taxes at checkout (typically $10 to $25 per night) but no additional redemption fees.

Before booking, note the cash rate for the same room and dates. Divide the cash rate by 5,000 to calculate your cents per point. If a room costs $150 per night and you are paying 5,000 points, you are getting 3 cents per point — triple the baseline 1 cent per point cash back value.

Let's make this concrete. You're flying into Nashville for a long weekend — maybe it's a bachelorette party, a music festival, or just a trip you've been putting off. You pull up Hyatt.com and search Nashville for a Friday–Sunday stay (two nights).

The Hyatt Place Nashville / Brentwood shows cash rates of $169 per night — that's $338 for your two-night stay before taxes. Totally reasonable for Nashville on a weekend, but $338 is $338.

Now look at the award column: 5,000 points per night. Two nights: 10,000 points.

You transferred 10,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points from your Sapphire Reserve to World of Hyatt last week (it took about 30 seconds, and at 1:1 every point landed). Your Hyatt account shows a 10,000-point balance. You complete the booking, pay the ~$30 in taxes at checkout, and you're done.

That's more than three times the value most people extract from their points programs. And those 10,000 Chase UR points? You earned them by putting your regular monthly spending on your Chase Sapphire card for a few months.

At the Hyatt Place, you'll check into a well-appointed room with a king bed, a sofa sleating area, and a bathroom that doesn't make you feel like you're in a budget motel. Hyatt House properties (also frequently Category 1 or 2) often include a complimentary hot breakfast — eggs, waffles, fruit — served every morning. In some suburban markets, these properties also offer free parking, turning your 5,000-point night into an even stronger value play when you factor in parking rates that might otherwise run $20–$30/night.

This isn't a flashy Park Hyatt penthouse suite. But it's a genuinely comfortable, predictably high-quality stay that you've effectively taken off your cash budget — freeing that $338 for experiences, food, or your investment accounts. That's the ChooseFI mindset applied to travel.

Stack your Hyatt Globalist benefits if you qualify. If you hold World of Hyatt's top elite status (Globalist, earned at 60 qualifying nights), you receive complimentary breakfast at most full-service properties and room upgrades. Even on a 5,000-point award night, your elite benefits apply. That free breakfast alone can add $25–$35 of value to every morning.

Use the Hyatt free night award from the World of Hyatt Credit Card. The World of Hyatt Credit Card (issued by Chase) comes with an annual free night certificate valid at Category 1–4 properties. Stack this with a paid or points night to effectively get one night free on a multi-night stay — no points required.

Book as far out as you can. The Hyatt booking window opens 395 days in advance. For peak travel periods — summer weekends, holiday weekends, major events — inventory at Category 1 properties can thin out. Getting in early locks your room and your rate.

Target Hyatt House properties for family trips. Hyatt House locations frequently feature suite-style rooms with full kitchens, separate living areas, and free hot breakfast included for all guests. A family of four can stay comfortably for 5,000–8,000 points and skip the cost of restaurant breakfasts entirely.

Earn points on the Bilt card on Rent Day. Bilt Rewards runs a bonus promotion on the first of each month — transferring points earned that day at elevated rates. Accumulating Bilt points through rent payments (no transaction fee) is one of the most efficient ways to build a Hyatt balance.

Don't transfer points speculatively. Even though Chase and Bilt transfers to Hyatt are instant, always confirm your specific dates show award availability before transferring. Points transferred to Hyatt cannot be moved back.

Don't ignore the expiration policy. World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. A single qualifying activity — a points transfer, a stay, a credit card purchase — resets the clock. Set a calendar reminder annually to ensure you don't lose your balance.

Don't overlook Category 2 properties. At 8,000 points per night, Category 2 Hyatts often include urban full-service hotels that provide dramatically more value than the jump in points cost suggests. Once you're comfortable with Category 1 redemptions, explore Category 2 as a natural next step.

This redemption was built for the travel rewards beginner — the person who has accumulated their first 10,000–20,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt points and isn't yet sure if the whole system is real. It's also for the seasoned optimizer who wants a reliable, low-friction redemption they can execute on short notice.

Minimum points needed: 5,000 for a single night. Most people engaging seriously with Chase UR earning will accumulate this through normal spending in a single billing cycle.

In the broader ChooseFI travel strategy, Category 1 Hyatt nights serve as the building blocks — the reliable, repeatable foundation that funds your domestic travel while you accumulate larger balances for the aspirational redemptions.

**Difficulty Rating: Easy — and we mean it.** This is the redemption we'd hand to someone who just got their first travel rewards credit card and wants to see if the points are real. The score of 5/5 on Beginner Friendliness reflects every dimension of the experience: earning the points is straightforward, the transfer path is clear, the booking interface is clean, and availability is abundant. **What makes this easy:** - **No complex routing rules.** There's no geographic zone logic, no partner airline ticketing, no stopover rules to navigate. You pick a hotel, check availability, transfer points, and book. That's the entire process. - **Instant transfers.** Both Chase Ultimate Rewards and Bilt Rewards transfer to World of Hyatt instantly. You can go from zero Hyatt points to a confirmed reservation in under five minutes. - **Reliable availability.** Category 1 properties are upper-midscale hotels with large room inventories. Award availability is rarely the bottleneck at this tier. **The one thing to watch:** Points don't live in Hyatt until you transfer them — and they can't come back once transferred. Always search hyatt.com *first*, confirm your dates show award space, *then* transfer. This single habit eliminates the only real risk in the process. **Tips for first-timers:** 1. Create your free World of Hyatt account before you need it — having your membership number ready speeds the transfer process. 2. Start with a one-night stay to build confidence, then scale up. 3. Screenshot your confirmation email and points balance after booking — it feels good, and it's good record-keeping. If you've ever booked a hotel room online, you can execute this redemption. Go do it.

Category 1 primarily includes Hyatt Place and Hyatt House properties in secondary markets, smaller cities, and suburban locations. These are upper-midscale hotels with consistently good quality — clean rooms, modern decor, and amenities like free Wi-Fi. Hyatt House properties often include complimentary breakfast and kitchen suites.

However, award availability itself can vary — popular properties during high-demand weekends may show no award availability even though the price remains 5,000 points when rooms are available.

At 5,000 points for a $100 to $200 room, you are getting 2 to 4 cents per point — two to four times the value of redeeming the same Chase Ultimate Rewards points as 1 cent per point cash back. Even compared to the Sapphire Reserve portal rate of 1.5 cents per point, Category 1 Hyatt bookings consistently deliver superior value. Note that Sapphire Preferred holders transfer at 4:3, so factor in the conversion when comparing.

Category 1 Hyatt hotels are the single best entry point into travel rewards for the FI community. At 5,000 points per night with cash values of $100 to $200, you consistently achieve 2 to 4 cents per point — a redemption rate that proves the system works before you ever attempt a complex international booking. #9060. Dezeen Awards-shortlisted housing project damaged in fire

Photography and video by Andorran Police unless otherwise stated

A fire has damaged the La Querola housing development in Andorra, designed by French studio Ateliers Jean Nouvel and Spanish studio Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos.

Located in the valley of Ordino, the project is shortlisted in the housing category of this year’s Dezeen Awards and recently won the awards’ public vote.

According to Andorran Police, officials were warned at 01:45 on 22 September about the fire, which spread to all seven buildings in the uninhabited development, affecting 10,000 square metres of housing.

The cause of the fire remains unknown, reported local newspaper La Veu Lliure. No official estimate of the damage has been released, and a date for reconstruction to commence has not yet been announced.

La Querola was completed in October 2025 but had not been occupied. Ateliers Jean Nouvel and Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos designed the housing to appear as if emerging from the natural landscape, with an angular exterior that evokes stratified, eroded rock.

The housing is made up of seven irregularly shaped blocks embedded into the sloping valley.

“The client’s brief called for a residential development within a landscape of exceptional natural value, a context in which any construction inevitably enters into dialogue with a protected mountain environment,” said Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos when entering the housing into the Dezeen Awards.

“The built volume is modelled as a fragmented, stratified mass, avoiding repetitive or generic gestures in favour of a form that reads as eroded geology.”

Clad in locally sourced slate, the building’s facades feature recessed windows and openings revealing outdoor terraces.

Duplex and triplex apartments were designed to have views of the surrounding valley, with wood lining the interior surfaces to add a sense of warmth.

“Voids and cavities pierce the volume, structuring the relationship between built mass and open territory, and generating terraces that function as habitable extensions of the building’s body,” said Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos.

“Openings are conceived not as conventional windows but as deep incisions and habitable cavities – spaces of varying depth that are occupied by fireplaces, bathtubs and other domestic fixtures, making the thickness of the envelope a place in its own right and allowing the geography to penetrate the deepest corners of the interior.”

Other buildings that have been shortlisted in this year’s Dezeen Awards include an off-grid home in Japan topped with a large metal roof and a renovated house in Japan with walls streaked in clay, soil and metal powders.

#9059. Ted Turner’s Western Art Collection to Sell at Christie’s for $20 M.

With Western art rising as an ascendant category on the auction block, Christie’s is selling works from the collection of Ted Turner, the media mogul who died earlier this year at 87.

According to CNN, the works are valued at around $20 million. That means the results for Turner’s works are unlikely to near the ones Christie’s achieved earlier this year when it sold a tranche of art about the American West from the holdings of William Koch, who will also part with works by Claude Monet and Paul Cézanne this November. Related Articles RM's SFMOMA Show Changed My Mind About Celebrity Curators Julia Stoschek Collection to Celebrate 20 Years with 'Selfish in Bed' Exhibition and Düsseldorf Reopening

And yet, the Turner collection could prove an unlikely hit, if the Koch sale is any proof. Pegged at $50 million ahead of the sale, the Koch works ended up selling in January for more than $84 million once premiums fees were counted in. According to Christie’s, the Koch sale now holds the record for a single-owner sale of American Western art.

The Turner sale is set to be headlined by an Alfred Bierstadt landscape that long hung above a fireplace in the businessman’s Montana ranch. Titled Yosemite Valley (1866), the painting depicts a placid vision of a tree-lined lake under a blue sky. There are no people here, suggesting that the land was untouched and free for the taking, even though Native Americans resided here.

Turner bought the painting at Sotheby’s in 2003, when the work was given a $6 million high estimate. It was at the time considered one of the most significant Bierstadt works to head to auction in two decades. This time around, the work once again has a $6 million high estimate. Bierstadt’s current auction record, set in 2008, stands at $7.3 million.

Also coming to auction from the Turner collection are two Thomas Moran landscapes depicting the Grand Canyon. The more expensive of the two Moran paintings, titled The Inner Gorge, Grand Canyon, comes to auction with a $6 million high estimate. Moran’s auction record, also set in 2008, is $17.7 million.

“These paintings meant a great deal to our dad, not only because of their beauty, but because they reflected so much of what he loved about nature and the outdoors,” the Turner family said in a statement. “While it’s difficult to part with pieces that were so dear to him, our family takes comfort in knowing they will be appreciated and cherished by others.”

The proceeds from the Christie’s sale will go to the Turner Foundation, whose stated mission is to “protect and restore the natural systems—air, land, and water—on which all life depends.”

“It’s an honor to share this amazing collection with the world,” Tylee Abbott, Christie’s head of American art, said in a statement. “The quality and depth is remarkable, with exceptional paintings by Bierstadt and Moran representing the country’s lasting love of the American landscape. In the context of Mr. Turner’s collection, with the proceeds benefiting his foundation, this takes on even further meaning and will surely resonate with to day’s great interest in the American West.”

American Western art is often considered a fraught genre, since it tends to place settlers, cowboys, and explorers front and center, frequently in a laudatory and admiring way. The genre has looked especially fraught this year, on the 250th anniversary of the United States, as institutions across the nation revisited American history, sometimes with a critical eye.

But any scrutiny over Western art’s themes and images seems not to have impacted sales.

“There has long been a very committed group collecting Western art, many of them based in the West,” Abbott told ARTnews earlier this year. “In the last couple of decades there has been an upswell of interest in American art through a combination of bidders based in the West and coastal clients acquiring homes in the West.”

#9057. Primary Architects crowns carpenter's studio in rural China with undulating timber roof

Chinese studio Primary Architects has topped a carpenter’s studio in China with a sinuous timber roof that responds to the local mountain terrain.

Located at the entrance of Haotang Village, Xinyang, in China’s central Henan Province, the building belongs to Zhang, a local carpenter.

It was designed by Primary Architects to incorporate his studio, as well as a woodcraft workshop that is also open to the public.

Primary Architects conceived of the project, called the Carpenter’s Home, as a lightweight timber structure nestled between the mountain and the village and aligned with the natural elevation of the terrain.

The 405-square-metre building sits at the foot of the mountain and is topped by a roof made up of hyperbolic curved beams that span up to 26 metres.

This sloping roof appears to gently descend from the mountainside and reconciles the elevation difference between the mountain and the village.

“The building responds to the rolling mountain terrain naturally by treating its roof as a gentle extension of the mountain ridge stretching into the village,” Primary Architects explained.

According to the studio, its undulating outline not only echoes the surrounding mountain terrain, but also forms a structural system that enables a flexible arrangement of internal spaces.

The roof’s structural system, which is comprised of glued timber and steel joints, was created through parametric control and digital modelling.

Prefabricated in a factory, the modular roof was assembled on site to improve construction efficiency.

Inside Carpenter’s Home, the ground floor houses the carpenter’s own woodworking shop as well as an area that is open to tourists and visitors, where exhibitions and tours are held.

A mezzanine floor has a tea room for visitors. Like the rest of the space, it is lit by a series of curved skylights that were incorporated into the timber-structured roof to introduce natural light into the interiors.

The angle of each skylight was carefully positioned in accordance with the movement of the sun to allow the interiors of the studio to be well-lit during working hours.

The open interiors were designed both to accommodate the traditional wood-working practice and to function as an education centre for the craft.

An expansive staircase that doubles as seating connects the studio space on the ground floor to the mezzanine tea room.

From here, visitors can observe Zhang’s working process, as well as his tools and material samples displayed on the side walls.

Primary Architects also created a series of working benches that can be combined and divided to support various aspects of the carpenter’s work.

“The Carpenter’s Home seeks to break through the existing formal paradigms of rural construction, responding to the land, craftsmanship and daily life in a more imaginative way,” said Primary Architects.

“With contemporary timber structure as its medium, it brings traditional woodworking back to rural daily life, making the building not only a space for accommodating activities, but also a continuously unfolding lifestyle,” it continued.

“For Haotang Village, it is not only a craft workshop, but also a timber vessel embodying local memory, artisan spirit and the vision of the future countryside.”

Primary Architects is a Beijing-based architecture studio founded by Xiang Huang in 2020. This project was shortlisted for workplace project (small) category at this year’s Dezeen Awards.

Elsewhere in China, Büro Ziyu Zhuang designed a museum cluster to “blend seamlessly” into a meadow, while RSHP completed a skyscraper in Shenzhen with a “striking butterfly layout”.

Chief architects: Xiang Huang, Songyan Mao Architectural design team: Cong Liu, Zhiyan Lin, Xiaoxia Wang, Junjie Liu, Xiaofeng Zhang, Yao Lu Grade A design institute: Zhongke Architectural Planning and Design Research Institute                                                                         Wood structure detailed design: Bowen Li Construction company: Shanxi Junchen Construction Co., Ltd. Client: Xinyang Pingqiao District Juxing Agricultural Investment and Development Co., Ltd. Building area: 405 square meters

Balenciaga is currently between creative directors after Pierpaolo Piccioli, who joined in July 2025, exited the company last week, and Croydon-born designer Martine Rose doesn’t start in the role for another week. But that hasn’t stopped artist Damien Hirst from having fun with a limited-edition collection nicknamed Damienciaga.

The collaboration kicks off Balenciaga’s 25th anniversary of its Le City handbag, which was designed by then-creative director Nicolas Ghesquière, now at the head of Women’s Collections at Louis Vuitton. Le City has become one of the brand’s signature pieces that all creative directors, from Alexander Wang and Demna to Piccioli, have played with. Hirst has added his own spin with his signature spots; artworks with the motif typically sell for millions of dollars at auction. Some of the other bags feature a butterfly made out of colorful spots; a mandala of wings; stickers of pills, hearts and other logos. The spots have also extended to T-shirts, scarves, wallets, while the sticker-style motifs appear on sneakers, hoodies, caps and bomber jackets. In an e-mail interview with Vogue, Hirst says that the Le City bag is a piece of fashion that “everyone knows it, don’t they? It’s one of the most iconic bags of the last 25 years. #9055. The Elie Khouri Art Foundation Appoints Sumayya Vally of Counterspace as Architect to Design the Foundation

Elie Khouri, the French-Lebanese philanthropist and entrepreneur, who is readying his contemporary art foundation, the Elie Khouri Art Foundation (Ekaf), to open in 2028 in Dubai, has appointed architect Sumayya Vally of Counterspace to design the foundation. This year, Khouri appeared on ARTnews’s Top 200 Collectors list.

The foundation will house its own permanent collection. Although, Khouri’s art collection features paintings by Julie Curtiss and Gunther Förg along with pieces by Carol Bove, Dana Schutz, Kehinde Wiley, and more. He started collecting in the late 2000s by acquiring a work by the Lebanese painter Nabil Nahas. Since then, he has been adding 30 to 35 works every year to his collection. Khouri also sits on Tate’s Middle East and North Africa Acquisitions Committee and the Museum of Modern Art’s Media and Performance Committee. Related Articles With Protests Quieting Down But Not Forgotten, Dealers Return to the Grand Palais for Paris Photo After a Historic Electoral Rout, Trump Again Asks the Supreme Court to Greenlight His Ballroom

“Art belongs in everyday life, not apart from it. My foundation will be a home for contemporary art, open to everyone,” said Khouri in a statement. “A place to inspire, challenge and spark dialogue. Above all, I want to give something lasting back to Dubai and the wider UAE, a country that has given me so much, by helping build a cultural legacy for generations to come.”

Ekaf will be located in Jumeirah 1, where Vally will be transforming an existing villa into a home for the foundation with galleries, pavilions and a garden, as well as hospitality and outdoor spaces.

“I think of buildings as having many lives. At EKAF, we begin with a house that has already held a world within it. Its doors, cornices, balustrades, and particular ways of receiving people and separating rooms contain the traces of another life,” said Vally in a statement.

The South African architect designed the 20th Serpentine Pavilion in 2021, making her the youngest to do so.

In January 2026, the foundation named art consultant Caroline Louca as its director; Louca previously held the position of managing director of Christie’s Middle East. Louca moved to the United Arab Emirates in 2008, helping the Abu Dhabi Tourism and Culture Authority build its network of museums, including the Louvre Abu Dhabi, Guggenheim Abu Dhabi and the Zayed National Museum.

“A building shapes what people do with art before a single work is hung. Our ambition is for EKAF to be a place where art is not only shown but properly looked at, questioned and talked about,” said Louca in a statement. “Architecture has a big part to play in that: how you arrive, how you move from one room to the next, whether you end up in conversation with a stranger. Counterspace treats a building as a place people use, not an object to admire, and that is the instinct we wanted.”

#9054. ZAV Architects extends house in Iran with ombre "architectural limbs"

Photography by Parham Taghioff unless otherwise stated

A series of overlapping arches shifts in colour from terracotta to blue on this home extension on the outskirts of Tehran, designed by Iranian studio ZAV Architects.

Named Golmorad, the colourful extension transforms the residence from a weekend villa, originally designed by Iranian studio Firouz Firouz, into a permanent home in the town of Kouhsar.

ZAV Architects‘ intervention extends both ends of the home into three adjacent orchard plots acquired by the client.

Constructed from masonry, the extension is coated in plaster to blend in with the earthen exterior of the original home, while its curved geometries set it apart from its predecessor.

Aiming to appear as if organically growing from the home, Golmorad emerges as a series of overlapping arched roofs.

At one end, the vaulted extension branches into two curved forms that gradually decrease in height – one wing containing a bedroom and ensuite, and the other an open-plan kitchen, living and dining room that opens onto an outdoor pool.

Openings between the overlapping roof planes let light into the home’s interior.

“Rather than approaching the extension as either a replication of the original structure or a distinctly separate addition, the project explores a third possibility: an architecture that emerges from within the existing building itself,” ZAV Architects told Dezeen.

“This intervention can be understood as a process of grafting, in which new needs and aspirations are grafted onto the existing body of the villa, giving rise to new architectural limbs that branch out and grow from it,” it continued.

“It is as though the original building, while retaining its underlying architectural logic rooted in thick-earth construction, has developed new and distinct organs of its own.”

ZAV Architects created a gradient effect across the building with terracotta tones fading into blue, intending to strengthen the appearance of the extension growing from the home.

“The uniform colour of the original villa develops into a chromatic spectrum that radiates outward from the existing core towards the newly formed branches,” the studio said.

“This transition makes the process of transformation visible, with each segmented shell expressing a distinct stage in the building’s evolution.”

Golmorad is shortlisted in the house extension category of this year’s Dezeen Awards. It recently won the awards’ public vote alongside a playground also designed by ZAV Architects.

Last year, ZAV Architects was among the winners of the Aga Khan Award for Architecture for the Majara Residence and Community Redevelopment, a colourful domed cultural retreat on the Iranian island of Hormuz.

#9052. German Art Historian Reattributes Renoir Print Previously Believed to Be a Fake

German art historian Henry Keazor has reattributed a work on paper to Pierre-Auguste Renoir that had previously been labeled a forgery.

Keazor is the founder of the Heidelberg Forgery Study Collection (HeFäStuS), which is “a collaboration with the three state criminal investigation offices of Berlin, Bavaria, and Baden-Württemberg, which provide forgeries from their evidence rooms as loans for research and teaching purposes,” according to its website. Students at the University of Heidelberg, where Keazor is a professor of modern and contemporary art history, have first-hand access to its 140 forgeries of artists like Vincent van Gogh, Salvador Dalí, and Alberto Giacometti, so they can “can become aware of the phenomenon of art forgery and learn how to recognize it,” according to its website. Related Articles Miami Art Dealer Sentenced to Nearly Four Years in Prison for Selling Fake Warhols French Police Foil Suspected Plot to Rob Fondation Maeght After Recovering Stolen Renoirs

In 2023, a private collector decided to offer the drawing to Keazor and the HeFäStuS as part of a “household clearance”; the owner had inherited the work in the 1970s from a friend who ran a New York gallery that “classed [the work] as a fake,” per a release. The gallery had also given the medium for the work as a pencil drawing.

“While unpacking it I noticed immediately that it was a print, not an original pencil drawing,” Keazor said in a statement. That led him and his students to begin conducting research into Renoir’s works on paper and subjecting the piece to paper and microscopic analyses, which revealed that the “the structure of the autotype paper” and confirmed that “signature is written by hand with black grease chalk,” according to Keazor.

They now believe that it is hand-signed lithograph, dating to around 1899 and depicting actor and singer Amelie Diéterle. The work matches one that Renoir produced for “Germinal,” an artist portfolio that also included works by Degas, van Gogh, and Toulouse-Lautrec.

Keazor now believes that the HeFäStuS print was a test for the portfolio works, which were produced in an edition of 100 and have their signatures printed on the work as opposed to handwritten. “The solution to the riddle is that the picture is a test print made with only one of the two print stones. Since the signature evidently lay on another stone, Renoir added it by hand, thereby making the proof a fully valid work,” Keazor said, noting that such test prints are rare in art history.

The work will go on view at the Kurpfälzisches Museum in Heidelberg from November 26 to March 21 as part of an exhibition titled “Riddle around Renoir.” Afterward, the HeFäStuS and the previous owner will decide “where to keep the print in future,” per a release.

#9051. Everyone Wants This Unapproved Weight Loss Drug—And Some Have Found a Way to Get It

For all the hype surrounding GLP-1 weight loss medications like Wegovy and Zepbound, these drugs don’t work for everyone. Nearly 17% of people on these medications are considered “non-responders,” leaving them looking for a different solution. But there’s a buzzy new medication waiting in the wings. While it’s not yet approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), people are already seeking it out.

It’s called retatrutide, and it’s a triple-agonist medication, which means it acts on three different receptors in the body. By comparison, Wegovy (semaglutide) acts on one receptor, while Zepbound (tirzepatide) works on two.

Retatrutide is already being hailed as a game changer in an area of health that’s already welcomed plenty of impressive medications in the past few years. In fact, clinical trial results show that it’s so effective for weight loss that some people have dropped out of the trials because they felt that they lost too much weight.

But retatrutide is still being tested in clinical trials. Eli Lilly, which makes reatrutide and Zepbound, hasn’t even submitted the trial results yet to the FDA for approval. So this is still an experimental medication—and versions of it are being sold online for cheap.

Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California, tells SELF that retatrutide is “not really available” for use just yet, short of signing up for a clinical trial. There is no set timeline for when it will hit the market, given that clinical trial results have not yet been submitted to the FDA.

If you’ve struggled with losing weight on a GLP-1 medication or just want to pay significantly less for what appears to be the next big thing in weight loss drugs, it’s understandable to be tempted to add this to your cart. Here’s why doctors recommend resisting the urge.

Retatrutide is similar to GLP-1 medications in a few ways. Namely, it’s used for weight loss and is given once a week through an injection. Like Wegovy, Ozempic, and Zepbound, retatrutide works by reducing appetite and slowing digestion.

But retatrutide has more going on than that. This medication acts on three hormone receptors in the body—glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP), and glucagon (GCG). “This is the first one in the pipeline to work on three different receptors,” says Dr. Ali. “The theory is that the more receptors it affects, the more effective the drug will be.”

The medication is currently in phase-three clinical trials, and it’s had some impressive results that suggest it could be the most effective drug for weight loss yet. The latest clinical trial results show that participants lost an average of 28.7% of their body weight on the highest dose of retatrutide over 68 weeks. By comparison, tirzepatide users lost an average of 15% to 22.5% over 72 weeks during clinical trials, and semaglutide users lost 10% to 15% of their body weight over 68 weeks during clinical trials.

It takes a little detective work, but there are some pharmacies that are selling the drug online.

In fact, this has become such an issue that the FDA issued a press release in early February, stressing that it’s illegal to sell retatrutide (and fellow experimental weight loss medication cagrilintide) right now. That includes picking up the medication from a compounding pharmacy.

“Retatrutide and cagrilintide cannot be used in compounding under federal law,” the release states. “Additionally, these are not components of FDA-approved drugs and have not been found safe and effective for any condition.”

The FDA also noted that its officials have issued warning letters to companies that are distributing these medications.

This is hardly shocking, but doctors really want you to take a pass on using retatrutide before it’s FDA-approved.

“People should wait to take medications until they are approved by the FDA to maximize safety,” Richard Siegel, MD, codirector of the Diabetes and Lipid Center at Tufts Medical Center and endocrinologist at Tufts Medicine Weight & Wellness Center–Stoneham, tells SELF. “All scientific data in animals initially and then humans are carefully reviewed by the FDA for any signals that a medication may be harmful.”

That includes side effects you might experience now or in the future, Dr. Ali points out. Compounding pharmacies have become a gray area. They’re able to legally produce and sell their own versions of popular medications when the FDA-approved versions are in shortage. But technically this is no longer legal once the medications are out of shortage.

But compounded drugs aren’t carefully regulated and may not even have the same ingredients or concentration as the medication they’re designed to mimic, Dr. Siegel says. “While these medications may be safe, there is less oversight in their production,” he says.

Dr. Ali warns against going directly through a compounding pharmacy, noting that it’s safer to work with your health care provider if you plan to go this route. “The worst-case scenario is that you’re getting something unsafe or ineffective,” he says.

But, with all medications, Dr. Ali says it’s best to use the FDA-approved version whenever possible. “It’s going to work in a predictable way, and the side effect profile will be well-studied,” he says.

Dr. Siegel points out that there are a lot of options to lose weight right now. And, if you haven’t had success on one, he recommends talking to your healthcare provider about trying a different medication or strategy. If you haven’t had luck while working with a primary care physician, Dr. Ali suggests seeing an obesity medicine specialist who will be more knowledgeable about treatment options.

“Medications for weight management are a powerful tool that should be used together with a comprehensive lifestyle plan focusing on self-monitoring, optimal nutrition, and an exercise prescription, including both aerobic and resistance components,” Dr. Siegel says. Meaning, people who have the best results do more than take medication—they also focus on nutrition and exercise.

If you’re interested in taking a weight loss medication or your existing treatment isn’t working, talk to a healthcare provider who specializes in this area. “These medications are designed for people with significant weight to lose,” Dr. Ali says. “Most likely, they will need to be taken long-term.” That makes getting a well-vetted medication from a reputable source even more important, he points out.

#9050. Viking legend informs ring-like viewpoint on Icelandic mountain ridge

Photography by Claudio Parada Nunes

Ring of Bjólfur is a mountain viewpoint in Iceland, designed by local studios Arkibygg Architects and Esja Architecture to evoke a giant silver ring left on the alleged burial site of a legendary Viking.

Located in Seyðisfjörður, a fjord in eastern Iceland, the viewpoint improves access to a ridge on Mount Bjólfur and celebrates its varied views over the town, valley and surrounding peaks.

Arkibygg Architects and Esja Architecture‘s design draws on the legend of Bjólfur, an Icelandic Viking settler believed to have claimed this landscape and been laid to rest on the mountain.

Local lore says Bjólfur was buried on the mountain with his most precious belongings, though they have never been found. The viewpoint, therefore, evokes a ring that has been left for him.

“The medieval Book of Settlements, or Landnámabók, tells of Bjólfur, the settler who first claimed land in Seyðisfjörður and gave the mountain its name,” Arkibygg Architects told Dezeen.

“The book says little about him, but local tales tell that he was laid to rest in a burial mound high up on the mountain,” it continued.

“By ancient custom, chieftains were often buried with their treasures, silver and jewellery. Bjólfur’s grave goods have never been found, but we let our imagination run free and left him a great silver ring.”

Arkibygg Arkitektar and Esja Architecture won a competition to design Ring of Bjólfur in 2021. The project was shortlisted in the small projects category of this year’s Dezeen Awards and also won the public vote for the same category.

Ring of Bjólfur takes the form of a perfect circle, measuring 32 metres in diameter. While emulating a ring, this was also designed to “work with views in every direction”.

Positioned on a mountain ridge 650 metres above sea level, the structure was built from post-tensioned concrete with stainless steel railings, chosen for durability and for colours that emulate silver. It partially cantilevers on one side.

“The ring can be used in many ways, and the view changes depending on where you are in the circle – and whether you are standing or sitting,” said Arkibygg Arkitektar.

“The choice of materials grew from the idea of creating a silver ring, while also having to withstand wind and weather at 650 metres, with the structure being submerged in snow for parts of the year,” said the studio.

A major focus for the studios was ensuring accessibility, creating “an experience that everyone can enjoy, including wheelchair users”.

To achieve this, they designed accessible parking next to the ring as part of the project. Further general parking is located further downhill to encourage people who are physically able to walk to the platform.

“The project has been very well received, not only by visitors but just as much by local residents,” it continued.

“The ring is already strengthening tourism in the town, and it has also become part of residents’ daily lives, widely used for outdoor recreation. People walk, cycle or even ski up there to take in the view.”

The landscape surrounding the viewpoint was preserved as much as possible, with any boulders that needed to be temporarily removed lifted back into place upon completion.

“The immediate surroundings – the soil and the rocks – matter a great deal. The aim was to disturb the ground as little as possible and to repair what was disturbed.

“Other areas affected by the works were restored with native vegetation. Having one clear destination also keeps visitors from wandering across the fragile ridge.”

Other viewpoints recently featured on Dezeen include an arrow-shaped structure in Denmark by Arup and the Lech Mountain Mirror by Snøhetta in Austria.

Adobe MAX is in full swing, and after this morning's keynote, I'm left feeling pleasantly surprised. I initially arrived with slight apprehension, expecting to leave fatigued and underwhelmed by the grand kickoff, especially regarding Adobe's ever-divisive AI developments. Instead, I must confess, I'm cautiously hopeful.

It's no secret Adobe is going full send on AI, after a full fleet of AI partnerships and Firefly taking centre stage, blossoming into a full-fledged creative studio. It could all start to feel a little existential, but beaming under the stage lights, future Adobe CEO Anil Chakravarthy assures me, "Adobe will meet you where you are”. And I start to believe him.

AI has persisted as a divisive topic among creatives, but Adobe has shown a refreshing self-awareness around the tension. Emerging on stage, vice president Deepa Subramaniam wastes no time addressing that "things feel uncertain” in the wake of AI.

Assurances of “reliability” and “safety” are thrown around, honing in on Adobe's legacy as a brand shaped and "built by creatives that care about the craft”. She assures the sceptics among the crowd (myself included) that for Adobe, "Creativity isn’t a side project; it’s a way of life,” and to my surprise, the typically eye-roll-worthy sentiment soothes me. At its core, it seems Adobe hasn't forgotten about the creatives that shaped its brand.

Deepa raises some valid points. In an increasingly content-driven world, more is asked of us. The humble graphic designer is now expected to be a web designer, motion designer, and social media maverick all in one – something that Adobe's “rich learning ecosystem” can solve, according to Deepa. Creatives are trapped in a battle with waning time and resources, with demand for content ever increasing. If handled correctly, time-saving AI could offer the respite we need, but it raises a moral dilemma. Where do we stop?

#9048. Kennedy Family Joins Litigation Opposing Trump’s Triumphal Arch

The opposition to President Trump’s 250-foot triumphal arch has gained a formidable ally: the Kennedy family.

Nine members of the Kennedy family moved on Tuesday to join ongoing litigation in Washington, D.C., seeking to halt the project before construction begins. Echoing a central criticism of the project, the Kennedys argue that the arch would cast a shadow over the graves of their relatives buried at Arlington National Cemetery. The filing adds that the structure would obstruct the solemn sightline from the eternal flame at President John F. Kennedy’s gravesite, across Memorial Bridge to the Lincoln Memorial, “destroying an essential element of the gravesite’s design.” Related Articles Federal Judge Temporarily Blocks Construction of Trump's Arch, Hours After it Gains Final Approval Trump Convenes Final Review for Triumphal Arch, Seeks Immediate Start on Construction

Two of the plaintiffs, Rory and Maxwell Kennedy, children of Robert F. and Ethel Kennedy, said in a statement to the New York Times: “A towering arch casting shadows across the graves of our father, mother, and uncles, as well as the graves of so many who have served our country, would also cast a shadow over our democratic principles, undermining the safeguards established by our elected representatives to protect this hallowed ground for generations to come.”

Since its unveiling last year, the president’s pet project has advanced in fits and starts. The Trump administration has pushed it past major hurdles, only to see federal courts repeatedly impose temporary blocks. The arch, whose various proposed designs have featured a flame, gilded angels, and a sniper’s nest, received final approval last Thursday from a commission allied with Trump. Only hours later, however, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a 14-day restraining order, accompanied by a 33-page opinion that that revisited several of the project’s chief legal and practical challenges: whether it required congressional approval, the costs it would impose on Virginia and the District of Columbia, and the potential disruption to traffic around the heavily traveled Memorial Circle.

The Kennedys, in their suit, reiterated the point: “Only Congress has the constitutional power to authorize an intrusion of this magnitude. Today, members of the Kennedy family are joining with the other litigants in this case to protect this historic site — and to defend the rule of law and separation of powers.”

Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman, told the Times that it was “unfortunate to see that some members of the Kennedy family have joined the litigation against the arch, as the project is intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery.”

He continued: “The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation. We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds.”
