Cathay Pacific or Qantas Business Class via Alaska Mileage Plan — no fuel surcharges

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Picture this: you're reclining in a fully flat bed at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Pacific, a glass of Château Léoville Barton in hand, watching the Australian coastline slowly materialize through your window. The cabin is hushed. The seat — Cathay Pacific's renowned Business Class throne on the Airbus A350-1000 — cocoons you in a private pod with a sliding door, direct aisle access, and a mattress pad that makes a five-star hotel bed feel like an afterthought. This is the LAX–HKG–SYD route in Cathay Pacific Business Class. And you booked it for 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles. Now consider what the person three rows up in economy paid in cash for their seat — and what the couple beside you in business paid for theirs. A Cathay Pacific Business Class ticket on this route typically retails between **$5,000 and $12,000**. That's not a typo. Premium cabin pricing on transpacific routes is notoriously aggressive, and Australia amplifies it further because of the sheer distance involved. At 55,000 miles for a one-way business class redemption, you're extracting somewhere between **9.1 and 21.8 cents per point (CPP)** — a range that makes most loyalty program strategists stop and stare. The ChooseFI community benchmarks a "good" redemption at 1.5–2 CPP for most programs. You are obliterating that benchmark. At the high end of this range, 55,000 miles is doing the work of $12,000 in cash. That is what the FI mindset calls asymmetric value. This is also a premium *experience*, not just a premium number. Cathay Pacific consistently ranks among the world's top airlines for business class. The A350-1000 is their flagship long-haul aircraft, featuring a 1-2-1 configuration with every single seat having direct aisle access. There are no middle seats. There are no awkward climbs over sleeping strangers. There is a full dine-on-demand menu, a curated wine list, noise-canceling headphones, and a ground service team that treats you like a valued guest before you even board. For the FI traveler, this redemption represents something rare: a genuine luxury experience — the kind that recalibrates your sense of what travel can feel like — made nearly free through a well-understood system. The math works. The experience delivers. And once you've done it, you'll understand exactly why the ChooseFI community talks about this one.

Alaska Mileage Plan is one of the most valuable frequent flyer programs in the world despite being a relatively small airline. The secret is their partner award chart: Alaska uses fixed pricing for partner airline awards, meaning costs do not fluctuate with demand the way dynamic programs do. This creates structural pricing inefficiencies — especially on premium cabin routes to Asia and Oceania — that savvy travelers can exploit. Alaska has partnerships with Cathay Pacific, Qantas, Japan Airlines, Emirates, Fiji Airways, and others. The primary way to earn Alaska miles is through the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card (Bank of America), through flying, or via Marriott Bonvoy transfers at a 3:1 ratio.

Here's the insight that transforms this from "interesting" to "actionable": Alaska Airlines Mileage Plan uses a fixed partner award chart, and that chart prices Cathay Pacific Business Class to Australia at 55,000 miles one-way — a number that hasn't kept pace with the explosive cash price inflation of premium cabin fares.

Most major U.S. loyalty programs have migrated to dynamic pricing, where award costs fluctuate with cash fare demand. Alaska hasn't done this for partner awards. Their chart is fixed. That means when Cathay Pacific's cash fares spike to $12,000 during Australian school holidays or peak summer travel, your award cost stays exactly where it was: 55,000 miles. This is the pricing inefficiency at the heart of this redemption, and it's why the ChooseFI community treats Alaska Mileage Plan as one of the most valuable programs in the industry.

Alaska Mileage Plan has only one meaningful transfer partner for most people: Marriott Bonvoy, at a ratio of 3 Bonvoy points to 1 Alaska mile. That's a steep ratio — you'll need 165,000 Bonvoy points to generate 55,000 Alaska miles — and transfer times run 1 to 5 days, so plan accordingly. There is no direct credit card transfer path into Alaska Mileage Plan from Chase, Amex, or Citi, which is why the "Easy to Earn" score for this redemption is a 2 out of 5. The miles must be earned directly: through Alaska's co-branded credit card (the Alaska Airlines Visa from Bank of America), through flying Alaska or its partners, or via Marriott transfer.

This is crucial and often overlooked. Alaska charges no fuel surcharges on any partner award bookings. This matters enormously for a Cathay Pacific redemption. If you were to book the same Cathay flight through Cathay's own Asia Miles program or through British Airways Avios, you could face fuel surcharges of $400–$900 or more on top of the points cost. With Alaska, your out-of-pocket cost is taxes and fees only — typically in the range of $50–$150 depending on the routing. That's it. A $12,000 experience for 55,000 miles and roughly $100 in fees.

Alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — a benefit that is genuinely rare among U.S. programs. On the LAX–HKG–SYD routing, this means you can build a stopover in Hong Kong at no additional points cost. Spend a few days exploring one of the world's most dynamic cities — the markets of Mong Kok, the skyline from Victoria Peak, the dim sum temples of Kowloon — then board your continuing flight to Sydney. Two destinations. One redemption. Same 55,000 miles.

The 55,000-mile rate applies to both Cathay Pacific and Qantas for business class to Australia. Cathay routes you through Hong Kong (HKG); Qantas has its own metal and routing options. If Cathay availability is thin, checking Qantas can open up alternatives without changing your points cost.

Do not start at Alaska's website. Alaska's own search tool for partner availability can be unreliable for Cathay Pacific. Instead, go to ba.com (British Airways' booking site) and run a one-way business class search for your desired route — for example, LAX to SYD or LAX to HKG. British Airways and Cathay Pacific are oneworld partners, and BA's search engine surfaces Cathay award availability with remarkable accuracy. Look for "Reward" seats in the business class (Club World or equivalent) cabin. Any dates showing availability on BA.com are almost certainly bookable through Alaska as well. Screenshot or note the specific dates before moving on.

Alaska opens its award booking window 331 days in advance. If you're targeting peak travel dates — Australian summer (December–February), for example — set a calendar reminder to search and transfer 331 days ahead. Your miles also never expire in Mileage Plan, which gives you flexibility to accumulate without pressure.

Confirm you have at least 55,000 Alaska miles available. If you're converting Marriott Bonvoy points, you'll need 165,000 Bonvoy points at the 3:1 ratio. Initiate transfers at least one week before you plan to call, as Marriott-to-Alaska transfers can take 1 to 5 days.

Log into your Marriott Bonvoy account, navigate to "Transfer Points," select Alaska Airlines as the recipient program, and enter your Mileage Plan number. Transfer in increments of 3,000 Bonvoy points (yielding 1,000 Alaska miles). Do not transfer until you've confirmed availability in Step 1 — points transfers are generally non-reversible.

This redemption cannot be booked online — Alaska's web portal does not support all partner award bookings, particularly for Cathay Pacific. Call Alaska Airlines at 1-800-252-7522. Tell the agent:

Have your Mileage Plan number, passport information, and a credit card for the taxes and fees ready. The call typically takes 20–40 minutes. Agents are generally knowledgeable, but if you encounter confusion, politely ask for a senior agent or call back.

If Cathay availability is limited on your preferred dates, ask the agent to check Qantas availability to Australia at the same 55,000-mile rate. Qantas Business (The Business) has its own award inventory and may have open seats when Cathay is fully allocated.

If you're routing through Hong Kong on Cathay, explicitly ask the agent to add a free stopover at HKG. This is a program benefit, not a favor — Alaska's routing rules allow one free stopover on one-way awards. Specify how many nights you want in Hong Kong before the continuing flight to Sydney.

The best way to find Cathay Pacific Business Class award availability is through the British Airways website (ba.com). Search for one-way flights from your U.S. gateway to Sydney or Melbourne, and look for dates showing Cathay Pacific-operated flights with Business Class availability. British Airways shows oneworld partner availability more reliably than most tools.

If Cathay Pacific shows no availability on your preferred dates, search for Qantas Business Class on the same route. Qantas availability can be found through the Qantas website or through British Airways. The Alaska Mileage Plan price is the same 55,000 miles for either carrier.

Earn miles through the Alaska Airlines Visa card sign-up bonus (typically 60,000 to 75,000 miles), through flying Alaska or partners, or by transferring from Marriott Bonvoy. If transferring from Marriott, allow 1 to 5 business days for the transfer to complete before your booking window closes.

Call Alaska Mileage Plan at 1-800-252-7522 and request a partner award booking on Cathay Pacific (or Qantas) Business Class. Provide your desired dates and routing. Ask about adding a free stopover in Hong Kong if routing through HKG. The agent will process the booking and deduct 55,000 miles plus taxes and fees (typically $50 to $150).

After booking through Alaska, manage your seat selection directly through the Cathay Pacific website or app using your booking reference. Select a window or aisle seat in the 1-2-1 configuration — every seat has direct aisle access, so there is no wrong choice. You can also pre-order meals and manage other preferences through Cathay's platform.

Let's make this concrete. You and your partner want to celebrate a milestone — a sabbatical, a paid-off mortgage, financial independence itself — with a trip to Sydney. Here's exactly how this redemption plays out.

The Route: Los Angeles (LAX) → Hong Kong (HKG) → Sydney (SYD), on Cathay Pacific Business Class, with a 3-night stopover in Hong Kong.

Cash Price: A quick search on Google Flights confirms what you suspected — this itinerary in business class retails for approximately $8,000 per person during the shoulder season. During the Australian summer or holiday periods, it climbs closer to $11,000–$12,000.

Your Cost: 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles + approximately $85 in taxes and fees. Per person.

CPP Calculation: At $8,000 cash value, your 55,000 miles are worth 14.5 cents per point — more than seven times what you'd get redeeming Alaska miles for domestic economy. At $12,000, you're at 21.8 cents per point, which is among the highest CPP figures available anywhere in the U.S. loyalty ecosystem.

In Hong Kong, Cathay Pacific's The Pier Business Class Lounge awaits during your stopover travel. It's widely regarded as one of the finest airport lounges in the world — noodle bar, live cooking stations, a spa treatment center, and a wine selection that rivals dedicated restaurants.

After three days exploring Hong Kong, you reboard for the six-hour SYD leg, arriving in Sydney ready — genuinely ready, not depleted — to start your adventure.

Total cost for two: 110,000 Alaska miles + roughly $170 in fees. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: extraordinary experiences made nearly free through a system anyone can learn.

Alaska's booking window opens 331 days out. Cathay Pacific releases business class award space to partner programs in limited quantities, and the best dates disappear quickly. Set a calendar alert for 331 days before your target travel date and be ready to search — and call — that morning.

The single best technique for this redemption: run your search on ba.com before calling Alaska. BA's search engine is faster, more reliable for Cathay availability, and lets you visually scan a full month of dates. Identify two or three date options before you pick up the phone. This dramatically shortens your call time and reduces the chance of getting an agent who says "I'm not seeing anything."

Don't treat the Hong Kong stopover as a layover — treat it as a destination. Alaska's routing rules explicitly allow a free stopover on one-way awards. Two to four nights in Hong Kong costs you nothing extra in miles. Pair this with a cheap positioning flight or use it as an anchor for a broader Asia itinerary.

This is the most common and most painful mistake. Marriott-to-Alaska transfers are generally not reversible. If you transfer 165,000 Bonvoy points to Alaska and then discover no award space exists on your dates, you're stuck with miles you may not use optimally. Always confirm availability on ba.com before initiating any transfer.

Book two one-way redemptions rather than a round-trip. This gives you full flexibility on return routing — you might come back on Qantas through another city, or extend your trip without penalty.

Since there are no major flexible currency transfer paths into Alaska (no Chase, Amex, or Citi transfers), the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature from Bank of America is your most efficient earning vehicle. The welcome bonus alone can cover a significant portion of this redemption. Pair with everyday spending in categories that earn elevated miles.

If Cathay availability is closed on your dates, Qantas Business Class to Australia prices at the same 55,000 miles. Qantas' "The Business" product on their A380 Sydney routes is exceptional in its own right — and availability patterns differ from Cathay, so checking both genuinely doubles your options.

This redemption is purpose-built for the FI-minded couple or solo traveler who is willing to invest some effort in the booking process in exchange for an extraordinary, nearly free experience. If you've been dreaming about Australia and refuse to pay $8,000–$12,000 for a business class ticket — but you're also not willing to spend 20+ hours crammed in economy for a trip this significant — this is your answer.

Minimum requirements: You need 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles per person. For two travelers, that's 110,000 miles. If you're building from zero through the Alaska Visa, factor in 6–12 months of earning runway before booking.

Within a broader FI travel strategy, this redemption pairs well with a Marriott Bonvoy credit card for point accumulation and an Alaska Visa for direct mile earning. It's a medium-complexity move with a very high ceiling on value.

This redemption earns a **moderate difficulty rating** — and that rating is honest. It's not complicated in concept, but it has two specific friction points that trip up even experienced travel rewards enthusiasts. **Challenge 1: Earning the Miles** Alaska Mileage Plan's isolation from major flexible currency programs (no Chase Ultimate Rewards, no Amex Membership Rewards, no Citi ThankYou transfers directly) means you can't simply funnel points you already have into Alaska. The primary path is the Alaska Airlines Visa (Bank of America) or a Marriott Bonvoy conversion at an unfavorable 3:1 ratio. Plan your earning strategy well in advance. **Tip:** Prioritize the Alaska Visa signup bonus as your foundation, then supplement with Marriott points if needed. **Challenge 2: The Phone Booking Requirement** You cannot book this online. The call-in process intimidates people who've only ever booked travel digitally. **Tip:** Do your homework on ba.com first, have your dates ready, and approach the call as an informed customer — not someone asking for help finding availability. Agents respond well to specific, prepared callers. **Challenge 3: Cathay Award Availability** Cathay Pacific releases partner award space selectively and often in small quantities. Availability rated 3/5. **Tip:** Search exactly at the 331-day booking window, keep Qantas as your backup at the same price point, and be flexible with travel dates by even one or two days — a Tuesday departure often has inventory when Saturday doesn't. The good news: once you've done this once, you'll understand the system deeply enough to replicate it. The ChooseFI community has members who've booked this exact route multiple times. The first time takes effort. After that, it's a process you know cold.

The fastest path is the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card from Bank of America, which typically offers a 60,000 to 75,000-mile sign-up bonus. That alone nearly covers the 55,000 miles needed. You can also transfer Marriott Bonvoy points at 3:1 (165,000 Bonvoy points equals 55,000 Alaska miles) or earn miles through flying Alaska and its partners.

Yes. You would book two separate one-way awards at 55,000 miles each. You could fly Cathay Pacific one direction and Qantas the other, or mix carriers based on availability. Each one-way can include its own free stopover.

Cathay Pacific typically releases Business Class award space 90 to 330 days before departure. The sweet spot for finding availability is usually 90 to 120 days out, when airlines release unsold premium cabin seats. Check frequently, as availability can appear and disappear quickly.

Alaska allows one free stopover on one-way awards. On a routing from the US to Australia via Hong Kong, you can stop in Hong Kong for any number of days at no additional miles cost. Simply tell the agent when booking that you want a stopover in HKG. This effectively gives you two destinations for the price of one redemption.

The Alaska Mileage Plan redemption for Cathay Pacific or Qantas Business Class to Australia is one of the most extraordinary sweet spots in travel rewards. At 55,000 miles for a seat that costs $5,000 to $12,000 in cash — with zero fuel surcharges and a free stopover in Hong Kong — this redemption delivers 9 to 22 cents per point. It requires more planning and effort than a simple hotel booking, but the payoff is a genuine luxury travel experience that proves the asymmetric value the FI community builds its travel rewards strategy around.

#9045. Liverpool Biennial Announces Artist List and ‘Age of Magical Thinking’ Theme

Executive Editor, ARTnews & Art in America

The 2027 edition of the Liverpool Biennial, scheduled to open June 5 and continue through September 19, will feature 25 artists and collectives assembled in mind of a newly designated theme: “The Age of Magical Thinking.”

“The title draws on psychologist Jean Piaget’s identification of a particular period in childhood development when the lines between reality and make-believe are blurred,” reads a press release. “This is an age when the imagination is powerful; tomorrow is charged with potential and when magical thinking can help to create new, alternative worlds.” Related Articles Wildfires Destroy Ancient Korean Temple, X-Ray Reveals That Joan Miró Painted Over His Mother's Portrait, and More: Morning Links for March 27, 2025 Ontario Museum Pressured Over Indigenous Curator Ouster, Abramović Performer Sues Over Sexual Assault, and More: Morning Links for January 24, 2024

Curated by Aimee Harrison and Lucía Sanromán, the exhibition across the city in North West England will include a public art project created by local young people and artist Harold Offeh for Williamson Square as well as new commissioned works by Francis Alÿs, Tania Candiani, and Laakkuluk Williamson. Venues for the show include the Bluecoat, FACT Liverpool, Walker Art Gallery, Open Eye Gallery, Victoria Gallery & Museum, Liverpool Cathedral, and the Exhibition Research Laboratory at Liverpool John Moores University.

About the theme, Sanromán, the cocurator, said, “As someone deeply committed to socially engaged and participatory forms of art, working on a Biennial informed by the perspectives and experiences of children and young people has given Aimee and I a lens to view and face the complexity of this particularly uncertain political moment, globally.”

Harrison added, “We have an opportunity to learn alongside children about living in a world that is both hard and full of possibility.”

Banks don't always have the most exciting branding, but Brazil's Caixa Econômica Federal, a huge state-owned financial institution with 165 years of history, has a good go. The bank's rebranded for the first time in almost three decades, and the new identity ticks all the boxes.

The new identity is a fine example of a redesign done right. It feels more modern, more human and approachable, and it remains instantly recognisable, maintaining a clever hidden symbolism.

See our guides to the best laptops for graphic design and the best monitors for graphics artists if you need new tools for your own work.

The Caixa rebrand was the work of the Brazilian agency Tátil. It looked to the bank's history and its existing identity, kept the elements that people most recognised, and turned them up.

The previous logo design had lasted 29 years, so it was doing something right, but it was starting to look drab and dated with the old corporate feel of those muted colours and slightly italicised all-caps letters.

The rebrand turns the colours up with more modern, vibrant hues. Tátil suggests the blue represents enduring solidity while the orange reflects the diversity of Brazil.

The wordmark gets a cleaner lowercase design, and the core X motif, which features in the wordmark and also stands alone, gets a significant refresh.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

The letter now more clearly resembles a box when applied in repeating patterns, reflecting the bank's name, which means box (as in savings box) in Portuguese. It also continues to resemble the roof of a house, reflecting the bank's role as Brazil's biggest mortgage lender.

You can see the evolution of the institution's branding in the video below.

"While every app was busy calling itself a bank, we went against the grain and found what only Caixa has, a bank that brings together the social and the commercial, today's needs and the drive to grow," Tátil says of the rebrand.

Editor’s Note: This story originally appeared in On Balance, the ARTnews newsletter about the art market and beyond. Sign up here to receive it every Wednesday.

Franklin Sirmans Elected Warhol Foundation Board Chair: The director of the Pérez Art Museum Miami succeeds scholar Deborah Willis as chair. The foundation also announced that Cheryl Finley, Candice Hopkins, and Suzi Kwon Cohen have joined the board, and that Naomi Beckwith and Cary Davis have completed their terms. Ming Smith and Pepón Osorio Receive 2027–29 CARA Fellowship: Administered by the New York–based Center for Art, Research and Alliances, the fellowship honors “mid-to-late career artists and artists’ legacies across disciplines, with an intention to uplift voices and knowledges that offer alternatives to established historical perspectives,” according to a release. That’s how much Christie’s expects Ted Turner’s collection of Western art to bring when it comes to the block on January 20. The top two lots of the approximately 20 works both carry high estimates of $6 million: Alfred Bierstadt’s 1866 landscape painting Yosemite Valley and Thomas Moran’s The Inner Gorge, Grand Canyon. The Bierstadt also had a $6 million estimate when it came to auction in 2003, where Turner bought it at Sotheby’s.

Much has been written about the great wealth transfer and what it might mean for the art world. Will the children of aging collectors be interested in the collections their parents assembled? In several recent instances, the answer appears to have been no, given the major sales dedicated to works from the collections of Rosa de la Cruz, S.I. Newhouse, and Patricia and Robert Weis. One fascinating case study is Ronald Lauder, the billionaire cosmetics heir who has been a fixture of the ARTnews Top 200 Collectors list since it began in 1990. This month, the Financial Times and the Wall Street Journal have both published features about the merger between the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Neue Galerie, Lauder’s Fifth Avenue museum dedicated to German and Austrian modern art, ahead of the latter’s reopening tomorrow. Lately, Lauder has been lending his art to museums less frequently and has stopped giving to political campaigns, and one dealer told the FT that he had sold works at Christie’s this past summer. All of this, a spokesperson said, is part of his “long-term philanthropic and estate planning.”

The merger with the Neue Galerie, which opened in 2001, will be completed by 2028. Interestingly, the two papers diverge on the value of the collection, with the Journal saying it’s worth $1.5 billion and the FT valuing it at more than $2 billion. The Met has also raised $200 million for the upkeep of the Neue Galerie, $50 million of which comes from the Lauder family. The FT article gives insight into just how big a role Lauder’s elder daughter, Aerin Lauder Zinterhofer, who joined the Met’s board in 2023, played in the deal. Her father calls her “the merger queen,” a talent he said she gets from both him and his mother, Estée Lauder. While Met director and CEO Max Hollein told the FT that Lauder had created “not only a beloved institution but a Gesamtkunstwerk, a total work of art,” he admitted to the WSJ that the Met could technically move the works in the Neue Galerie around and that they would fall under its general collection-management policies. Lauder, however, insisted that the “Klimts have to stay in the Klimt room.”

#9042. Hauser & Wirth Now Represents rafa esparza, Maker of Adobe Sculptures and Paintings That Center Community

Hauser & Wirth, one of the largest galleries in the world, now represents Los Angeles–based artist rafa esparza, who is best-known for his installations, sculptures, and paintings made from adobe. The representation will be done in collaboration with LA’s Commonwealth and Council, the artist’s longtime gallery.

The news makes esparza one of the few living Latinx artists to be represented by a mega-gallery. Hauser & Wirth also represents Firelei Baéz and Angel Otero.

esparza will have his first solo show with the gallery in fall 2027 in one of its New York spaces, and he will debut a new work at Hauser & Wirth’s Art Basel Miami Beach booth next month. Next February, Zolo Press will publish his first monograph, titled rafa esparza: Works on Adobe. Related Articles Frieze London Brings 400-Year-Old Paintings and Collectors in Their 20s Painter Lucy Bull Joins Hauser & Wirth as Her Market Continues Its Ascent

Since 2014, esparza has been working with adobe, a building material that combines loam, straw, manure, and water, typically to make bricks that are then baked in the sun. esparza learned the technique from his father, whose family has been using adobe for generations in Durango, Mexico.

Initially, esparza began making adobe bricks that he would use to transform and challenge the art spaces in which they are exhibited: The organic materials in adobe counter museums’ strict climate control settings, while the “brown architectures,” as the artist calls his creations, take on their white cubes. Many of his interventions allow for visitors to walk directly on the adobe, which begins to crumble during the exhibition’s run.

He memorably presented these works at the 2016 Made in L.A. biennial (on an outdoor terrace) and the 2017 Whitney Biennial (in the Whitney’s ground floor gallery). The Whitney Biennial work took the form of a rotunda which esparza invited Latinx artists who were not formally part of the biennial to exhibit their work or stage performances; his collaborators included Beatriz Cortez, Gala Porras-Kim, Eamon Ore-Girón, and Nao Bustamante. The bricks used in the Whitney installation were then transported to Marfa, Texas, where they were installed on the facade and interior of Ballroom Marfa.

More recently, esparza has begun painting directly onto the adobe, creating works intimate portraits, medium-sized translations of photographs documenting important historical moments, and large-scale sculptures that are supported by metal armatures that are visible from behind. Tratos: Después de Pedro Valtierra Entre Redadas (2025–26), for example, had a US flag embedded in the metal structure, which supported a painting of a police officer manhandling a protester.

He has staged performances and had solo exhibitions at the Museum of Contemporary Art Los Angeles (in 2018), the Institute of Contemporary Art Los Angeles (2018), Performance Space New York (2019), and Artists Space (2023). With Cortez, he has had two-person exhibitions at the Americas Society in New York (2025) and the Museo Anahuacali in Mexico City (2026). Other important group shows that his work has been featured in include “Xican-a.o.x Body” at the Cheech (2023), “At the Edge of the Sun” at Jeffrey Dietch in Los Angeles (2024), the Prospect.6 triennial in New Orleans (2025), and the Latinx painting survey “Let us Gather in a Flourishing Way” at the Buffalo AKG Art Museum (2026).

“We are thrilled to join Commonwealth and Council in representing rafa esparza, an artist of profound humanity and dedication to community,” Hauser & Wirth president Marc Payot said in a statement. “rafa brings real warmth to a conceptual practice that is enormously rigorous and disciplined, drawing the earth quite literally into works that mark time and the human hand while harkening to centuries of challenging questions about ownership, agency and belonging. It will be an honor to share his art with increasingly international audiences and new generations.”

#9041. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review: A sublime remake that enhances and enchants in equal measure

Ocarina of Time is a stunning remake, but beneath its enchanting visuals and smoother controls enabled by modern technology, its core remains faithfully intact, reminding us why it still deserves to be regarded as one of the greatest games of all time.

Gorgeous, detailed and enchanting visuals

Original story and quests faithfully retained

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Since its 1998 release, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has been revered as the greatest game of all time, influencing many games, though few have ever tried to replicate its formula beyond subsequent 3D Zelda titles. That is, until Breath of the Wild blew open the doors, reinventing Nintendo's most beloved series in the modern open-world age of player agency and freedom, and its sequel, Tears of the Kingdom, reached new, unimaginable heights.

Returning to the N64 classic then might feel like a quaint relic of the past. So it's a revelation that, for the series' 40th anniversary, revisiting this beloved masterpiece remade for Nintendo Switch 2 has achieved an alchemy that rekindles the magic of what it must have been like to play Ocarina of Time for the first time 28 years ago.

This technically isn't the first time that Ocarina of Time has been remade, but whereas the 3DS update was largely a refurbishment that nonetheless stuck to the original blueprints, this Switch 2 remake has been fully rebuilt from the ground up for a new generation. The most notable difference, of course, is the art direction, which isn't just an exercise in Unreal hyper-realism. There's such attention to detail, from every blade of grass to the ridiculously detailed patterns and textures that adorn Link's hat and tunic. What's remarkable is that, unlike most modern games, all this visual density hasn't come at the expense of readability. I'd argue it's even easier to make out the cracked walls that bombs can blow up, while dungeons like the infamous Water Temple have improved architecture that makes navigation less confusing.

Despite initial divisive responses to the new Zelda character designs (but then, I'm old enough to remember the 'Celda' reactions to Wind Waker), I soon found myself enamoured by the ornate puppet-style aesthetic reminiscent of fairy-tale and fantasy media from the 80s, while the still-mute Link says a lot just with his subtle facial expressions. Admittedly, Sheik is much less androgynous than the original game (though the twist is about as non-spoiler as Luke Skywalker's father), but Zelda herself is also an improvement over the dainty damsel, with a voice distinct from the stereotypical princess in the newer games.

It's also however not a 'reimagining' in the vein of Resident Evil 2 where the original story has been adapted to a modern iteration of the series, nor is it just a primarily graphical overhaul like Metal Gear Solid Delta: Snake Eater that otherwise plays almost identically. After Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom's vast open world, trekking across Hyrule Field in a matter of minutes should feel ridiculously small, yet I have to give kudos to Nintendo for not succumbing to the temptation of stretching it out and then stuffing it with filler content, though the original side quests, from item-trading to hunting down Gold Skulltulas, are intact.

There's still a majesty to this finite adventure of a courageous boy journeying across time to save the world that still evokes so much, whether it's when you first pull out the iconic Master Sword or just stand in the middle of Hyrule Field and just make out the surrounding locations based on their distinct landmarks without the need for waypoint markers. A maximalist Final Fantasy 7 Remake approach that stretched the narrative with many more things to do would have diluted, rather than enhanced, the experience.

Still, plenty of modern additions make for a much smoother playthrough, from a free-moving camera to 60FPS performance in stark contrast to the original's barely stable 20FPS, and a clear quest log that also weaves a beautiful tapestry chronicling your adventure. There's even a dedicated jump button for Link, which admittedly took me a while to adjust to, since I kept falling off platforms when I expected an auto-jump; you can just dash instead of the original's hack of rolling around ad infinitum.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

You can also see some of the newer games' design incorporated, such as being able to quick-select items, though die-hards may lament that this means getting rid of the ability to map three items at once - it's balanced out by having some items like the lenses of truth or iron boots being mapped to respective buttons on the D-pad. Weapons like the slingshot, bow, and hookshot can also use gyro aiming, and while this was introduced in Ocarina of Time 3D, those still retained the original's first-person perspective, whereas now it's third-person like the newer titles, and you can move around at the same time.

Personally, my favourite new feature exclusive to Switch 2 hardware is being able to play the iconic ocarina songs by humming the tunes into the console's built-in microphone. For sure, it's a gimmick, but a very apt one, and I found it so much more intuitive than trying to memorise the button inputs, which is also a testament to how memorable Ocarina of Time's music continues to be.

If there is a downside to all the modern polish, it's that playing through Ocarina of Time is perhaps a little too breezy. That's certainly true of all the target and archery minigames, where, with the intuitive gyro aiming, I could get the top prizes on the first go without breaking a sweat. That also speaks to the absence of a more challenging option such as a Hero mode (you can opt to not increase your hearts, which is easier to do as you have to press a button to pick up heart containers), though an obvious choice would have been a Master Quest mode that remixes the dungeons, which could still happen post-launch either as a free update or paid DLC.

But Ocarina of Time was never as hardcore as Dark Souls; it was more about the pleasure of discovering new items you could put to ingenious use, especially against its brilliantly designed bosses, including an improved multi-stage finale. It's also nice that one of the remake's genuinely new features is a museum of all the enemies you've encountered, which lets you jump into boss rematches and even boss rushes.

If the overall changes to the game and story are relatively minor – voiced cutscenes are fine but hardly a gamechanger, though it's nice that Matt Mercer reprises his role as Ganondorf – it's really a testament that the original 1998 release was already such a defining moment in gaming that it doesn't require a radical overhaul to remind you just how great it still is. More importantly, in a post-BotW world, it's a relief that an adventure of this size can still feel epic and timeless.

#9040. Having ‘Boring’ Conversations Is Really Good for You, Psychologists Say

It’s tempting to try to bypass coworkers in the break room or limit small talk with the person waiting next to you in an effort to avoid what you suspect will be a dull conversation. But new research makes a solid argument for leaning into these “boring” chats.

The study, which was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that people who actually engage in these conversations thought that they were much more interesting and enjoyable than they expected. But beyond that, there is data to suggest that having these “boring” conversations could do your mental and physical health a solid.

“These moments are small, but they are not trivial,” Nicholas Allan, PhD, psychologist and assistant professor in the department of psychiatry and behavioral health at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF. Here’s why.

The research focused on nine experiments featuring 1,800 participants. During the experiments, participants were asked to predict how much they would enjoy talking about a range of topics they identified as boring. These included World Wars I and II, nonfiction books, math, onions, the stock market, cats, and vegan diets. These chats happened with either strangers or friends, and were in person or online.

The researchers discovered that while participants said they expected the conversations to be pretty lame, they reported afterward that they enjoyed them much more than they thought they would. This even happened when both people in the conversation thought a topic was boring.

“We decided to conduct this research because so many people avoid conversations they think will be boring. We cancel small talk, dread networking events, and assume that certain topics, like the weather, commuting, or daily routines, just won’t be interesting,” Elizabeth Trinh, lead study author and a doctoral student at the University of Michigan, tells SELF. “If conversations are generally good for us, why do we so often expect them to be dull or draining?”

Ultimately, the researchers found that being engaged in the conversation was what really mattered. “Engagement drives enjoyment more than topic does,” Trinh says. “People assume that interest comes from having a fascinating subject. But in reality, what makes conversations enjoyable is the sense of connection like feeling heard, responding to each other, and discovering unexpected details about someone’s life. Even a mundane topic can become meaningful when two people are actively engaging with each other.”

People are social creatures by nature and connecting over a topic that feels boring, like onions, is still a social connection, Aaron P. Brinen, PsyD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, tells SELF. Thea Gallagher, PsyD, clinical associate professor of psychology at NYU Langone Health, agrees. “Sometimes people will predict that a conversation will be awkward or uncomfortable. But if you try to connect and listen in a conversation, there can be great benefits,” she tells SELF.

As a result, Dr. Gallagher says she encourages her patients to have conversations everywhere they go. “Being a lifelong learner can be very powerful,” she says. “At the end of the day, connecting with humans can make us feel good.”

These chats can seem pointless, but experts stress that they’re actually not. Not only will you likely find that you enjoy “boring” conversations more than you expected, it could keep you from feeling lonely.

“Loneliness is not just about how many people someone sees. It is about whether interactions feel connecting and meaningful,” explains Dr. Allan. Side-stepping a “boring” chat is likely to increase your sense of loneliness, Dr. Brinen says. “Even if you didn’t want to be a part of that conversation, you’re still lonely,” he points out.

Loneliness on its own is a horrible feeling, but it can also have a big impact on your health. Feeling lonely or socially isolated raises the risk of a slew of serious health conditions, including heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, depression, anxiety, dementia, and early death, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). “When we find a way to be engaged with other people, it meets that need to connect with others,” Dr. Brinen says.

Over time, those small “boring” moments can build on each other, Dr. Allan says. With that, your feelings of loneliness—and health risks that can come with them—decrease.

Of course, some interactions with others aren’t great. “Not all social contact is beneficial,” Dr. Allan says. “More contact is not automatically better. What seems to matter most is whether the interaction feels respectful, reciprocal, and emotionally safe. Positive connection helps. Depleting or hostile interactions do not.”

Ultimately, Trinh recommends keeping an open mind when it comes to future conversations. “We may be missing out on connection because we misjudge how conversations will feel,” she says. “If we avoid talking to someone because we assume it will be boring—like a coworker at the coffee machine, a stranger at an event, or a neighbor in the elevator—we may be unnecessarily depriving ourselves of small moments of connection that could improve our mood and sense of belonging.”

#9039. After a Historic Electoral Rout, Trump Again Asks the Supreme Court to Greenlight His Ballroom

One day after the historic rout by the Democrats nationwide on Election Day a week ago, Trump took to the construction site of the sprawling ballroom he is constructing on the grave of the East Wing of the White House, which he abruptly razed in October 2025. “Trump invited reporters into a cavernous construction site and talked about the building project for nearly 20 minutes,” reported PBS, “without mentioning sweeping Republican defeats around the country the night before.”

The next day, Solicitor General D. John Sauer filed a petition asking the Supreme Court to greenlight the 90,000-square-foot construction project, including the 22,000-square-foot ballroom-cum-military complex. He asked the justices to rule on whether a district court, at the behest of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, erred in August in enjoining the ongoing “renovation” of the East Wing. The $400 million project has been the subject of heated debate and lawsuits since its inception. Sauer asks that the court reverse a lower court’s ruling outright or hear oral arguments, explains SCOTUSblog. Related Articles President Trump Moves to Make Oval Office a Public Monument Former Presidents Obama, Clinton Mock Trump's White House Interiors With Comparisons to 'Saddam Hussein' and 'Liberace's Bathroom'

The petition starts off by claiming the injunction was granted “at the behest of a single passerby claiming she will dislike how the new building looks.” That passerby was Alison K. Hoagland, a member of the board of the National Trust for Historic Preservation. The question of whether she has legal standing to sue is a central issue in the ongoing argument.

Sauer claims she has no standing, because the court has ruled that “mere offense, disagreement, or distaste does not qualify as a concrete and particularized injury.” He further calls the ballroom a “vital national-security effort taking place on the White House grounds with the President’s personal involvement,” arguing that it is necessary because the president faces “an onslaught of assassination attempts.” (There have been, counting generously, three.)

A consultation with the Secret Service and the National Parks Service, says the petition, determined that demolition and rebuilding would be the most cost-effective course of action and would be best “to ensure that the East Wing remains minimally visible from public spaces.”

The old structure couldn’t support the ballroom’s necessary security features, says the White House, including blast-proof windows, fortified walls, and missile-resistant columns. Nor could the underground military installation be built under the existing structure.

In April 2026, US District Court judge Richard J. Leon wrote a searing 35-page opinion, employing some 18 exclamation marks, rejecting Trump’s plan for the ballroom, saying that “the President of the United States is the steward of the White House for future generations of First Familes. He is not, however, the owner!”

The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia froze Leon’s order to allow the court time to consider the government’s appeal, outlines SCOTUSblog. A three-judge panel upheld Leon’s ruling in August but pushed its effective date back two weeks to allow the federal government to go to the Supreme Court. The majority wrote that only Congress has the power “to regulate the construction and demolition of White House structures.” A dissenting judge said Hoagland had no standing.

The Trump administration called Leon’s ruling “extraordinary and unlawful,” and Sauer asked the justices to pause the ruling, saying construction was “vitally required by national security” and that Hoagland’s “dislike” for the new construction doesn’t constitute a legal injury.

In August, a federal court ruled that Trump lacked the authority to build without Congressional approval, but the Supreme Court greenlighted the construction project in a stay issued by Chief Justice John Roberts; the Court ruled 5–4 for the White House on August 31. Roberts dissented and, along with Ketanji Brown Jackson, Elena Kagan, and Sonia Sotomayor, ruled that the construction “is likely unlawful” and that the majority decision was “no victory for the separation of powers” and that Hoagland did have standing.

In any event, there’s no turning back now, says Sauer, writing that the project is 70% complete, “and, in turn (sic), there remains no sound way now to redesign or unwind the massive superstructure that is currently standing at the White House.”

The Gate of Vanaheimr is a 3D-environment artwork created with the idea of building a fictional world that I want to see and experience. The majority of my inspiration comes from Norse mythology. I focus on creating atmosphere through light, shadow, and composition, allowing viewers to feel as if they have stepped into a world of freezing temperatures and overwhelming grandeur.

Creating artwork that can make viewers feel amazed requires what I call ‘epic scale’, which is a technique I specialise in. It focuses on placing a tiny figure in front of enormous architecture, emphasising the contrast between the small figure and the vastness of the environment.

The software I use for my entire 3D workflow is Blender, with additional adjustments and post-processing done in Photopea (see our guide to the best 3D modelling software, and you might want one of the best laptops for 3D modelling).

First, I arrange pre-made models to establish the composition, setting up the camera and gradually adding surrounding details. The enjoyable part is experimentation. If something doesn’t fit, you will immediately notice.

Most of the textures came from Poly Haven and photos I’d captured. I use Ambient Occlusion, Bevel and Fake Bump Nodes to add depth and dimension.

I prefer creating the lighting while working on the composition, which allows me to observe the direction of light interacting with the entire scene. Lighting can hide many imperfections, even when models aren’t perfect.

I’m usually searching for the lighting angle that makes the image look its best. I often use Sky Texture, Spot Lights, and Environment Texture, sometimes combining them to achieve the desired atmosphere.

The final step after rendering the raw image from Blender is additional editing in Photopea (which has a similar workflow to Photoshop). I add fog, smoke and dust, making small lighting adjustments to enhance the overall mood.

However, I don’t usually rely heavily on colour grading, because I’m generally satisfied with the colours and atmosphere already achieved through compositing in Blender.

#9037. Mori AI home robot "resembles a contemporary table lamp"

Robotics startup OKA has released a lamp-shaped artificial intelligence robot designed to offer companionship by greeting people, dancing to music and playing nature sounds.

Mori by OKA (One Kind Artificat) is 26.4 centimetres tall, with a cloth-covered base and an illuminated, dome-shaped head that lifts to reveal cartoonish eyes that blink and swivel.

According to OKA, Mori “resembles a contemporary table lamp” and was designed to “help people feel calmer, more at ease, and more connected to the world around them”.

“We wanted Mori to feel like a familiar object in the home rather than an unfamiliar machine,” OKA told Dezeen. “Many robots look technical, mechanical, or overly human, while a lamp is something people already live with comfortably.”

The robot exists in two modes: a lamp setting, when it’s compact and at rest, and a responsive setting, when the head is lifted and tilted.

Powered by the start-up’s proprietary AI system, the robot’s responses include playing audio informed by rain and other nature sounds, changing the colour of its lamp top and performing nonverbal communication through multi-axis neck and body movement.

Users tap the top of Mori’s head and it “retracts its face and becomes a quiet lamp”. As another part of its calming offerings, grabbing its base triggers a breathing exercise.

It also makes small sounds as part of these interactions.

“Mori’s soft silhouette and tactile materials let it blend into domestic interiors,” said OKA. “Its warmth, brightness, and subtle changes can suggest comfort, curiosity, or calm, which lets Mori express itself through illumination, sound, and movement instead of screens or conversation.”

According to the company, Mori will remember occupants, routines, and interaction history and adjust its behaviour accordingly, such as using “judgment to decide when to proactively engage or remain quiet”.

The AI model is based on the concept of Attentive Intelligence, built upon research by OKA co-founder Weizhe Chen. Attentive Intelligence is an emerging framework within AI, wherein a model is proactive versus reactive to prompts.

“It reads the room before responding and weighs whether to join in, so sometimes a small nod is enough and sometimes it stays quiet,” said OKA.

“Its responses are shaped by VIBE (Vitality, Interaction, Bonding, Emotion), an inner state that drifts with time and experience, so the same greeting can come out lively one day and gentle the next.”Mori comes in a variety of soft colourways and is rechargeable with a 2.5-hour battery life. However, OKA suggests keeping it plugged in.

OKA was founded in 2024 in Cambridge, Massachusetts, by entrepreneur and designer Hua Wang and robotics researcher Weizhe Che. The company is focused on creating robotic projects that “integrate seamlessly into human life rather than forcing human life to adapt to technology”.

OKA plans to release five major “artifacts” or products in its lifetime, according to the team. The Mori robot is the first.

Mori joins a growing number of home robots released recently with “embodied AI” – or the act of inserting an AI model into a robotic body.

Other home robots include the Droxel “droid butler” and Neo, a humanoid robot dressed in a cloth bodysuit.

#9036. With Protests Quieting Down But Not Forgotten, Dealers Return to the Grand Palais for Paris Photo

As soft music crooned through the halls of a softly lit, glittering Grand Palais in Paris Tuesday evening, VIPs trickled in for a private dinner hosted by the Prix Pictet as part of the Paris Photo fair, which opens to the public on November 12. Wandering through the fair’s aisles featuring 246 exhibitors this year, it was unsettling to imagine that just three weeks ago, Art Basel Paris had to evacuate the very same venue. Booths were dismantled early, the night before protests planned for October 24. The fair’s closure two days sooner than planned was unprecedented and came as a shock to many, ultimately necessitating Art Basel to offer a 20 percent discount on booth fees to all exhibitors. Related Articles The Art Market Wanted to Go Global--It Didn't Plan for Everything That Means Dealers Scramble to Get Works Out of Paris After Surprise Art Basel Announcement

Though civil unrest in France has not returned to the fever pitch experienced in October, and the government has exerted some greater control over the situation, demonstrations are continuing here, in an effort to bring attention to rising costs of living and under-funded public schools. How then, are Paris Photo organizers and exhibitors navigating it all?

“We are, of course, watching the situation closely to see how things evolve,” Photo Paris director Florence Bourgeois told ARTnews. “At this stage there is nothing new to report, and nothing alarming. In fact, for two weeks the demonstrations have been taking place peacefully, and generally in the east of Paris. So we are not alarmed, and we remain vigilant so that we can respond if necessary.”

Bourgeois said that the fair has closed early once before, after the 2015 terror attacks in Paris; despite lacking appropriate insurance at the time, organizers reimbursed 20 percent of booth fees. “But that’s no indication of what might happen in 2026,” she said. “It was an extremely different situation to that of the current protests.” (She declined to comment further on the fair’s current insurance policy.)

“If we ever do face something along those lines, our decision would be made based on protecting everyone’s safety. That’s the priority,” she added.

For German gallerist Thomas Zander, who exhibited at the shortened Art Basel Paris and is now back for Paris Photo, the city is the biggest draw. “It’s strange in a way, but I love Paris,” he said about returning so soon. He characterized this year’s Art Basel Paris as inspiring a “difficult feeling” in him. The early closure cost him “two good days” of sales, he said, adding, “Now we are in a better situation this week, and there are not so many demonstrations in the center, and it’s quieter than the week of Art Basel Paris.”

At the fair, his booth has on view what he described as “museum-quality works” because “all the museum people come here, to Paris Photo.” This includes a set of six dye transfer unique master prints by William Eggleston from 1968 to 1973, priced together at €1 million ($1.11 million); a rare series of 41 vintage gelatin silver prints of pinball machines by Candida Höfer, which are being sold as a single display for €600,000 ($665,570); and 16 works from Zoe Leonard’s “Analogue” series (1998–2009) about New York’s changing Lower East Side and offered for a total of €140,000 ($155,300).

In terms of price point, Paris Photo is a much more accessible fair than Art Basel Paris, where artworks are frequently offered in the six-, seven-, and even eight-figures. While some exhibitors at Paris Photo might make a sale over $1 million, the prices for other works can start as low as a few hundred dollars, with artist-signed books even costing under $100.

Despite having lower prices than the markets for contemporary painting and sculpture, the photography market has not been immune to the rest of the cooling that the global art market has faced in the past few years, according to Bourgeois, who said that more than ever closing a sale “comes down to a question of quality, which is why we’ve worked hard to represent the best that photography has produced over the last 200 years.” Even still, “for top quality photographic works, prices remain high and are not falling,” she added.

Several dealers said that approachability and a perceived distancing from the billionaire’s club of collectors often play to the favor of Paris Photo, as protestors demand greater social equality. (In October, there were calls to protest outside Art Basel Paris and “take back the Grand Palais” from the wealthy few.)

“By taking part in a fair, we are not ignoring the realities of life around us, nor disconnected from it,” Bourgeois said. “We also represent part of the economy: there are galleries that make a living from this, that represent artists, give them visibility and support them by selling their work. I believe all of this is very important.”

“I’ve been hearing from a lot of people that Paris Photo doesn’t have quite the same image as Art Basel,” Paris dealer Anne-Laure Buffard said. “It’s a fair that has less of a connotation symbolizing a certain concentration of wealth, or an elitism reserved for the extremely rich.” With the recent closure in mind, in light of the protesters who have calmed, Buffard said, “We’re all trying to stay optimistic.”

She is presenting salt-washed and painted, crystalline photographs taken in the Dead Sea, on the border between Israel, Jordan, and the West Bank, by Ilanit Illouz, priced from about $2,000 to $17,750; as well as painted and drawn photographs by Vasantha Yogananthan chronicling the impact of tourism on the northern Indian region of the Himalayas, priced between about $3,300 and $11,100.

Elsewhere, Pace Gallery is offering a jewel of a 1926 vintage gelatin silver print on a treated postcard by André Kertész for $500,000. It is thought to be one of only six or seven in the world. On the more affordable end, medium-sized still life photographs by Kiki Smith have already sold for $8,500 apiece.

“It’s been a very strong first day, with a number of significant sales made in the first hours of the fair, reflecting the strong demand for photography,” Pace senior vice president Lauren Panzo said. “It’s particularly encouraging to see so many new collectors coming through” alongside existing clients.

On Tuesday evening, Panzo told ARTnews that while the gallery has considered the possibility of further interruptions to the fair from ongoing protests, she is “personally not concerned—there are always protests here,” and the current ones seem to be more “under control.” She expects that over the weekend there will be lines to get into the Grand Palais as there have been in years past. “People in Paris love photography. I think there’s such a love for this medium. It’s so accessible,” she said. “Photography is different.”

Greeting visitors upon entering the Grand Palais is a large installation of works spanning the career of German photographer Thomas Ruff, a collaboration by his five galleries: David Zwirner, Konrad Fischer, Mai 36, Lia Rumma, Sprüth Magers. Other highlights include a selection spotlighting women photographers, who now make up 38 percent of artists represented at the fair, up from 20 percent when the program launched in 2018, and around 100 newly acquired and unseen photographs from the Centre Pompidou’s collection. The Prix Pictet also now has a dedicated booth, featuring works by this year’s winner: Valérie Belin’s Still Life, showing an accumulation of plastic goods and memento mori, and Alfredo Jaar’s The End, which documents the receding Great Salt Lake in Utah.

A curated selection of artworks spread throughout the Grand Palais represents every decade since the creation of photography, which is marking its 200th anniversary this year. On one end are Serge Plantureux and Atelier 41, which have on view works by the pioneer photographer, Joseph Nicéphore Niépce, who made what is considered the world’s oldest known existing photograph, View from the Window at Le Gras (1825).

Among contemporary examples in the Voices section is an installation of new works by Alessandro Calabrese in the booth of Milan’s Viasaterna gallery. Priced between $2,440 and $8,430, these dreamy images are made by printing on the “wrong” side of glossy photo paper, resulting in painterly, electric-hued prints. “In the end, it creates a sort of watercolor painting, but [made] automatically,” Calabrese told ARTnews. “All my research is based on looking for the limit of the figurative side and the realism in photography, and trying to challenge it.”

Make precise cuts in wood, acrylic and metal with our pick of the best CNC machines.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The best CNC machines let you make precise, repeatable cuts in metal, wood and other materials right from your desk, and we think it's the start of a revolution in small business crafting. The latest generation of desktop CNC machines are typically enclosed, work quietly, and are automated enough that you don't need to be a trained machinist to use them.

They do cost a fair few bob, starting at $1,199 but venturing into the $5000 territory, so they aren't craft machines for the people at this stage.

CNC machines work in the opposite way to the best 3D printers or the best UV machines. Rather than building an object up layer by layer, they carve it out of a solid block with a spinning cutter. That means you can create strong, precise parts in metal, wood and stone, built to last.

I've picked the best CNC machines available to consumers today, along with two promising Kickstarter models that we're excited to see materialise.

Makera launched as a company in 2019, with the aim of lowering the cost of precision desktop manufacturing. Two years later they made a big splash with their first CNC machine, Carvera, which debuted on Kickstarter and is still popular today: we've put it as number two on our list. But the Z1, which launched in 2025, again on Kickstarter, has shaken up the market by driving the cost of entry even lower.

Despite being the cheapest on this list, it does everything a beginner will need. It's built on a cast aluminium frame and fully enclosed. It offers automatic probing and levelling, a built-in camera you can connect to your phone, and an air blast that clears chips as it cuts. And its software offers one-click toolpaths, so you don't need to learn complex software before you get started.

The tradeoff for the cheap price is that it's more limited in terms of size and power. The 200 x 200mm work area also means you can only work with small parts, while the 150W spindle requires shallow, patient passes in metal. Another drawback compared to the Carvera is that you'll need to change tools by hand via a quick-release lever.

If you're seeking your first CNC machine, though, this is our top pick.

The Carvera has been around since 2021 but remains Makera's flagship. With this CNC machine you get a six-slot automatic tool changer, letting you swap between different milling bits mid-job, saving you from having to fiddle about with your hands. It's capable of cutting and milling wood, plastics, acrylics, carbon fiber, FR4 (PCBs) and non-ferrous metals like aluminum and brass.

Other features include an automated wireless probe for surface mapping and bed leveling, built-in dust collection and a 2.5W laser for engraving and engraving and PCB labelling. The enclosed design keeps noise to around 65dB: not silent, but still quiet for a CNC. You can cut wood, plastics, PCBs and non-ferrous metals like aluminium and brass well, and if you want to make circuit boards at home, Makera will sell you a dedicated bundle for that.

The 200W spindle is modest, and Makera doesn't recommend you try to cut steel or titanium. And while the crowdfunded rivals below promise more power at a similar price, remember that they're not actually available yet. This is, and has years of independent tests and positive customer reviews behind it.

Twotrees produces affordable laser engravers and 3D printers, and the ED1 is its latest CNC machine. It offers automatic tool changing, like the Carvera above, but at a more affordable price.

While the ED1 is closer to shipping that the CNC machines below, it's only available for pre-orders, which will ship from January 2027. That means it hasn't yet been independently tested, so at this stage we can only go on the specs.

They do, though, look very impressive. The five-slot changer is said to swap cutters in around 10 seconds, the 600W spindle has three times the power of the Carvera's – Titanium is on its list of materials – and the 300 x 200mm work area is a decent size. You'll also get auto levelling, a built-in camera and AI-assisted software.

These CNC machines haven't shipped yet, so we haven't included them in our main list. Both are due to arrive in early 2027, though, so assuming all goes well, they're well worth keeping an eye on.

Infimaker was founded in Shenzhen in 2024 by former DJI engineers, and the K1 is not just its CNC machine but its first product at all. The Kickstarter closed in September, but late pledges are still open, with delivery estimated for February.

So what's different about this one? Well, most desktop CNC machines are 3-axis: the cutter moves left and right, back and forth, and up and down. This adds two more axes: tilting and rotating the workpiece as it cuts, which allows you carve complex shapes like impellers and sculptures in a single setup, rather than having to re-clamp the part by hand.

This CNC machine features a 1.5kW spindle, a six-tool automatic changer and AI-assisted software. Be aware, though, that you'll need a strong desk, as this weighs a hefty 110kg.

The Tooldance X1 is a crowdfunded CNC machine with a 1.5kW permanent-magnet spindle that aims to deliver high torque at low speeds, enabling you to work with stainless steel and titanium. It promises the largest work area on this list at 400 x 265 x 180mm, along a nine-slot automatic tool changer that uses RFID tags to track its cutters, and sensors that measure your stock for you.

The Kickstarter is still live, with delivery estimated for March 2027. So as you'd expect, there've been no independent tests yet. If you're in the US, also note that the spindle's output drops to around 1kW on a 120V supply.

CNC machines and 3D printers work in opposite ways. A 3D printer is additive: you build up objects up layer by layer, usually from plastic. A CNC machine, in contrast, is subtractive. You begin with a solid block of material and it carves sections away with a spinning cutter.

If you want to make parts from wood, aluminium, brass and even steel, a CNC machine is a better choice than a 3D printer. You'll typically get a stronger, smoother finish than most 3D prints. Be aware, though, that it's much more difficult to make hollow or enclosed shapes than with a 3D printer.

A 3-axis machine moves the cutter left and right, forwards and back, and up and down. This is usually all you need for flat parts, signs and reliefs. With 4-axis machine, you also get a rotary attachment that turns the workpiece. This allows you you to carve around cylinders. A 5-axis machine adds the option to tilt the part, so the cutter can reach almost any angle in one setup. This makes it easier to make complex shapes.

Imagine stepping off a long-haul flight, exhausted and slightly rumpled, and walking into the Park Hyatt Tokyo — the hotel made iconic by *Lost in Translation* — and being handed a room key to a suite with floor-to-ceiling views of Mount Fuji. Or picture arriving at the Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme, where Haussmann architecture frames your every view and the concierge greets you by name. Or standing in the Park Hyatt New York, 25 floors above Midtown, watching the city sprawl in every direction from a room that costs more per night than most people's monthly car payment. Now imagine paying nearly nothing for it. That's the power of the World of Hyatt award chart — and the Park Hyatt sweet spot is one of the most emotionally resonant redemptions in all of travel rewards. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community's collective jaw drop: a single night at the Park Hyatt New York regularly retails for **$1,200–$2,000**. The Park Hyatt Tokyo commands **$800–$1,500** per night. The Park Hyatt Paris? Easily **$1,000+** in peak seasons. Yet every one of these properties sits at **Category 7**, bookable for just **25,000–30,000 World of Hyatt points** per night. At 30,000 points for a $1,500 room, you're extracting **5 cents per point (cpp)** — in a world where most loyalty programs are engineered to deliver 1–1.5 cpp if you're lucky. The CPP range for this sweet spot runs from **2.7 cpp all the way to 6.7 cpp**, meaning even a modest redemption delivers 2–3x the value of a typical points transaction. Why does this gap exist? Because Hyatt uses a **fixed award chart** anchored to categories, not real-time cash pricing. When demand spikes — New Year's Eve in New York, cherry blossom season in Tokyo, Paris Fashion Week — cash rates explode upward while your points cost stays locked. The hotel's revenue management team can't touch your award rate. That's the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community is built to exploit. This isn't aspirational travel for the ultra-wealthy. This is FI-minded travel: understanding the system, earning points intentionally, and converting them into experiences that would otherwise require an extra year of saving. A two-night stay at the Park Hyatt Tokyo for 60,000 points — points you can earn from a single credit card welcome bonus — is the kind of redemption that reframes what financial independence actually looks like in practice.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: World of Hyatt prices its awards on a fixed category chart, while Park Hyatt properties punch dramatically above their category ceiling in cash value.

Here's how the Hyatt award chart works: properties are assigned to Categories 1 through 8, with standard award nights running from 3,500 points (Cat 1) up to 45,000 points (Cat 8). Park Hyatt properties — the absolute pinnacle of the Hyatt portfolio, a collection of ultra-luxury city hotels that competes directly with Four Seasons and Ritz-Carlton — fall predominantly into Category 7 (25,000 points/night) and Category 8 (40,000 points/night). But unlike Four Seasons or Ritz-Carlton, which have largely abandoned fixed award charts in favor of dynamic pricing that tracks cash rates, Hyatt has held the line on fixed pricing. This is a rare and increasingly endangered feature in hotel loyalty, which is exactly why the ChooseFI community should be actively using it now.

The transfer path that makes this accessible is Chase Ultimate Rewards. Chase transfers to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, and the transfer is instant — meaning you can spot availability, transfer your points, and book within minutes. Bilt Rewards also transfers to World of Hyatt at 1:1, also instantly, giving you two powerful earning pipelines into the same program.

This matters enormously for strategy. Chase Ultimate Rewards is arguably the most flexible points currency in travel rewards — earned through cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve — and the fact that it flows directly into Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio without any degradation is a genuine gift. 30,000 Chase UR points become exactly 30,000 Hyatt points. No conversion fees, no waiting period, no surprises.

Another critical mechanism: World of Hyatt charges zero fuel surcharges on award redemptions. With hotel awards this is less of an issue than with airline programs, but it reflects Hyatt's broader philosophy of clean, predictable award pricing. What you see is what you pay — taxes and fees on hotel awards are typically minimal.

Now layer in Globalist status, and the value compounds further. World of Hyatt's top-tier elite status (earned at 60 qualifying nights per year) unlocks complimentary suite upgrades at check-in (space available) and free breakfast for two guests daily. If you're a Globalist checking into the Park Hyatt New York and you receive a suite upgrade, you've just added hundreds of dollars of daily value to an already exceptional redemption — and free breakfast at a Park Hyatt can easily run $60–$90 per person.

The booking window is 395 days out, which matters for high-demand dates. The Park Hyatt Tokyo during cherry blossom season (late March to early April) or the Park Hyatt New York around major events will see award availability evaporate quickly. Understanding that you can search and book nearly 13 months in advance is your single biggest tactical advantage for locking in prime dates.

Finally, it's worth understanding what you're getting at the property level. Park Hyatt is not Hyatt Regency or even Andaz — it's Hyatt's true ultra-luxury tier, with butler service, marble bathrooms, curated art collections, and some of the best city-view room designs in the world. The points-to-experience ratio here is genuinely exceptional.

Before anything else, inventory what you have. Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards account and note your balance. You need a minimum of 25,000 points for a Category 7 Park Hyatt night or 40,000 points for a Category 8 property. If you're planning a multi-night stay, multiply accordingly — 30,000 points per night at a Category 7 is a reasonable planning number that covers most Park Hyatt sweet spots.

Decide which property you're targeting. The flagship three for this redemption are:

Go to hyatt.com and use the hotel search. Enter your destination city and dates. In the rate filter, select "Use Points" to display award availability. The site will show you the points cost per night — if you see the Category rate (25,000 or 40,000), availability exists. Note that peak and off-peak pricing can adjust these numbers slightly, so check a few date combinations.

Search flexibly. If your first-choice dates show no availability, shift by a day or two — award inventory at Park Hyatt properties is released in small blocks and replenished irregularly. Use the calendar view to scan multiple dates at once.

This is critical: do not transfer points until you've confirmed award availability exists on your target dates. Point transfers to Hyatt are irreversible. Once you've found open award space, note the exact dates and room type, then move immediately to Step 4.

If you're using Chase Ultimate Rewards: Log into your Chase account, navigate to "Pay Yourself Back" → "Transfer to Travel Partners" → select World of Hyatt. Enter the amount (in increments matching your need) and confirm. The transfer is instant — your Hyatt account will reflect the points within minutes.

If you're using Bilt Rewards: Navigate to the "Rewards" tab, select "Transfer Points," choose World of Hyatt, and confirm. Also instant.

Return to hyatt.com immediately after the transfer confirms. Search your target dates again, select the award rate, and complete the booking. You'll pay any applicable taxes (typically modest for hotel awards) and your points will be deducted. Print or screenshot your confirmation.

Award inventory at Park Hyatt properties is genuinely limited. If you lose availability between searching and transferring (rare, but possible), call the World of Hyatt member line (1-800-304-9288) — agents sometimes have access to inventory not visible online. Alternatively, set calendar reminders to check again; properties occasionally release additional award space within 30 days of arrival as booking patterns clarify. Remember: the booking window opens 395 days out, so planning ahead dramatically expands your options.
