#8969. Can You Actually ‘Boost’ Your Metabolism?

Few bodily processes are as focused on and as misunderstood as metabolism. It seems like just about everyone wants to “boost” or “speed up” their metabolism in the hopes of burning more calories and, as a result, losing body fat. In reality, this is not an easy task, but you wouldn’t know that from the countless TikToks claiming it’s as simple as taking a shot of apple cider vinegar, hopping into an infrared sauna, or braving a cold plunge.

The truth? Many of these supposed hacks don’t have much research backing them up, and the ones that do won’t meaningfully move the needle when it comes to your weight. Improving your metabolism actually boils down to a few basic tenets that aren’t flashy or sexy but can have long-term benefits for your overall health and well-being. We’ll get into all that, but first, a little background on what your metabolism even is.

Metabolism is commonly thought of as the mechanism that controls your weight. Having a “fast” metabolism means your body burns calories rapidly, making it easier to maintain or lose weight, while having a “slow” metabolism means you gain pounds more easily and have a harder time taking them off. This isn’t wrong, per se, but it doesn’t tell the whole story. Your metabolism is the way your body turns food into energy. This energy is then used to power your heart and lungs, build and repair tissue, regulate hormones, and perform other critical functions.

Put more succinctly, “metabolism is all the chemical processes that keep our body alive and functioning,” explains Jonathan Gabison, MD, an assistant professor of family medicine at the University of Michigan who is board-certified in obesity medicine.

For example, about 20% of the energy your metabolism provides goes to your brain, building neurotransmitters and keeping signals going, so having an efficient metabolism is critical for cognitive health.

In short, yes. Your metabolism is influenced by loads of factors, from genetics and age to weight. But that doesn’t mean your metabolism is fixed. It’s actually highly modifiable, says Shebani Sethi, MD, a clinical associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University and the founding director of the world’s first academic metabolic psychiatry clinical program.

That said, taking shots of apple cider vinegar in the morning or picking up “metabolism-boosting” supplements won’t do the trick. Research shows that improving your metabolism requires consistent long-term habits. Here are five that can make an impact.

Every time you move your body, it burns calories and raises your metabolism—both during the moment and for a period afterward. Think of your metabolism like a pie: Two thirds of the energy you use every day is devoted to keeping you alive (that’s your basal metabolic rate), and the rest goes toward digesting food and moving your body. Being more active is the most straightforward way to up your metabolism. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity a week.

This can include dedicated exercise, like a jog, hike, or workout class. (The CDC recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity a week.) But it also extends to all the movement you do outside of formal exercise, known as NEAT (non-exercise activity thermogenesis). Increasing your daily step count, prioritizing physical hobbies like gardening and walking your dog, or even taking on more household chores and grocery runs all count toward upping your overall movement.

Strength training helps build and maintain muscle mass. Muscle tissue is metabolically active, which means sustaining it burns more calories than maintaining fat tissue. Therefore, having more muscle mass will give your metabolism a slight boost.

By strength training you’re also improving your overall health. For instance, since muscle tissue uses the majority of the glucose in your bloodstream, more muscle mass can increase your body’s capacity to use glucose and help prevent blood sugar spikes. Plus, research has shown that having more muscle helps improve insulin sensitivity, including in individuals without diabetes.

Those same CDC exercise guidelines suggest including at least two days of strength training every week. That can include body-weight moves like push-ups and lunges; lifting weights with dumbbells, kettlebells, barbells, or cable machines; or utilizing resistance bands. Dr. Gabison says what’s most important is being consistent with your exercise routine, so it’s best to choose workouts you’re likely to stick with. And remember, if you’re just starting out, it’s important not to push yourself too hard early on and risk injury.

Protein is having a major moment right now. While things may be getting a little out of hand (hello, protein popcorn), consuming sufficient amounts of high-quality protein has well-established benefits for your metabolism. That’s because the nutrient is the building block of muscle, so eating enough of it helps support muscle growth and maintenance, especially if you’re resistance training.

Protein also has the highest thermic effect of all three macronutrients, meaning digesting it burns more calories than carbohydrates or fats. Plus, it’s the most satiating macro, so increasing your protein intake can help you feel fuller and fend off cravings, which may help with weight management.

However, balance is key. Sun Kim, MD, MS, a board-certified endocrinologist and associate professor of medicine at Stanford, says doctors and health care providers have different viewpoints on how much protein is enough for optimal health. In her opinion, “most Americans eat plenty of protein without trying,” she says, cautioning that consuming excessive amounts won’t magically speed up your metabolism and could even worsen insulin sensitivity in some cases. So unless you’re extremely active, there’s no need to get hundreds of grams a day.

For most healthy adults, the recommended dietary allowance for protein is 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight per day. That means a 120-pound person needs roughly 43 grams of protein a day, which is about what you’d find in two four-ounce hamburger patties. If you incorporate some protein into every snack and meal throughout the day, you should easily hit the mark. That said, some groups need more. People who are pregnant, breastfeeding, or highly active may need up to 2 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day. Older adults and those taking GLP-1s should also be mindful of their intake, as reduced appetite can lead to inadequate protein intake and muscle loss, particularly when coupled with reduced physical activity.

An often-overlooked habit for better metabolism is getting quality sleep. A lack of sleep dysregulates your metabolism, causing a cascade of issues, including worsened glucose management, more intense hunger the next day, and reduced energy expenditure. (Sleepy people are less likely to move their bodies.) When this happens consistently, it can lead to an increased risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. Sleep also has an impact on hormones that can slow down the metabolism.

There isn’t a specific number of hours you should sleep each night, but research shows that most adults do best with seven to nine hours of quality rest most evenings.

Prolonged stress keeps your cortisol (stress hormone) levels chronically elevated, which can break down muscle tissue and slow your metabolism. Constantly pulling out your hair can also disrupt your appetite-regulating hormones, triggering cravings that may prompt you to eat more. All of these things can affect your weight. Research shows chronic stress can increase your risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and related cardiometabolic complications too.

There is, sadly, no quick fix for reducing stress, so some trial and error might be required to figure out what works best for you. Some places to start are doing yoga, meditating, practicing breathing exercises, going for walks outside, journaling, spending time with loved ones, engaging in relaxing hobbies, or starting therapy to talk through whatever is weighing on you.

Sure, supporting a healthy metabolism can increase the number of calories you burn and help with weight management. But it can also improve what’s known as your metabolic health, which encompasses measures such as blood pressure, cholesterol, insulin sensitivity, and total body fat. Having good metabolic health is essential for preventing chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes and heart disease. The healthier your metabolism, the more calories you burn and the better your metabolic health.

#8968. What Does Dark Green Poop Mean? Causes, Diet, and When to See a Doctor

Bum nuggets typically sport a classic brown, so glancing back into the loo and spying on greenish-colored poop can throw you for a loop.

Most of the time, green poop reflects a leafy diet or your body’s unique way of breaking things down. But if the green becomes a recurring (fecal) matter, it might be something else.

Continue reading to learn more about poop color, its meaning, and when it’s time to make an appointment with a healthcare provider.

Spotting green or another unexpected color in the toilet can be startling, but it’s more common than you might think. From dietary influences to your body’s digestion speed, several factors can change poop from earthy tones to other shades. Let’s check some out.

Are you chowing down on lots of green leafy veggies like spinach, kale, or broccoli? These foods are high in chlorophyll, which can dye your doodles green. Chlorophyll doesn’t always break down entirely before reaching your intestines, meaning it passes through your system and colors your stool green.

Have you ever had a St. Paddy’s Day-themed milkshake or a brightly colored cake? Artificial colors in foods and drinks can change poop from brown to green. It’s not magic! It’s just the dye in green food passing through your gut unchanged.

When your digestive system processes food too rapidly, it doesn’t allow for the full breakdown of bile, a yellow-green fluid that aids digestion. This often results in a greenish stool, especially during fast-moving episodes of diarrhea.

Have you recently been taking antibiotics? These meds can reset your gut’s bacterial crew. Since these tiny critters play a big part in the shade of your stool, introducing antibiotics might cause green poop sometimes.

If you’ve had certain medical treatments, it can affect digestion and cause bright green poop. One example is graft-versus-host disease, which may occur with bone marrow transplants. This tricky condition can bring about less-than-welcome guests, like diarrhea and green stool. It’s a clear signal from your body that things are out of sync.

Some uninvited microscopic guests like Salmonella bacteria, the water-loving mini parasite Giardia, and norovirus can also be a reason for your poop turning green. These critters can hustle your digestion at an unnaturally quick pace, turning your stool green as they disrupt your gut’s usual rhythm.

Babies can surprise you with a whole crayon box of poop colors, and green is definitely in the mix.

For infants, green stool might stem from the same factors as adults, like dietary changes. This includes adjustments when they start eating solids or changes in a parent’s diet if chestfeeding.

Another harmless cause could be ingesting a small amount of amniotic fluid in the womb. So, if you notice your little one sporting some spring grass-colored diapers, it’s usually no biggie.

If the green theme park in your toilet isn’t closing down, or if it’s accompanied by other symptoms like severe stomach pain, nausea, or diarrhea, it might be time to call in the pros. Persistent changes in stool color may signal underlying health issues that need medical attention.

Dark green poop can result from eating lots of leafy greens or foods with green coloring. However, it can also indicate that food travels quickly through the digestive system.

While liver issues can change stool color, they usually turn it pale or dark, not green. If you’re worried about liver health, look for pale or clay-colored stools instead.

If you haven’t been on a kale-eating spree, dark green poop might be from iron supplements or constipation remedies, which can also give poop a greenish tint.

Dark poop could be a sign of your diet or medications. However, if it’s black and tar-like, it might mean bleeding in your upper gastrointestinal tract. In that case, chatting with a healthcare professional is a must.

While green poop can def throw you through a loop, it’s usually not a sign of anything serious. It’s often your body’s way of dealing with what you eat or how fast you digest. So, unless it’s paired with other worrying symptoms, there’s probably no need to panic.

#8967. built99 positions india’s contextual intelligence on the global stage

built99 introduces an annual selection of 99 nominated studios. backed by designboom and archdaily, the initiative champions low-impact construction, regional craft, and deep contextual intelligence.

mariana rodrigues November 12, 2026 3 min

Built99 arrives to bridge Indian architecture and design with the global creative sphere, spotlighting practices defined by low-impact construction, native materials, and cultural responsiveness. Backed by designboom and ArchDaily, the initiative introduces an annual list celebrating 99 nominated studios whose work actively challenges conventional building practices. The goal is clear: ensure this regional contextual intelligence takes its rightful place in shaping the future of contemporary architecture and design.

Steering clear of pay-to-play rankings, Built99 acts as an independent cultural institution dedicated to deep architectural substance. Focusing on responsible construction and lasting cultural value, the platform keeps standards rigorous through a strictly nomination-based model, open only to studios with at least a decade of proven built work across India. Out of roughly 250 reviewed candidates, the final 99 practices earned their place through the real-world impact of their built spaces and critical thinking.

Curated by editors and design voices across DAAily platforms, designboom, and ArchDaily, including Martin Zelger, Timo Behrend, Iñaki Laguardia, and Susanna Moreira, the selection relied on five core pillars. The team examined spatial clarity, contextual intelligence, and the ethics of making, with a clear focus on local labor, native materials, and regional craft. Civic footprint and lasting relevance carried equal weight, spotlighting studios that enrich their communities with architecture built to outlast fleeting fads.

The resulting index mirrors the regional variety of Indian architecture, refusing to limit itself to primary metropolises or singular aesthetics. From dense urban hubs like Mumbai, Delhi, and Bengaluru to practices embedded across Kerala, Punjab, Tamil Nadu, Raipur, and Udaipur, the 99 studios chart a truly decentralized landscape. Here, established figures share the stage with hands-on ateliers and collaborative workshops, united by clear spatial thinking, local roots, and genuine civic commitment.

Securing physical permanence in print, the Built99 hardcover book launches this November to document the projects, research, and material methods of all 99 studios. The release pairs global coverage across designboom and ArchDaily with features across leading Indian titles like Forbes India, Fortune India, Robb Report, and GoodHomes. With the full index now live since November 10, leading up to an invitation-only gathering and forum on November 14 at New Delhi’s ITC Maurya, held alongside event partners Amici, Marmo Solutions, and Within.

#8965. what’s a primate to quantum mechanics? in conversation with daniel birnbaum and jacqui davies

at OGR torino, the quantum effect consider how quantum theory travels through cinema, popular culture and contemporary art, from kubrick to schrödinger’s cat.

annalise kamegawa November 12, 2026 9 min

At OGR Torino, The Quantum Effect, an expansive exhibition on art and quantum theory, illustrates the seemingly unknowable principles of quantum mechanics with mirrors, monkeys, and monoliths. To enter the exhibition, one must pass through a series of mirrors that create a dizzying sense of disorientation. Turn a corner, and there’s a projection of those reflective halls being played back to the viewer. It’s a visual collapsing of perception that speaks to the uncertainty of the universe.

In conversation with designboom, curators Daniel Birnbaum and Jacqui Davies discuss how they connected Mark Leckey, Yayoi Kusama, and Tomás Saraceno with Heisenberg’s Uncertainty Principle and Dirac’s Equation. On the interdisciplinary nature of the show, Davies remarks, ‘By placing artworks, experiments and equations in dialogue, the exhibition affirms the validity of each of these languages while resisting their collapse into a single explanatory framework. The show operates – to quote the title of Ryan Gander’s installation – as a ‘school of languages.’ It unfolds across sign systems.’

The curators for the show at OGR Torino consulted Professor Ulf Danielsson, professor of theoretical physics at Uppsala University and Secretary of the Nobel Committee for Physics, to highlight equations important to the field. On this collaboration, Birnbaum notes, ‘Our exhibition tries to stage the co-existence of these symbolic systems without privileging one over the other… [Danielsson] selected the equations that best capture the essence of phenomena such as entanglement, superposition, teleportation, parallel universes or the beginning of quantum computing. Most of us of course cannot read them but Ulf likes to emphasize their beauty.’

Within the exhibition, when staring up at the black monoliths – a wink to Stanley Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey – these equations appear on the screen as scenes from The Matrix, Star Trek, and footage of Schrödinger’s cat appear from towering heights. Davies, who created the monoliths in a series called Cinematic Blossomings, notes that she, ‘reassembled fragments [she remembers] from cinema, TV and pop culture to make new film-works which resemble ideas from quantum theory,’ in order to create the work.

Although they are not perfect reflections of these scientific principles, this media begins to hint at a shared understanding of the universe. ‘That is what we mean with the quantum effect,’ Davies emphasizes. ‘Even if they remain incomprehensible on an analytical level we are all familiar with some of these phenomena. In The Terminator, Star Trek,  TRON, or Wonder Woman, or David Cronenberg’s The Fly we see bodies shimmer, dematerialize and re-materialize elsewhere. We all grew up with teleportation as something almost normal, happening every day on TV. Other films employ different ideas from quantum physics in imaginative ways.’

On the inclusion of pop culture, Birnbaum acknowledges that, ‘Clearly they have sometimes been simplified or even vulgarized, but we are all familiar with visually extremely powerful imagery,’ citing Kubrick’s film as a prime example. ‘One can find versions of the Many World Interpretation of quantum physics in any number of science fiction movies and speculative works of literary fiction, from Jorge Luis Borges to Philip K Dick or the Matrix. In that way some of the bewildering paradoxes explored by physicists have entered an imaginary that we all share.’

‘Although quantum concepts have become trendy in the artworld in recent years their aesthetic reverberations can be traced throughout the twentieth century.’ Birnbaum remarks, emphasizing that not just pop culture, by the fine arts, have been a site for this exploration. ‘Long before ‘quantum’ became a catchphrase, one finds moments in which science seem to converge in surprising ways. We think Marcel Duchamp’s Large Glass, with it’s exploration of many dimensions, is an example of such convergence.’

Within the exhibition is the persistent fanning out of Duchamp’s influence, pointing to his persistent use of repetition, breaking, and glass. There’s an explicit reference with the inclusion of a photo taken by Man Ray in 1923 of Duchamp holding his work Glissière Contenant un Moulin à Eau (en métaux voisins) (Glider Containing a Water Mill [in Neighbouring Metals], 1913–15). There’s also Sturtevant’s Duchamp descendant l’escalier (1992), a black-and-white photographic interpretation of Duchamp’s painting Nude Descending a Staircase, both of which depict the repetition of a body as it, frame by frame, moves across the canvas.

More subtly, there’s Cerith Wyn Evans’s Phase-shifts )( manifest [after D.T.] (2026), a mobile of cracked windshields, with D.T. in the title standing for ‘delay in time.’ The breaking of glass continues in Mark Leckey’s 2021–22 film, To the Old World (Thank You for the Use of Your Body), in which a man launches his body through a bus stop glass wall, the shards and fragments of which splay into a dark void upon impact. ‘Many of the works explore the possibility of breaking through the glass that separate us from another reality,’ says Davies on the recurrence of the material, ‘One of our curatorial starting points was the novel Locus Solus by Raymond Roussel, an early example of what today is called quantum fiction. In that novel a scientist guides a party through extraordinary, unbelievable things are presented, always behind glass.’

Duchamp’s influence carries on into the primate-heavy works in the exhibition. There’s Rirkrit Tiravanija’s untitled or (the savage detectives) (2025), in which two man-ape figures are crouched on the ground, bearing sticks and staring at a replica of Duchamp’s Peigne, a comb with the inscription, ‘3 or 4 drops from a height have nothing to do with savagery.’ This continues into the liminal space of Ryan Gander’s office space, where School of Languages (2023) and Chronos Kairos 01.01 (2025) are being shown. In a white-walled room, an ape named Brenda cowers underneath a corner desk, only visible when you traverse to the other side of the room and peer underneath. Hanging is a digital clock with the time 88:88, which doesn’t exist on our traditional 24-hour clock.

Once again, there’s a heavy reference to perhaps what can be considered a time before man, the primates that preceded us. With the heavy referencing to Kubrick’s film, one can’t help but think again of that moment where the monolith appears, interrupting linear time with its presence. Here, the curators are calling back to the idea that maybe this straight progression of time, one where we can easily track fish to ape to man, is perhaps more complicated than we may believe.

What emerges in The Quantum Effect is less a definitive explanation of the universe than an invitation to reconsider how we understand it. Like the intricate webs of Tomás Saraceno, whose glowing structures trace paths of seemingly incomprehensible complexity, the exhibition brings together a constellation of references, ideas, and artistic gestures that resist a single point of interpretation. ‘For Tomás they are ciphers of the universe itself. He can talk for ever about string theory in front of these complex creations by spiders,’ says Brinbaum. ‘Good art is never just an illustration of theories. But sometimes one detects this strange convergence between languages.’ From quantum equations and fractured reflections to primates, monoliths, and Duchampian repetitions, the works unsettle familiar understandings of time, perception, and human progress.

Even with the most advanced mathematics and scientific theories, the universe remains fundamentally elusive. Rather than attempting to resolve these uncertainties, the exhibition embraces them, finding in the unknown a space for speculation, connection, and wonder. Ultimately, The Quantum Effect suggests that understanding the world may not be a matter of finding definitive answers, but of remaining open to the possibilities that emerge when art and science meet.

#8964. How to Calculate Your Rising and Moon Sign: A Beginner’s Guide

The sun sign is the *it girlie* of the “big three” elements in astrology.

But do you know about your moon sign and rising sign?

We chatted with an astrologer to understand what they are and how to calculate them.

According to Olga Verkhotina — astrologer and personal coach — the big three in astrology are your three most significant chart elements:

“While a natal chart contains so many more intricate details beyond just three elements, the big three is a way to determine the main highlights that make up your personality and overall temperament,” Verkhotina says.

Verkhotina explains that a rising sign is the zodiac sign that falls at the beginning of your First House — basically, the beginning of your natal chart.

“The First House in astrology is associated with a person’s identity, individual activity, even their appearance, and the sign that houses that theme gives its characteristics,” she says.

“Knowing your rising sign describes the way others may perceive you, the way your behavior comes across, as well as how you approach new situations in life.”

You’ll need: date, time and place of birth.

“Knowing the accurate time is important here because even 10 minutes can make a difference in the sign,” Verkhotina explains.

“Once you have the data, you can trust astrology software to calculate it for you. There are a lot of natal chart calculators online, so you can just search ‘rising sign calculator,'” Verkhotina says.

Pro tip: Verkhotina suggests reading horoscopes from your rising sign instead of your sun sign, saying it will likely give more personalized insights on which areas of your life might be impacted by current cosmic events.

“A moon sign describes the position of the moon on the zodiac wheel at the moment of your birth,” Verkhotina says.

She explains that the moon in astrology symbolizes:

“The moon sign helps you better understand how these themes demonstrate themselves in your life,” Verkhotina says.

Unlike the rising sign, you don’t have to have the precise time of birth to know your moon sign, although Verkhotina says it’s still recommended.

You can also use an online calculator to find your moon sign or refer to the ephemeris — a table showing the daily positions of planets.

Verkhotina describes the sun sign as the most important planet in your chart.

“It’s the center of your vitality, your ego, consciousness, and individuality at its core. That’s why it’s the most commonly known element in astrology,” she says.

It represents the zodiac sign the sun was in at the time of your birth, which Verkhotina says gives your individuality certain qualities associated with its specific sign.

“It’s important to understand that although the sun is a huge element in astrology, it doesn’t cover the nuances of one’s character,” Verkhotina explains.

Instead, she says it just represents overall traits.

Verkhotina adds that the specifics of your character are covered in the rest of your astrological chart. “This is why sometimes no two leos are the same,” she says.

This one is easy peasy — you don’t have to have your time or place of birth.

“The sun cycle is very similar every year, so you can look it up by the date, month and year of your birth. Each sign corresponds to a calendar date that year,” Verkhotina says.

Here’s each astro sign, in a nutshell, according to Verkhotina.

Your sun sign is important, but your moon and rising signs add extra details.

Your rising sign reflects your identity and how others see you, while your moon sign reveals your emotions and behavior.

To find these signs, you can use online birth chart calculators. Just make sure you have your birth date and time handy for accurate results.

Last medically reviewed on August 2, 2024

#8963. 7 Tips for Building a Healthy Diet With Canned, Frozen, and Packaged Goods

Certain influencers have built entire social media empires out of making everything from scratch. Oftentimes, their videos carry an implicit sense of moral superiority, suggesting that you’re not a good parent (or at least not as good as them) if you’re resorting to pre-packaged store-bought items. Those who pick their own produce and painstakingly hand-craft their own candy necklaces simply work harder, love their children more, are fundamentally better.

But this suggestion is hardly fair. For the vast majority of people—meaning those who don’t make their living off of wellness content or have near-endless amounts of time and money to burn—canned, frozen, and packaged stuff is almost always a far more practical option. “Groceries are a fortune,” after all, Anthea Levi, MS, RD, a Brooklyn-based health writer and the founder of Alive+Well Nutrition, tells SELF—and fresh items tend to be the most expensive, as a trip to the produce section of the supermarket will readily prove.

Besides the lower price point, canned, frozen, and packaged foods have one other major advantage: their staying power. “You can keep them in your freezer for months, so that often gives people confidence” in the purchase, since they know they don’t have an expiration date hanging over their head, Desiree Nielsen, RD, a recipe developer with a focus on plant-based nutrition, tells SELF. This, in turn, leads to reduced food waste: “Fresh salad greens are notorious for going slimy in the fridge, but you’ll never have that issue with frozen spinach. Ditto for fish. Fresh fish needs to be cooked ASAP before it turns, while frozen fish and canned or tinned fish last until you’re ready to use them,” Levi says.

Nielsen also takes issue with the basic idea that these options are somehow inherently inferior—“a big, big misconception,” in her eyes. “There has been a lot of confusion about the nature of these foods in general. Just because something is processed or packaged does not mean it’s unhealthy,” she says.

In other words, canned, frozen, or packaged items are often perfectly fine to include in your diet—and you shouldn’t feel embarrassed, ashamed, or inadequate if they make frequent appearances in your meals (or if they’re your first resort over fresh). “Constant access to fresh foods is, unfortunately, a luxury. If canned, frozen, or packaged items are the only way you’re able to put a fruit or vegetable on your plate, go for it,” Levi says. But if you’re still concerned about the health aspect, there are a few key ways to maximize the nutritional value and improve the overall experience. Here’s what to know to make the most of your freezer stash.

“Typically, the fewer ingredients, the better,” Levi says—a rule of thumb to consider while shopping. While canned, frozen, and packaged items have a reputation for being ultra-processed—rife with additives and lower in nutritional value—there are actually plenty out there “that are made from just one or two whole-food ingredients, such as canned peas, frozen fruit, and canned salmon,” Levi says. “These are as close to fresh foods as you can get, and just as nutritious.” Many jarred peanut butters only contain dry roasted peanuts and salt, for example. (By contrast, Ritz peanut butter crackers, which have an ingredients list several rows long, are a very different story.)

That said, this issue can be nuanced. “Just because an ingredient looks fancy or technical or like a chemical does not necessarily mean that it's bad for you,” Nielsen points out. Many processed foods—including bread, milk, and breakfast cereal—are fortified with healthy vitamins and minerals that you might not otherwise consume enough of in your diet. Take vitamin C—which may appear under the name “ascorbic acid”—as an example. “You might not recognize that what you’re looking at is vitamin C, so you don't want to scare yourself off of potentially nutritious and valuable food because you see things on the ingredients label that you don't recognize,” Nielsen says.

In Nielsen’s experience, canned foods are often considered even less “healthy” than frozen, but the stigma isn’t necessarily warranted. Canned beans, which boast fiber, plant-based protein, and minerals like iron and zinc, are an excellent example of a canned food that amounts to an “incredible nutrition source,” she says. Still, this category does have one major drawback: Staples like veggies, soups, and, yes, beans can contain a significant amount of sodium, a mineral that can cause high blood pressure and related issues like heart disease and stroke when overconsumed. Tinned fish like TikTok’s beloved sardines can suffer from the same issue, as the brine inside the tin can be heavy on added salt as well.

Given that many brands offer sodium-sensitive alternatives, try to prioritize those options instead to keep your sodium intake in check and avoid potential health consequences, according to Nielsen. Look for labels like “No salt added,” “Low sodium,” or even “No sodium” to steer you in the right direction. If you can’t find anything fitting that bill at your local store, draining and rinsing canned products before use can also drastically cut down on the sodium content—by up to 40%, according to some estimates. (Just keep in mind this method may also cause losses in other nutrients, like vitamin C.)

“In terms of packaged and processed foods, I'm always looking for a couple of nutrients to minimize and a couple of nutrients to optimize,” Nielsen says. Sodium is one to limit or avoid, as we’ve already covered, but there are others too—like added sugars and saturated fat. “Peaches that come canned in sugary syrup aren’t as nutritious as peaches that come canned in water, or are purchased frozen or fresh,” for example, Levi says.

On the other hand, when you’re reading over a nutrition facts label, “what you want to see is fiber,” Nielsen says—and “protein is a big bonus.” Multiple vitamins and minerals in a product is also often a positive sign. Even breakfast cereals, which are often thought of as unhealthy, “can be incredible sources of minerals like iron and zinc—things that we need that help to keep our metabolism running, that keep us energized,” Nielsen says.

Trying to decide between two (or more) similar products? Comparing and contrasting the ingredients can help you narrow it down, according to Nielsen. Take breakfast cereal: You’ll want to ask yourself, “‘Which one of these cereals gives me the most fiber, the most protein, has the least sugar?’” she says. In this case, the relative content of vitamins and minerals can also be a helpful clue. Seeing that a cereal contains 10% to 20% of your recommended dietary allowance, as many do, can be “your sort of gut check that this is actually a really nutritious food,” Nielsen says.

Even though frozen veggies are affordable and durable, they do have one big downside compared to fresh: Their taste and texture can take a hit—and, in turn, “you do have to adjust your cooking somewhat,” Nielsen says. To prevent sogginess, cook frozen veggies from frozen rather than letting them defrost first, according to Levi. And you’ll want to use heat-based cooking methods (like air-frying, baking, roasting, and stir-frying) “as opposed to water-based methods like boiling or steaming,” she says.

“Many of us are working more than ever before—maybe working two or three jobs—and we don't have a lot of time to put a home-cooked meal on the table,” Nielsen says. Strategically pairing your canned, frozen, and packaged items is an easy way to boost efficiency in the kitchen without sacrificing nutritional value. If you’re having canned soup for dinner, you can dump in a can of lentils to boost the fiber and protein, for example. (Bonus tip: You can also use this approach to stretch out your leftovers. Need a batch of spaghetti to last longer? Toss some frozen peas on top or some frozen broccoli on the side.)

“Stocking your freezer and pantry with budget-friendly canned, frozen, and packaged items can help make balanced meals a breeze,” Levi says. Follow the tried-and-true “plate method” to guarantee a nutritious result, according to Nielsen: Reserve a quarter of your plate for whole grains or starchy vegetables, another quarter for protein, and the remaining half for fruits and non-starchy veggies. You could make rolled oats with chia seeds, frozen berries, and peanut butter for breakfast, or pasta with tinned sardines and frozen broccoli for dinner, for example, Levi says. “It sounds way too simple, but it is backed by so much science to help you balance your diet without counting anything,” Nielsen says. “As long as you stick to that plate method, you will be eating a nourishing diet”—yes, even if your ingredients don’t come to you direct.

#8962. Yoga and Overweight: Health Benefits and Tips for Getting Started

Part of the beauty of yoga is its accessibility for everyone. Yoga practitioners come in all shapes and sizes and are hella modifiable. If you have overweight, there’s 100% a place for you in the world of downward dogs, crescent lunges, and resting pigeons.

Check out these benefits of yoga for overweight.

For wellness, you’d be hard-pressed to find a more holistic practice than yoga. Your physical and mental health can get a boost from busting out your mat.

The limb-stretching, muscle-engaging, bodyweight-bearing nature of yoga has many physical benefits.

For starters, yoga may enhance your metabolism. An older study found that people who practiced had greater metabolic efficiency and lower weight than non-yogis.

It’s clear, too, that yoga’s combo of cardio and strength torches calories. A 160-pound person can burn around 180 calories per hour, popping in and out of poses. A 2021 study revealed that both Hatha and vinyasa yoga led to weight loss, with an average of 3.4 kilograms (7.5 pounds) lost over a 6-month.

Extra strength and flexibility are two other well-known upsides of the practice. Research shows that even sedentary folks can build these elements of fitness by taking up yoga. One study showed that, after 8 weeks of practicing at least twice a week (180 minutes), people with no prior yoga experience had greater muscle strength, endurance, flexibility, and cardio-respiratory fitness.

On the surface, yoga might look like mere stretching — but the practice goes far beyond the physical. Yoga engages the mind in all sorts of ways that may have benefits for overweight.

By training your brain toward calm and focus, yoga sessions encourage mindfulness. A mindful outlook can have far-reaching effects in multiple areas of life, like promoting mindful eating and greater body awareness.

As a form of self-care, yoga can also promote a healthier body image. In a 2018 study, young adults who made it a habit reported higher satisfaction levels with their bodies. Better self-esteem and motivation have also been linked to the practice.

Then, too, yoga’s stress-relieving effects might follow you off the mat and into the dining room. Some research has found that people who do yoga binge eat less often.

Wanna get started with yoga but aren’t sure how? We got you.

It all starts with setting realistic goals and expectations. If you’ve never practiced before, you won’t be pretzel-ing yourself into challenging poses like scorpion or crow overnight — and that’s OK. Consider setting smaller, step-wise goals, such as attending a 30-minute class twice a week or mastering a few basic poses. Little by little, you’ll work your way up to a more advanced practice.

It’s also wise to select a class (or video) for beginners. Check your gym or yoga studio’s schedule for introductory sessions, and don’t be afraid to let an instructor know before class that you may need some modifications. Most are happy to provide adaptations to make the class a better experience for beginners.

Meanwhile, if you’re pursuing a yoga practice for weight loss, remember to pair it with other healthy lifestyle practices for best results. Though stretching and holding poses burn calories, yoga might not take you to your weight loss goal alone. A balanced diet, cardio exercise, and sufficient sleep are other keys to achieving a healthy weight.

Yoga stereotypes of scantily clad gym babes in impossible contortions might make you feel somewhat intimidated about in-person classes. If you’re concerned that a gym session will make you self-conscious, start with an at-home practice. (YouTube is a treasure trove of classes and instructors explicitly geared for people with overweight.) All by yourself in your living room, there’s no one to impress.

Or, if you’re up for in-person yoga, let your instructor know your needs again. Modifications are always possible.

No matter where you practice, credit yourself for showing up for your health. And, at the beginning of your session, don’t forget to set an intention you find motivating or encouraging, such as “I am caring for my body” or “I am worthy of love and respect.”

Overweight doesn’t have to be a barrier to taking up yoga. Start small, knowing that you’ll get more comfortable with each session. With all the physical and mental health benefits a yoga practice provides — and all the modifications that make it more accessible — it’s worth a try, regardless of weight.

Last medically reviewed on August 31, 2024

A will (technically a "last will and testament") is a legal document that specifies how your assets should be distributed after your death. It must go through probate — a court-supervised process that validates the will, pays debts and taxes, and distributes assets to beneficiaries. A living trust (specifically a revocable living trust) is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. When you die, the successor trustee distributes those assets according to the trust terms — without court involvement.

You need both: A trust does not name guardians for minor children (only a will can do that), and a trust only controls assets that have been formally transferred into it. A pour-over will acts as a safety net — it directs any assets not in the trust at your death to pour into the trust, where they are distributed according to the trust terms. The pour-over will still goes through probate, but it ensures nothing falls through the cracks.

The term "living trust" almost always refers to a revocable living trust — one you can change, amend, or dissolve at any time during your lifetime. You remain the trustee, manage the assets as you always have, and pay taxes on trust income using your personal Social Security number. For income tax purposes, a revocable trust is invisible — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist.

An irrevocable trust is fundamentally different. Once established, you cannot easily modify it, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. This permanence provides two powerful advantages:

The federal estate tax exemption is $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples) in 2026, but this historically high exemption is scheduled to sunset after 2025, potentially dropping to approximately $7 million per person. FIRE households who have built $3 million to $10 million in net worth through decades of saving and investment growth should monitor this sunset closely. If the exemption drops, irrevocable trusts become relevant at much lower wealth levels.

For most FIRE households with $1 million to $5 million in net worth, a revocable living trust provides the right balance of control, flexibility, and probate avoidance. Irrevocable structures become compelling only when estate tax exposure is real or asset protection needs are elevated.

Estate planning is governed primarily by state law, and the value of a living trust versus a will varies significantly depending on where you live.

Nine states are community property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin. In these states, most assets acquired during marriage are owned 50/50 by both spouses regardless of whose name is on the title. At death, only the deceased spouse's half passes through their estate plan.

The remaining 41 states follow common law (also called "equitable distribution"). Ownership depends on whose name is on the title. This distinction affects how assets pass at death and whether a trust or will provides better spousal protection.

Use this framework to determine whether you need a trust, a will, or both:

A revocable living trust is strongly recommended if:

Remember that a trust only controls assets titled in the trust's name. After creating a trust, you must fund it by re-titling your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust. Unfunded trusts — trusts that exist on paper but hold no assets — provide zero benefit. The pour-over will catches stragglers, but relying entirely on the pour-over defeats the purpose because those assets still go through probate.

The most common estate planning mistake with trusts is failing to fund them. Creating a trust document costs $1,500 to $5,000, but if you never transfer your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust, it provides zero probate avoidance. After signing your trust, immediately re-title assets into the trust name. Your attorney should provide a funding checklist. An unfunded trust sitting in a drawer is an expensive piece of paper — not an estate plan.

Yes. A pour-over will catches any assets not transferred into your trust during your lifetime and directs them into the trust at death. A will is also the only legal document that can name guardians for minor children. Every trust-based estate plan should include a pour-over will.

A revocable living trust prepared by an estate planning attorney typically costs $1,500 to $5,000, depending on complexity and your location. This usually includes the trust document, pour-over will, powers of attorney, healthcare directives, and initial funding guidance. Online trust services cost $200 to $500 but may not address state-specific issues or complex situations.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as both the grantor (creator) and the trustee (manager). You maintain full control over all trust assets during your lifetime. You name a successor trustee who takes over only if you become incapacitated or die.

A revocable living trust does not reduce estate taxes — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist for income and estate tax purposes. However, a trust can be structured with provisions (such as an A/B trust or disclaimer trust) that maximize the use of both spouses' estate tax exemptions. For estate tax reduction, irrevocable trusts are the primary tool.

A revocable trust can be changed, amended, or dissolved at any time. You maintain full control. An irrevocable trust generally cannot be changed after creation, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. Revocable trusts provide probate avoidance and incapacity planning. Irrevocable trusts provide estate tax reduction and asset protection.

Without a trust, each state where you own real property requires a separate probate proceeding (called ancillary probate), multiplying costs and complexity. Transferring out-of-state property into a living trust eliminates ancillary probate entirely — the successor trustee can transfer or sell the property without court involvement in any state.

#8960. Starvation Mode: How Caloric Restriction Affects Your Body

Cutting back on calories but not losing weight? You might wonder if you’ve gotten stuck in the twilight zone of so-called “starvation mode.”

Everyone from your personal trainer to your grandma may have warned you about this metabolic frenemy that keeps your body holding onto weight. But is starvation mode really a thing — or just an urban legend?

The concept of starvation mode is that when you restrict calories, your body has a “hold it right there” response. To prevent you from losing weight rapidly, your metabolism slows, conserving energy by reducing the calories it burns.

Research shows starvation mode — formally called adaptive thermogenesis or metabolic adaptation — is a legit phenomenon. It’s well documented that sometimes, the more weight you lose (and the more rapidly you do so), the more your body resists the process.

Evolutionarily speaking, this may be a holdover from when humans faced food scarcity and needed a mechanism for self-preservation. But in today’s world, starvation mode can be a frustrating roadblock to weight loss.

What does this metabolic hiccup look like? These symptoms may indicate that starvation mode is becoming a problem for your health:

Starvation mode isn’t the same thing as actual starving. In today’s modern food environment, true starvation is rare. If you’re eating regularly, you won’t experience life-threatening starvation.

However, your body might exhibit some of the same early signs as real starvation. These include the symptoms listed above.

Most commonly, though, starvation mode involves stalled weight loss. You may have hit the wall of adaptive thermogenesis when restricting calories and increasing physical activity without losing weight.

Getting into starvation mode can take just a few days, especially if those days involve severe calorie restriction.

So what counts as severe calorie restriction? Many experts advise not going below 1,200 calories per day for women and 1,500 calories per day for men unless supervised by a doctor. Anything below these numbers could land you in starvation mode faster.

Fortunately, getting your body out of starvation mode isn’t complicated.

First, there’s the obvious solution: Eat a few more calories. But we don’t mean just any calories. By adding a few more nutrient-dense foods (especially those with fiber and protein), you may find weight loss becomes easier, not harder. Both of these nutrients have links to weight loss — so they might help you get out of starvation mode without gaining weight.

If you’re feeling extremely depleted, you might take a temporary break from a weight loss diet to replenish your nutrient stores.

Choosing the proper exercise could also bump you out of starvation mode. Resistance exercises like weightlifting, yoga, push-ups, squats, and others build muscle, which increases your metabolic rate.

According to a 2014 study, people who participated in a 9-month resistance exercise program increased their resting metabolic rate — aka how many calories they burned at rest — by an average of 5%.

Weight loss is a balancing act. It’s normal to experience physical and emotional ups and downs.

That said, it’s time to see a doctor if you’re noticing symptoms like extreme fatigue or lethargy, constipation that lasts more than a few days, sensitivity to cold, or unusual mood changes. Your healthcare team can help you hit the sweet spot of weight loss without lingering in starvation mode.

Despite its name, being in starvation mode doesn’t mean you’ll starve. Instead, it’s a state in which your body has adapted to your weight loss efforts, giving you pushback on how many calories it burns. With strategies like tweaking your calorie intake and adding strength training, you can get out of this mode and back on the path to sustained weight loss.

Last medically reviewed on August 31, 2024

#8959. Text Neck Exercises: Simple Moves to Ease Digital Strain

Whether you’re caught up in doomscrolling or just checking your work emails, chances are you’re spending a lot of time on your phone. But all that screen time can lead to a pesky condition called “text neck.” Hunching over your device can leave you with some severe aches and pains.

So, hold your phone up to eye level and check out these easy tips to get rid of text neck fast!

Also known as “tech neck,” text neck is a term coined by a chiropractor to describe the neck pain you might feel after spending too much time looking down at your phone.

Most of us check our phones with our heads tilted forward and down. When you do this for too long, the muscles in your neck get strained. The muscles in the back are overstretched, while the ones in the front are compressed.

If you have text neck, here’s what you might be dealing with:

But don’t get bent out of shape about overusing your favorite device. There’s no solid proof that your phone habits are to blame for your neck woes. Several studies found no connection between using your device and having neck or shoulder pain.

You could get a sore neck from overusing your muscles for many other reasons, like genetic factors, weight issues, or bad posture. “Text neck” might be a term concocted by a chiropractor to get your business. But, hey, we’re not judging.

To help ease text neck pain, try these simple exercises.

Aside from these cubicle-friendly exercises, here are some ideas to help keep text neck from being a regular pain in the y’know:

“Text neck” is the popular term for the head and neck pain caused by hunching over your device for too long. But don’t throw away your beloved device just yet. More research is needed to link “text neck” to your tech time.

In the meantime, sit up straight and do gentle exercises like neck rolls, chin tucks, and shoulder rolls. To prevent text neck from hitting you up on the reg, take regular breaks from your phone and seek out habits that help lengthen and strengthen your body. Your neck will thank you!

#8958. Renovation delays pose "Notre Dame-like" fire risk for Houses of Parliament

Image by Pandora Pictures courtesy of Shutterstock

A government report has found that risks of a major fire at the Palace of Westminster are rising as health and safety incidents increase at the UK parliament building in London, amid continuing delays to its renovation.

Released last week by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), the report said that maintenance costs for the UNESCO-listed structure are expected to rise from £1.5 million to £2 million a week if no action is taken. According to the latest report on the restoration, the overall cost of the renovation will rise by £420 million for each year the project is delayed.

Parliament voted in 2018 to vacate the Palace for restoration, however this has been delayed by ongoing disagreements about how fully the House of Commons and House of Lords should leave during the anticipated decades-long renovation.

“Political allergy” to updating the building

According to Public Accounts Committee chair Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, current fire risks could result in “Notre Dame-like flames” at the parliament building, which in 2023 was reported by the committee to be at “constant risk of fire”.

“There has long been a political allergy to gripping the nettle that is R&R [repair and renovation],” Clifton-Brown said.

“Consider the impact of global rolling news footage of Notre Dame-like flames licking out of the building’s roof, resulting in the destruction of our heritage, or worse, injuries or loss of life,” he continued.

“These are not notional possibilities, but real and rising risks which our committee identified three years ago.”

Renovation strategy to be decided by 2030

The report outlines four strategies for the renovation of the building laid out by the R&R Client Board, with one needing to be selected by parliament by 2030 for the programme to progress.

Two of these strategies have been recommended by the board in a bid to speed up the decision-making process. These are fully leaving the building, which is estimated to cost between £11.1 billion to £15.6 billion and take 19 to 24 years, and the partially vacating the building, which is estimated at £19.5 billion to £39.2 billion and could take up to 61 years.

Approving either of these recommendations would require parliamentary approval.

“All options ahead involve extremely high figures with very big ranges,” Clifton-Brown said.

“At a time of national fiscal constraint, we would expect the parliamentary authorities to examine these figures extremely carefully to see how they can be reduced before the vote.”

The PAC’s report also found that there are areas that still need costing, including aspects like decommissioning, relocation of the building’s services, and the restoration of the medieval cloister court.

The cross-party committee has urged the clerks of both House of Commons and House of Lords to set out remaining cost estimates and provide a detailed schedule for the works.

“It is crucial that we preserve the palace as a symbol of our democracy,” the report said. “A failure to act would have serious consequences for taxpayers and future generations.”

The renovation of the adjacent Elizabeth Tower was recently completed by architecture studio Purcell, and last year was awarded a RIBA London award.

#8957. Reading the City from Above: Drone Imagery and the Material Layers of Urban Environments

Beyond their buildings, infrastructure, and streets, cities can be understood as territories shaped by materials, resources, and processes of transformation that define their physical environments. As drone technology becomes increasingly integrated into architectural documentation and urban analysis, aerial imagery offers new opportunities to examine these different layers at multiple scales. As Jane Jacobs once suggested, "Cities are the mines of the future."

Beyond their buildings, infrastructure, and streets, cities can be understood as territories shaped by materials, resources, and processes of transformation that define their physical environments. As drone technology becomes increasingly integrated into architectural documentation and urban analysis, aerial imagery offers new opportunities to examine these different layers at multiple scales. As Jane Jacobs once suggested, "Cities are the mines of the future."

From documenting building surfaces and identifying patterns in material distribution to observing how construction systems and urban landscapes evolve over time, drones can provide valuable information to architects, engineers, surveyors, urban planners, and researchers, supporting their work and informing their workflows. When combined with photogrammetry, thermal imaging, geographic information systems (GIS), and automated image processing, aerial observation is no longer limited to a single discipline or field of application. Instead, it opens up broader discussions about surface conditions, environmental performance, and material resources.

Large industrial warehouses, extensive green spaces, and residential complexes of varying scales can be distinguished from above, whether we are looking out from the top floor of a residential tower or sitting beside an airplane window. Aerial views make it possible to recognize the material dimension of cities through elements that, when observed from the ground, are often perceived in isolation. From a bird's-eye perspective, rooftops, pavements, facades, industrial surfaces, and open spaces form a kind of material mosaic, revealing patterns of construction and occupation, building periods, and even design decisions in relation to their surrounding environments.

Beyond visual identification, remote sensing and spatial data processing technologies can help locate, quantify, and assess the material resources embedded in the built environment. Nevertheless, they cannot necessarily determine a material's exact composition, structural condition, or potential for reuse without complementary information, such as technical surveys, construction records, specialized sensors, or ground-level inspections.

"Urban mining. Scoping resources for circular construction," by Areti Markopoulou and Oana Taut, introduces MatterSite, a research project developed as part of the Master in Robotics and Advanced Construction at the Institute for Advanced Architecture of Catalonia (IAAC) in Barcelona. The project explores how drone photography, robotics, and computer vision systems can be combined to identify and classify building materials and components in existing structures, particularly those approaching demolition. By investigating how certain elements could retain their construction value rather than becoming mixed with waste and losing their potential for recovery, the research proposes an approach based on the prior digitization of buildings. Through automated image processing, it aims to locate recoverable materials and components, record their positions, quantify their presence, and assess their condition to inform subsequent decisions about selective dismantling and reuse. By connecting available materials with project requirements, this survey becomes more than a documentation tool: it can also help plan a building's transformation and the management of its material resources.

When Material Surfaces and Environmental Performance Come Into Play

Connecting the material composition of cities with their environmental performance makes it possible to move beyond considering materials as isolated elements and instead examine how accumulated construction decisions influence temperature, solar absorption, water infiltration, and vegetation availability. By combining aerial imagery with thermal sensors and spatial analysis tools, researchers can investigate temperature differences across rooftops and pavements, the distribution of impermeable surfaces, the presence and continuity of green roofs, how different urban areas respond to solar radiation, and the relationships between vegetation, materials, and urban microclimates. These observations provide an architectural and territorial perspective on concepts such as urban heat islands, albedo, thermal performance, and urban permeability.

Connecting the material composition of cities with their environmental performance makes it possible to move beyond considering materials as isolated elements and instead examine how accumulated construction decisions influence temperature, solar absorption, water infiltration, and vegetation availability. By combining aerial imagery with thermal sensors and spatial analysis tools, researchers can investigate temperature differences across rooftops and pavements, the distribution of impermeable surfaces, the presence and continuity of green roofs, how different urban areas respond to solar radiation, and the relationships between vegetation, materials, and urban microclimates. These observations provide an architectural and territorial perspective on concepts such as urban heat islands, albedo, thermal performance, and urban permeability.

For example, the study "Combating the Heat Island Effect with Drone-Based Thermal Visualization," by Keenan Gibbons, proposes using high-resolution thermal imagery to examine a five-block urban corridor along Huron Street in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The research explores how different materials and exposure conditions influence surface temperatures. Using a drone equipped with thermal and RGB cameras, maps were generated to distinguish temperature variations across paved surfaces, rooftops, vegetation, and shaded areas. While vegetated surfaces and tree canopies recorded temperatures close to the ambient air temperature, sun-exposed concrete sidewalks reached approximately 11°C (20°F) above air temperature. Shaded concrete surfaces were considerably cooler than those exposed to direct sunlight, while some dark, bituminous roofing materials reached surface temperatures of approximately 82°C (180°F).

As Gibbons explains, heat is not distributed uniformly across the urban environment; rather, it is influenced by what lies beneath our feet and above our heads. The research highlights the significant impact of material properties on thermal conditions. Dark, dense surfaces, particularly asphalt and black roofing materials, absorb solar radiation and store heat, which is subsequently released back into the surrounding environment. In contrast, lighter-colored surfaces, vegetation, and tree canopies can reduce heat absorption and limit direct solar exposure, resulting in lower surface temperatures. Nature-based solutions also benefit from evapotranspiration, a process through which water evaporates from surfaces and is released by plants into the atmosphere, contributing to ambient cooling.

Ultimately, heat is not only distributed unevenly across urban space but also varies over time. Repeated drone surveys conducted before and after construction, and across different years, can help monitor how nature-based solutions and alternative material finishes perform under changing environmental conditions. By comparing thermal data over time, researchers can assess whether these interventions maintain their cooling potential and how their performance responds to seasonal variations, material aging, and changes in vegetation.

Tracking Material Transformations Over Time

When examining materials from an aerial perspective, periodic surveys also make it possible to track how built surfaces change, new materials are introduced, and existing infrastructure is transformed. Just as cities are constantly evolving, their material composition is continuously changing. These transformations can be observed in the replacement of existing buildings with new construction, the conversion of industrial areas to other uses, the addition of green roofs, rainwater harvesting systems, and solar panels across different urban environments, as well as the ongoing evolution of public spaces.

Temporal comparisons make it possible not only to observe how much a city grows, but also how its material composition changes over time. Periodic surveys allow researchers to compare different stages in the development of the same territory while also examining natural processes. Through photogrammetry, orthomosaics, point clouds, and three-dimensional models, it becomes possible to identify geometric changes, measure volumes, and document the evolution of surfaces.

The study "Dune Belt Restoration Effectiveness Assessed by UAV Topographic Surveys (Northern Adriatic Coast, Italy)," by Regine Anne Faelga, Luigi Cantelli, Sonia Silvestri, and Beatrice Maria Sole Giambastiani, uses drone-based monitoring to evaluate a dune restoration project in the protected natural area at the mouth of the Bevano River, along the northern Adriatic coast near Ravenna, Italy. Coastal dunes are important ecosystems that provide protection against flooding, support groundwater storage, help prevent saltwater intrusion, provide habitats for different species, and offer recreational opportunities. However, their dynamic nature also makes these landforms particularly vulnerable to environmental changes and human activity.

The study evaluates the impact of fences installed to support dune development by measuring sand accumulation and changes in vegetation cover over a five-year period. The researchers used a systematic data-processing workflow based on Structure-from-Motion (SfM) photogrammetry and Geomorphic Change Detection (GCD), comparing drone surveys conducted in 2016 and 2021. By analyzing elevation data from both surveys, the results showed that the fences effectively promoted dune recovery and growth. Significant sand deposition was recorded along the dune toe and front, covering a total area of 3,799 m², with a volume of 1,109 m³ and an average deposition depth of 0.29 m.

Advances in drone technology and Structure-from-Motion photogrammetry have made monitoring geomorphological changes and estimating sediment budgets increasingly practical, both in research and in real-world applications. Beyond documenting changes in the built environment, these methods demonstrate how repeated aerial surveys can help track the movement and accumulation of natural materials, offering valuable insights into the evolution and resilience of urban and coastal landscapes.

The value of drone imagery extends beyond documenting the physical appearance of cities. When combined with photogrammetry, artificial intelligence, geographic information systems (GIS), and other digital tools, aerial images can become a source of "material intelligence." By transforming aerial photographs into georeferenced maps, 3D models, and point clouds, these technologies facilitate the identification of changes in building surfaces, the estimation of material volumes, and the monitoring of resource flows across urban and natural environments. In this way, the focus shifts from simply observing the built environment to generating data that can inform material inventories, selective demolition, and circular construction strategies.

#8956. How Taking a GLP-1 Could Affect Your Bone Health

When it comes to treating obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other chronic health conditions, GLP-1 agonist drugs—such as Ozempic, Zepbound, and Wegovy—have been a game changer for literally millions of Americans.

But as with any medication, these drugs can deliver unwelcome side effects. And a recent study that just garnered a bunch of attention raised the possibility of new ones.

The research, which was presented at the 2026 American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons annual meeting in March and has not yet been peer-reviewed, found a link between GLP-1 use and increased risk of bone issues, including osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones) and osteomalacia (soft bones). The study also found a link between GLP-1 use and heightened risk of gout, a type of arthritis that causes pain and swelling in the joints.

The lead study author said he became interested in whether GLP-1s might affect bone and other connective tissue after some of his patients “developed serious tendon tears following relatively minor injuries,” according to NBC News. After analyzing five years of medical records from nearly 147,000 adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity, the study authors concluded that GLP-1 use was associated with a “significantly increased” risk of osteoporosis, osteomalacia, and gout.

Of course, this news is likely unsettling for anyone on these medications. But should we be legit worried about these findings? And how exactly could GLP-1s harm bone health in the first place? We tapped two experts for answers, along with practical tips for protecting bone health while taking GLP-1s.

First, some relieving news: As of now, there is “no sound scientific evidence” that suggests GLP-1s directly increase the risk of osteoporosis or osteomalacia, Marci Laudenslager, MD, an obesity medicine physician with The Johns Hopkins Healthful Eating, Activity & Weight Program, tells SELF. (Same goes for gout, she adds.)

Dr. Laudenslager, who was not involved in the study, points out that it was observational in nature, meaning it looked at correlation…not causation. “While well-conducted observational studies can reveal a potential relationship between a medication and a clinical outcome, they cannot determine whether a medication directly causes that clinical outcome,” she explains.

Another limitation of the study is that it relied on medical records alone, which means it assumed that all patients who were prescribed GLP-1s, as noted in their medical records, were actually taking the drug. In reality, many patients who are prescribed GLP-1s are unable to take them because of cost or medication shortages, Dr. Laudenslager says. Moreover, people who do start taking don’t always continue due to insurance, cost, or problems tolerating the drug, she adds.

Beyond that, the study didn’t take into account factors that commonly impact bone health, like exercise habits, nutritional habits, and other lifestyle factors, Kelyssa Hall, an exercise physiologist and certified strength and conditioning specialist at Hospital for Special Surgery, tells SELF. “These factors can play a huge role in bone health with or without the addition of GLP-1s.” The study also didn’t account for certain endocrine conditions, cancers, alcohol use, family history, and steroid use–all of which can also play a role in bone health, Dr. Laudenslager adds. And the study didn’t note which specific GLP-1 drug people used and the dosage, she adds.

Lastly, the study findings have not yet been peer reviewed–a step that Dr. Laudenslager describes it as “essential” in the scientific process. As Hall puts it: The study “highlights the need for more research on these topics.”

Okay, so that particular study has its limitations. But other research supports the notion that these drugs may be linked with declining bone health. So…is there actual cause for concern?

According to Dr. Laudenslager and Hall, taking GLP1-s can indeed decrease bone density for some people. But that’s likely due to the volume and rate at which people lose weight while on these drugs—and not anything specific to the medication itself, Dr. Laudenslager says.

“When you take GLP-1s, there can be rapid weight loss which means there is less load being carried around on the skeleton,” Hall says. “Bone formation or strengthening is improved with load to the skeletal system,” she explains, “so losing weight decreases the regular load on the bones overall.”

Over time, this decrease in loading can translate to a decrease in bone density, Dr. Laudenslager says. But, again, this isn’t unique to GLP-1s: “Significant weight loss through any mechanism—lifestyle change, medications, or surgery—can impact metabolism as a whole and bone metabolism, in particular,” she says. Basically, whenever you lose a bunch of weight—regardless of how you lost those pounds—there’s always a risk of bone loss.

In short, while it’s true that some people taking GLP-1s have had changes to their bone health, these changes seem to “be driven primarily by magnitude of weight loss rather than a direct, negative consequence of the medications themselves,” Dr. Laudenslager says. That said, the use of GLP-1s and bone health “is an active area of study,” she adds. More research is needed to fully understand the impact of GLP-1s on bone density.

Resistance training is important for pretty much everyone—and that includes folks on GLP-1s. One of its many benefits is that it’s been shown to improve bone density, Hall says. That means it can be a helpful strategy to bolster bone health when you’re on a GLP-1. Plus, strength training can help guard against muscle loss that can happen when you’re losing weight. “Retaining muscle mass is important for strength and stability,” she says. And it can also help support your overall metabolism, she adds, which can help your body sustain weight loss results for the long haul.

If you’re new to strength training, Dr. Laudenslager recommends gradually building up to a routine of two to three sessions a week, with at least a day off in between each workout to allow your muscles the time they need to recover. Before getting started though, make sure to check with your doctor or other medical provider so they can advise what type of workouts are safe and recommended for you.

A common side effect of GLP-1s is appetite suppression, which can sometimes lead people to follow a really low calorie diet. Calorie restriction can suppress bone growth and increase the risk of fractures, according to research, which is one of the reasons you want to make sure you’re still eating enough to support your overall health while on a GLP-1. “Hunger is an essential hormonal cue we all need in order to sustain health,” Dr. Laudenslager says. The ideal amount of calories is highly individualized, but if you’re unsure that you’re getting what you need, bring it up with your doctor or another qualified expert, such as a registered dietitian.

Protein is often touted for its muscle-building benefits, but it’s also vital for bone health, as it helps to build bone mass. The recommended dietary allowance for adults is 0.8 grams of protein per kilograms of bodyweight a day—a general guideline that Dr. Laudenslager also suggests for people taking GLP-1s. She suggests a slightly higher intake for people at greater risk of bone health issues (such as older adults and postmenopausal women) and lesser amounts in people with kidney disease. Just make sure that as you prioritize protein, you don’t skimp on important components of a well-rounded diet, including fiber, water, healthy fats, and essential vitamins, minerals, and nutrients, she adds.

Rapid weight loss can be harmful for bone health, so to mitigate this risk, strive for a more gradual reduction in pounds. The recommended rate of weight loss depends on your starting weight, but as a general guideline, Dr. Laudenslager recommends losing 5% to 10% of your total weight over the course of about six months. This translates to an average of about 0.5 to 2 pounds lost a week. So if you notice that taking a GLP-1 is causing you to lose weight at a faster pace, bring it up with your doctor. They may want to adjust your medication dosing to help slow your weight loss rate into a more ideal, gradual range.

Bone loss isn’t an overnight thing. In fact, clinically significant bone loss typically happens over the course of years, Dr. Laudenslager says. “This means there are a wealth of opportunities throughout a person’s weight loss journey to prevent and treat bone loss early on if it’s detected through surveillance.” So if you have any bone health concerns, mention them to your doctor (though hopefully your provider is proactively thinking about this too).

On that note, Dr. Laudenslager strongly encourages people interested in obesity treatment to seek care from a board-certified obesity medicine physician. She recommends the American Board of Obesity Medicine and the Obesity Action Coalition websites as resources for finding a board-certified provider.

GLP-1s can be a true game-changer for people struggling with chronic health conditions. Unfortunately, there’s still a lot of societal stigma and misunderstanding surrounding obesity, including the misconception that “anti-obesity medications are dangerous and should be avoided,” Dr. Laudenslager says. In truth, though? “The medication side effects are quite manageable when prescribed by providers who are well-versed in current practice guidelines,” she says.
